title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
summary: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.
full_text: One sample, the whole team's future. generates every robot's future camera views and action chunk together; training it to predict the whole team's future teaches each robot to coordinate with its teammates. Left: two real robots, each with three private cameras and no shared global camera; in laundry-bag collection both lift the bag to hold it open while Agent~2 loads the garment. Right: two to four simulated arms; in Camera Alignment each agent's private view is predicted six control steps ahead within a 24-step joint sample, whose first eight steps are executed before replanning (a read-only shared global camera provides context). fig:teaser Introduction sec:introduction Robots will increasingly work in teams to tackle complex tasks in the physical world. In homes and factories, robots may need to hand objects to one another, jointly manipulate deformable materials, or carry loads together. In these tasks, each robot observes the scene from its own viewpoint, but its actions change the shared environment and shape what its teammates can do next. A grasp may alter the shape of an object held by another robot, while a handover may enable a teammate to begin its next operation mandi2024roco,qin2025robofactory . Successful collaboration therefore requires robots to coordinate their actions and timing to achieve a shared goal. Viewed this way, collaborative manipulation is a process in which robots jointly shape the future of their shared physical world. This motivates us to formulate it as a multi-agent world-modeling problem: jointly predicting the team's shared future and the action sequences that produce it. Existing approaches to multi-robot collaboration largely fall into three categories. (1) Decentralized policy coordination retains a separate execution policy for each robot while learning coordination mechanisms. Although readily scalable, these policies may lead to idle waiting or oscillatory behavior in tightly coupled tasks because of mismatched coordination patterns or desynchronized execution pmlr-v305-he25a,dong2026mimic,park2026distilling . (2) Joint trajectory and action generation methods model multi-agent trajectories or generate coordinated controls but lack explicit predictions of their visual consequences NEURIPS2025_0895de15,zhu2024madiff . (3) Language- and logic-guided task coordination uses planning, dialogue, or temporal logic to organize collaboration, but does not explicitly predict the visual consequences of joint actions chen2024scalable,kannan2024smart,mandi2024roco,meng2026ltldiff,zhang2026ma . These methods either decentralize decision-making, lack physical foresight, or rely on task-level guidance; none jointly generates executable team actions and their corresponding visual futures. World models offer a natural path toward addressing this lack of physical foresight, yet existing research still separates multi-agent future prediction from executable joint control. Multi-agent world models can reconstruct shared states or disentangle per-agent dynamics for planning zhang2025combo,zhao2026empowering , and in video generation they can produce multi-view-consistent futures savva2026solaris,zhu2026shareverse,wu2026multiworld,liu2026gamma . However, these video models treat actions only as conditioning inputs and do not produce policies that can be directly deployed in the physical world savva2026solaris,wu2026multiworld,liu2026gamma . In robotics, recent world-action models jointly learn visual prediction and action generation, demonstrating that future-prediction representations can improve control by capturing the dependencies between actions and anticipated scene evolution guo2024prediction,li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel,NEURIPS2025_89a3b655,ye2026world . However, these models are still organized around a single robot's control stream. Multi-agent video generation models thus predict without producing executable joint control, whereas multi-robot policies act without jointly modeling the visual consequences that each agent will encounter. This leads to a central question: how can a unified generative model jointly predict a robot team's future observations and generate coordinated actions for manipulation in a shared physical world? We introduce , a multi-agent world-action model that learns coordinated control by jointly modeling each robot's actions and the team's future camera views. A shared Transformer connects all agents' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention and jointly denoises them. Each generated sample pairs executable action chunks with synchronized future views, predicting both how the team will act and how the scene will evolve (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Joint prediction needs to preserve which observations and controls belong to each robot while distinguishing its identity from its task responsibility. uses an explicit view--agent map to associate multiple private camera streams with their owner, together with per-agent state and action tokens that retain each robot's control interface. Regular-simplex rotary identities assign the same identity code to all views of a robot, an action-to-video bias ties its action tokens to those views, and separate task-role embeddings specify its responsibility. This allows multiple robots to share a task role without merging their observations or controls: for example, two camera holders can share a role while retaining separate states and action outputs. To adapt GR00T~2~ nvidia2026gr00t2 , a single-robot world-action model, to team control, we use two training stages. During warm-up, the model learns from one robot's views, state, and actions at a time, adapting to the cameras and controllers. Team training then enables cross-agent attention and role conditioning, using synchronized demonstrations to jointly supervise the robots' actions and future views. Randomized identity assignments and complete-agent-group shuffling expose each role to varied identity codes and sequence positions while preserving each robot's observation--action correspondence. At deployment, joint denoising produces the team's future views and action chunks. The robots execute their actions in synchrony, then use updated observations to condition the next joint prediction. We evaluate on three real-robot tasks: laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover. Using three private cameras per robot and no shared global camera, achieves 67.8 mean success, outperforming MA-VLA by 18.9 percentage points under the same demonstration and camera setup. We further evaluate on eight tasks with two to four arms, including camera alignment, collaborative photography, and multi-stage delivery, achieving 90.3 average success. Ablations show that removing cross-agent attention reduces four-arm relay success from 95.0 to 39.0 , while removing future-video supervision in team training lowers Place Food success from 78.0 to 47.0 . Additional ablations demonstrate the benefits of task-role conditioning, randomized agent identities, and single-robot warm-up for coordinated manipulation. Our main contributions are: We propose , a multi-agent world-action model that jointly denoises all agents' future-view and action tokens through cross-agent attention. Joint video-action flow matching enables a single sample to contain synchronized visual futures and executable actions for the entire team. We design an agent-attributed representation that explicitly associates each robot's private views, state, and actions, combining regular-simplex agent identities with separate task-role embeddings. This preserves each robot's observation and control interfaces while allowing multiple robots to share a task responsibility. We further develop a two-stage training scheme: single-robot warm-up adapts the pretrained world-action backbone to the target cameras and controllers, and synchronized team training learns cross-robot interactions with randomized identity assignments and agent-group shuffling. We demonstrate coordinated manipulation on three real-robot tasks and eight simulation tasks with two to four arms. improves mean success over MA-VLA by 18.9 percentage points on real robots and exceeds its published simulation average by 6.9 percentage points. Ablations examine the representation, future supervision, cross-agent interaction, and training recipe. Related Work sec:related Coordinating robot actions. These approaches coordinate robot actions or task plans, but do not jointly generate executable team actions and their corresponding visual futures. unifies the two in a single joint sample, coupling all agents' action chunks with synchronized future views to model the visual consequences of the team's actions. Predicting multi-agent worlds. Shared-world prediction provides a complementary perspective on collaboration. COMBO reconstructs shared state from egocentric observations for compositional planning, and SeqWM models multi-robot dynamics sequentially with intention sharing zhang2025combo,zhao2026empowering . Solaris, ShareVerse, MultiWorld, Gamma-World, and population-scalable video models develop consistent multi-agent views and scalable video generation savva2026solaris,zhu2026shareverse,wu2026multiworld,liu2026gamma,zhao2026population . Action-conditioned video models predict how supplied robot or player controls change the scene. For coordinated manipulation, the policy must also generate the controls that participate in that change. learns a joint distribution over the team's visual futures and low-level actions. Learning actions with visual futures. Joint visual and action prediction connects generative world models to robot control. DreamZero learns aligned visual futures and robot actions; Motus unifies world modeling, policy learning, inverse dynamics, and joint video-action prediction, while Motubrain develops multiview and cross-embodiment modeling ye2026world,bi2026motus,team2026motubrain . Recent work also clarifies how a policy can use future information. Fast-WAM and SelfWAM retain future supervision with action-only deployment paths, and RIFT constructs a future key/value interface in one backbone pass yuan2026fast,pan2026selfwam,zhang2026keep . These designs connect a robot's actions to anticipated scene evolution. In a team, that evolution also depends on what the other robots do. extends joint world-action modeling to these cross-robot dependencies: all agents' action chunks and private-view futures interact within one generative process. Each robot's predicted behavior is thereby modeled alongside the future that the team jointly creates. sec:method predicts each robot's actions together with the future the whole team will see. It extends a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone to generate the whole team's future views and action chunks in one sample (Figure~ fig:method ). Cross-agent attention couples the robots' predictions; simplex identities attach every view to its robot, and an action-to-video bias and role embeddings attach its actions and task role. title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems
summary: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
full_text: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems Ivan A. Fernandez Jingdao Chen Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems. Introduction Motivation Agentic systems increasingly combine perception, state estimation, reasoning, and autonomous action to interact with dynamic environments pati2025agentic,sapkota2025agentic . In cyber-physical applications, degraded or manipulated sensor observations can therefore influence downstream autonomous decisions. This concern is particularly relevant to Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) architectures, where detection, tracking, classification, and sensor fusion may support subsequent decision and response functions. Recent U.S. defense requirements similarly emphasize robust C-UAS sensing, tracking, multi-target handling, and operation under challenging conditions usarmy2026mobilecsuas,usaf2026csuas . The operational relevance of drone and counter-drone technologies has also increased substantially in recent conflicts mittal2025drone . Real-world datasets remain essential for evaluating C-UAS sensing and tracking; however, they provide limited control over the occurrence, severity, and repeatability of individual stress conditions. Standardized C-UAS evaluation efforts have likewise emphasized scenario-based testing, repeatability, and quantitative performance metrics decubber2025standardized . Multi-modal datasets such as MMAUD provide synchronized camera, LiDAR, radar, and other sensing data for anti-UAV research yuan2024mmaud , while synthetic datasets such as SynDroneVision demonstrate the value of simulation for increasing scenario diversity and supplementing real-world data lenhard2025syndronevision . This work develops a lightweight synthetic C-UAS testbed for security stress testing of perception and tracking components that may feed agentic decision pipelines. The objective is not to reproduce high-fidelity aerodynamics or fully calibrated sensor physics. Instead, the testbed emphasizes repeatable target motion, known ground truth, configurable scene conditions, and controlled sensing degradation so that downstream algorithm behavior can be observed under systematically varied conditions. Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed Figure~ fig:framework_analysis summarizes the synthetic testbed. Scenario parameters specify target trajectory, range, sensor configuration, and environmental conditions. A simplified quadrotor-shaped Universal Scene Description (USD) target is propagated using prescribed kinematic trajectories, while Isaac Sim generates synchronized multi-modal observations together with known target state and sensor geometry. The target follows repeatable trajectories including straight flight, hover, climb or descent, acceleration, and turning motion. Because target state is known directly from the simulation, generated observations can be paired with ground truth for quantitative evaluation. The RGB camera provides rendered imagery, while RTX LiDAR produces three-dimensional returns from target and scene geometry. An illustrative IR-like channel provides a third modality for preliminary multi-modal experiments; it is intended as a thermal-like synthetic representation rather than a physics-based long-wave infrared model. Target range, viewing geometry, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability can therefore be varied while preserving a common underlying trajectory. From a security perspective, these controls provide a basis for repeatable observation-level perturbations that may affect downstream autonomous behavior. Candidate stress cases include sensor dropout, reduced update rate, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, false or ghost observations, and ambiguous multi-target encounters. Such conditions can support studies of when uncertainty or inconsistency should trigger monitoring, fallback behavior, or human oversight. Synthetic Data Exemplars Three representative sensing configurations demonstrate the current testbed: a near-range target in a relatively clear scene, an increased-range target, and a target observed in clutter with partial occlusion. Figure~ fig:exemplars shows paired RGB and RTX LiDAR observations generated from the same underlying scene state. These scenarios demonstrate controlled multi-modal data generation rather than sensor-model fidelity. Future experiments will introduce security-relevant sensing perturbations while retaining the same ground-truth trajectory and evaluation structure. Nonlinear EKF Tracking Exemplar LiDAR-based UAV detection and tracking has previously been explored using spatiotemporal point-cloud processing and filtering approaches liang2024cluster,khosravi2026lidar . Here, the EKF is used only as an exemplar for demonstrating how the proposed testbed can expose a tracker to controlled measurement degradation. A nonlinear coordinated-turn EKF is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. The filter state is where , , and denote target position, is horizontal speed, is heading, is vertical velocity, and is turn rate. The LiDAR measurement is represented as where is the target position and is the LiDAR centroid measurement error. The visible-surface centroid is therefore treated as an imperfect target position measurement. Figure~ fig:framework_analysis demonstrates quantitative tracking evaluation. Uncertainty remains bounded during regular LiDAR updates and increases as target returns become sparse and measurements are lost, illustrating how sensing degradation propagates into estimator state and uncertainty. Conclusion Future Work This work presents an NVIDIA Isaac Sim testbed for controlled generation of synthetic C-UAS observations and repeatable security stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms. Scripted quadrotor motion and synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like sensing support multi-modal evaluation. A nonlinear coordinated-turn EKF demonstrates quantitative assessment of tracking error and uncertainty under degraded sensing. Future work will introduce sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, false observations, occlusion, environmental degradation, and multi-target interactions. These scenarios will support studies of how perception and tracking failures affect downstream agentic behavior and inform monitoring, resilience, fallback, and human oversight.

title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,gr00t couple pretrained vision-language backbones with action heads learned from demonstrations, whose scale and quality strongly determine performance. Collecting such demonstrations through teleoperation is particularly difficult for high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) humanoids. Whole-body controllers (WBCs)~ sonic,twist2 coordinate balance, locomotion, and bimanual control but do not remove this data bottleneck. Real-to-sim-to-real (R2S2R) systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ legs,vlk,3dgs instead reconstruct deployment scenes and generate whole-body trajectories without teleoperation. Policies trained on these synthetic demonstrations can transfer to hardware, but residual appearance and dynamics gaps still require learning from deployment experience. Reinforcement learning can improve a behavior-cloned (BC) policy under compounding errors and residual sim-to-real mismatch, but VLA post-training requires long-horizon rewards and optimization through diffusion or flow action heads. Offline-to-online methods often update simple MLP policies~ hu2023imitation,yang2024robot,huang2024mentor , limiting expressiveness through their tractable action densities. Advantage-weighted methods support richer policies~ wu2025robocopilot,intelligence2025pi,peng2019advantage, chen2025conrft , but often require human DAgger interventions. RL-100~ lei2025rl differentiates the PPO objective~ schulman2017proximal through the full denoising process at high computational cost. Steering~ wagenmaker2025steering , residual methods~ xiao2025self,ankile2025residual , and DICE-RL~ sun2026prior adapt pretrained policy outputs more directly. Nevertheless, these approaches rely on continued real robot interaction or fixed offline data, neither of which supports exploratory whole-body humanoid learning. Learned world models (WMs) shift policy optimization away from hardware by predicting future observations under candidate actions. Existing systems use either compact dynamics representations or generative video models. Latent dynamics models and explicit 3D digital twins~ dreamer,wu2022daydreamer,drema,diwa enable sample-efficient learning, but are usually scene-specific and do not provide the open-world visual inputs required by VLAs. Generative video WMs instead adapt large pretrained models to robot actions. VLAW~ vlaw treats successful WM rollouts as behavior-cloning targets, while WMPO~ wmpo and related methods optimize policies on generated trajectories~ world4rl,rise,worldgymnast,worldvlaloop . WoVR~ wovr , WorldSample~ worldsample , and PlayWorld~ playworld improve rollout initialization, transition selection, and autonomous data collection, respectively. However, these methods remain limited to fixed-base tabletop manipulation and use human teleoperation data during training. These limitations raise a central question: how should scalable synthetic data and limited autonomous policy rollouts be combined for whole-body humanoid VLA post-training without teleoperation? uses simulation to train the initial VLA and broaden the WM's dynamics coverage. Autonomous real robot rollouts then close the remaining visual sim-to-real gap in its predictions, after which the video WM serves as the policy-improvement environment. This forms the flywheel shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Our contributions are: 0.2 0pt 0pt We build , to our knowledge the first WM-RL system for whole-body humanoid VLAs beyond fixed-base tabletop manipulation, coupling egocentric video generation with whole-body dynamics and dense progress rewards. We develop autonomous whole-body play data for WM mid-training: manipulation play improves contact-dynamics prediction, while locomotion play improves consistency under large egocentric viewpoint changes. We study how photorealistic simulation and a video WM can form a teleoperation-free policy-improvement flywheel. Experiments on three loco-manipulation tasks show that simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM provides a more useful environment for policy improvement. Background The LEGS Simulator sec:legs The LEGS simulator~ legs is an R2S2R data engine for the Unitree G1. It combines a 3DGS reconstruction of the static scene with interactable object meshes recovered using SAM 3D~ sam3d . MuJoCo~ mujoco models robot--object contacts, while the 3DGS scene provides background rendering. SONIC~ sonic tracks scripted locomotion and manipulation primitives, producing teleoperation-free trajectories with state, contact, and action data for base-VLA training and WM adaptation. Dense Progress Reward Models sec:reward SARM~ sarm estimates progress hierarchically: it first predicts the current semantic stage, then conditions a second estimator on that stage to predict continuous within-stage completion. Dataset-level stage-duration priors combine both outputs into normalized task progress. SARM2~ sarm2 generalizes this hierarchy across tasks with a mixture-of-experts stage estimator. Its rollout adaptation uses segment-level labels of fast progress, slow progress, adjust, or mistake, together with final task progress. DreamDojo: A Whole-Body-Control World Model sec:dreamdojo DreamDojo~ dreamdojo is an action-conditioned video WM built on Cosmos~ cosmos . Given a single seed frame and a sequence of achieved 43-DoF joint states, it predicts future frames in fixed-length chunks, . Its post-training on real Unitree G1 WBC trajectories provides a whole-body prior, while autoregressive error accumulation~ diffusionforcing,selfforcing,weaver motivates broad play data and bounded rollout horizons. Reinforcement Learning for Flow-Matching Policies sec:rl A flow-matching action head generates an action chunk by integrating a learned velocity field, but its implicit likelihood complicates standard policy gradients. We consider three alternatives. DICE-RL~ sun2026prior searches modes of a frozen flow prior and learns a local residual correction: where candidate action chunks are evaluated by an -member critic ensemble, and is selected. AWR~ peng2019advantage performs advantage-weighted supervised regression: where is the estimated advantage and is a temperature. ReinFlow~ reinflow converts the deterministic flow ODE into an SDE with learned noise; each discretized step is Gaussian: This gives tractable per-step log-likelihoods for on-policy optimization such as PPO~ schulman2017proximal . title: RefreshGrad: An Online Adaptive Data-sampling Method for Diffusion-based Visuomotor Learning
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.
full_text: [] #1 Unequal and dynamic window value to the policy motivates online re-scoring and reweighting. (a) Windows sliced from demonstration episodes have unequal value to the current policy at the same training step; each window's value changes over training (illustrative). (b) periodically re-scores windows with the current policy using policy-native signals, applies rank-based sampling with uniform coverage, and updates the policy under the same training objective. Introduction Adapting visuomotor and vision--language--action (VLA) policies to downstream manipulation tasks relies heavily on demonstration supervision brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,chi2023diffusion . However, a fundamental yet under-appreciated property of demonstration datasets is the severe disparity in data value across temporal windows. Across episodes, demonstrations inevitably mix clean executions with visual corruptions---such as dim lighting, sensor blur, and background texture shifts---as well as demonstrator inconsistency. Even within a single successful episode, temporal segments vary sharply in supervision utility: repetitive free-space reaching motions offer diminishing returns once mastered, fine contact and articulation transitions demand concentrated optimization, and hesitant or occluded intervals can induce conflicting parameter updates. Treating all segments equally under uniform sampling wastes optimization budget on redundant motions while allowing corrupted or inconsistent windows to degrade policy learning. Our analysis shows that training value is both window-dependent and policy-dependent: windows within the same episode contribute unequally ( (a)), and per-window signals that are stable between adjacent refreshes decorrelate steadily as training proceeds, under both RefreshGrad and uniform sampling ( ). A fixed assessment of data quality therefore cannot fully capture a window's current learning value. A clean but already-mastered window may offer limited additional supervision, whereas an imperfect window may still contain learnable transitions. This observation motivates adapting exposure to the evolving learner, beyond static offline selection sirigiri2026faktual,dass2025datamil . Since high loss can also reflect corruption or inconsistent actions, this adaptation requires feedback about both learning progress and prediction consistency. Motivated by this insight, we propose , an online adaptive data-sampling framework that repeatedly estimates window utility from the current policy and reallocates training exposure accordingly ( (b)). Following a uniform warmup, scores windows using learning progress, cross-episode gradient agreement, temporal prediction consistency, residual disagreement, and photometric sensitivity under deterministic diffusion probes. These complementary signals distinguish actively learnable windows from redundant or unreliable supervision. Robust normalization and temporal smoothing yield comparable, stable utilities, which a rank-based sampler combines with a uniform coverage floor to update anchor sampling probabilities. Alternating scoring with policy updates allows exposure to track changing window value while preserving nonzero support for every valid segment. The procedure requires no external scorer or rollouts and leaves the policy architecture, per-sample loss, and inference pipeline unchanged. We instantiate on an action-chunking Diffusion Policy backbone chi2023diffusion and evaluate it across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks. As summarized in (c), improves perturbed success over Uniform on all ten tasks, raising the average from 60.7 to 76.1 . It also exceeds the 68.2 achieved by FAKTUAL sirigiri2026faktual and improves clean success from 57.4 to 81.3 , supporting the effectiveness of online adaptive window allocation. Our contributions are threefold: Characterization of demonstration data value. We reveal that temporal-window value is non-uniform and evolves with the learner, and identify its principal sources as learning progress, cross-episode gradient agreement, temporal prediction consistency, residual disagreement, and photometric sensitivity. This provides a policy-native account of why different windows contribute unequally. Data-value-driven online window allocation. We introduce to periodically estimate these value cues from the current policy and adapt training exposure through rank-based sampling with a uniform coverage floor, without environment rollouts or inference overhead. Empirical and mechanistic validation. We evaluate across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks and show gains in both perturbed and clean success. Training-trace diagnostics, sampler controls, and signal ablations support multi-cue valuation and periodic online adaptation. Related Work Visuomotor and vision--language--action policies. Modern robot manipulation policies map visual observations---often paired with language instructions or multimodal prompts---directly to control actions brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,jiang2023vima . At the action-generation level, action-chunking transformers and diffusion policies model temporally extended control sequences zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion , building on denoising and score-based generative modeling ho2020ddpm,song2019score,song2021ddim,nichol2021improved as well as diffusion formulations for planning and offline reinforcement learning janner2022diffuser,wang2023diffusionql . Standardized manipulation benchmarks further emphasize long-horizon temporal structure, task diversity, and robustness to environmental variations liu2023libero,mees2022calvin,james2020rlbench . While these advances establish expressive policy architectures and evaluation protocols, they typically rely on uniform sampling over collected demonstrations during training. addresses the complementary problem of dynamically allocating training exposure across demonstration windows as optimization progresses, and is instantiated here on an action-chunking Diffusion Policy backbone chi2023diffusion to isolate sampling effects from language-grounding confounds. Data selection and valuation for imitation learning. Offline imitation learning studies consistently show that demonstration quality, diversity, and composition critically govern downstream policy performance mandlekar2021robomimic . In general machine learning, active learning and coreset selection allocate supervision toward informative or representative subsets cohn1994active,sener2018active , while gradient approximation, gradient matching, validation-guided selection, and influence functions estimate sample utility from model gradients mirzasoleiman2020craig,killamsetty2021gradmatch,killamsetty2021glister,koh2017influence . Extending data curation to robot manipulation, DataMIL leverages datamodel attribution and surrogate losses to select task-relevant demonstrations offline dass2025datamil , whereas FAKTUAL introduces a fast, model-free trajectory-kernel entropy metric to curate diverse demonstration subsets without policy access or rollouts sirigiri2026faktual . Despite their effectiveness, offline curation and static reweighting schemes fix data importance prior to or early in training: model-free diversity curation does not account for within-trajectory quality disparities or visual corruptions, and static selection cannot adapt as the policy masters simple motions and shifts its learning bottleneck (window-utility rank correlation falls from 0.80 between adjacent refreshes to 0.10 between the first and last refresh). Moreover, trajectory-level hard filtering permanently discards excluded episodes that may still contain valuable contact transitions. In contrast, operates at the fine-grained temporal-window level, periodically recomputing priorities online from the evolving policy while preserving nonzero support across all demonstrations. Online adaptive sampling and robustness cues. Dynamically adjusting sample priorities during training has a long history, notably in prioritized experience replay (PER), which weights reinforcement learning transitions by temporal-difference error schaul2016prioritized . However, in supervised demonstration learning under uneven data quality, prioritizing samples solely by loss magnitude is brittle: our training-trace analysis shows that high window loss correlates negatively with cross-episode gradient consensus and temporal action consistency, reflecting demonstrator noise or visual corruptions rather than learnable skill deficiencies. While overlapping action-chunk averaging has been used at inference time to smooth execution zhao2023act , and visual robustness research applies domain randomization or augmentations during training tobin2017domain,hendrycks2020augmix,hendrycks2019corruptions , prior work has not unified these properties into an online data-valuation mechanism. Rather than altering training images or adding auxiliary losses, is the first to formalize cross-episode gradient agreement, shift-aligned temporal consistency, inter-noise residual disagreement, and read-only photometric sensitivity under deterministic diffusion probes as online window-utility dimensions, separating genuinely learnable transitions from noisy or redundant segments while preserving the native training objective and inference pipeline. Observations on Window-Level Data Value sec:observations Building on the window-value disparity in (a), we first analyze theoretically what makes a demonstration window valuable. In diffusion-based imitation learning, raw training loss only reflects instantaneous fitting error, which conflates actively learnable transitions with unlearnable noise. From an optimization perspective, we hypothesize that a window's true training value is governed by five complementary factors spanning three requirements---active error reduction, spatiotemporal supervisory coherence, and prediction stability under input perturbations: (1) Learning progress. A static loss cannot separate a window where the policy is actively improving from a mastered reaching segment or a persistently noisy transition; only loss reduction across checkpoints indicates where supervision is actively being absorbed. (2) Cross-episode gradient agreement. Even when loss decreases locally, an isolated demonstration window can mislead the policy if the demonstrator hesitated or took an idiosyncratic path. Since a parameter step changes the loss of another visually similar window to first order by , positive gradient alignment across episodes is theoretically required for updates to generalize rather than conflict. (3) Temporal prediction consistency. Action-chunking policies predict overlapping future action sequences at adjacent frames; coherent supervision requires adjacent predictions to agree on their shared future horizon rather than inducing jerky control transitions. title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery. Introduction Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into effective actions across a wide range of robotic manipulation and embodied control tasks~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,li2026safetyembodiedaisurvey,chen2026hazardarenaevaluatingsemanticsafety . In dynamic environments, agents must reason over long spatiotemporal horizons and adapt their actions as conditions change. Most VLA models rely on large-scale offline pretraining~ intelligence2025pi,liu2023libero,o2024open,khazatsky2024droid,lin2026evodepthlightweightdepthenhancedvisionlanguageaction . They perform well on in-distribution tasks but struggle in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, where they encounter tasks and environmental variations that pretraining data rarely cover~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi,wang2026libero . Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a way for VLA models to respond to distribution shifts during deployment~ sun2020test,bai2025evolve,park2026test,liu2026fly . As a robot acts, incoming visual observations and the resulting environmental feedback provide supervision without expert action labels~ ji2026vane . These signals can help the model adapt its perceptual representations and action decisions while retaining knowledge acquired during pretraining. On-device fine-tuning with first-order (FO) optimization remains difficult because the memory and compute demands of backpropagation (BP) can exceed the resources available on robotic platforms, particularly those that use low-bit quantized weights for inference~ dettmers2023qlora,malladi2023fine . Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization reduces the memory cost of TTA by estimating gradients from forward evaluations under perturbations~ berahas2021theoreticalempiricalcomparisongradient,wang2026fozo,zhang2026curvature,zhang2026zotta . MeZO uses this approach to fine-tune large language models with near-inference memory usage and achieves performance comparable to first-order fine-tuning on several downstream tasks~ malladi2023fine . Dust, a state-of-the-art ZO optimizer, uses activation-space perturbations and parallel evaluations to match or exceed the performance of backpropagation at large perturbation population sizes~ dahal2026backprop . In our preliminary VLA-TTA experiment (Figure~ fig:placeholder ), Dust quickly approaches AdamW's task success rate~ kingma2014adam,loshchilov2017decoupled . After 6 , 000 steps, Dust's success rate plateaus and then drops substantially, eventually reaching a level comparable to that of SignSGD. We refer to this pattern of stagnation followed by decline during long-horizon ZO adaptation as the performance plateau problem. The performance plateau problem motivates Dune (Dust Using Nodewise Error-feedback), a memory-efficient ZO optimizer that uses regression over historical statistics to recover reliable update directions when perturbation noise overwhelms the dominant error signal. At each step, Dune constructs regression features from model output residuals and time buckets that encode the stage of adaptation. It uses historical statistics with decaying weights to predict layerwise error signals from these features. Dune then forms a weighted combination of these predictions and the current ZO perturbation observations to preserve the dominant direction of the error signal and suppress high-frequency perturbation noise. Finally, it updates the historical statistics with the raw perturbation observations from the current batch, allowing the regression to track changes as adaptation proceeds. This mechanism stabilizes long-horizon VLA-TTA while retaining the memory efficiency of ZO optimization. Our paper mainly makes the following contributions: Dune Paradigm. To overcome performance plateaus in VLA-TTA, Dune predicts layer-wise error signals via online ridge regression over output residuals and flow-matching time buckets, fusing them with current perturbation observations for stable updates without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Performance Plateau Theory. Under Gaussian perturbation and convex quadratic objectives, we establish a loss recursion showing how estimation variance limits convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, theoretically motivating historical error regression. Extensive Experiments. Across LIBERO benchmarks and real-world robots, Dune substantially boosts long-horizon task success rates with a significantly reduced memory footprint, while ablations confirm improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery. Related Work Vision--language--action models. Large-scale robot datasets and multimodal pretraining support the learning of general-purpose manipulation policies conditioned on vision and language~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,team2024octo,kim2024openvla . Follow-up work has explored continuous action generation and efficient deployment~ black2024pi_0,li2024cogact,shukor2025smolvla . To improve planning on complex tasks, other approaches integrate intermediate reasoning into action generation through embodied chain-of-thought~ zawalski2024robotic , visual subgoals~ zhao2025cot , and latent planning~ huang2026thinkact . These approaches strengthen policies through model architecture and training design, while adaptation at deployment addresses failures on tasks that pretraining data do not adequately cover. Test-time adaptation for VLA models. Tent and CoTTA established approaches for online and continual adaptation, respectively~ wang2020tent,wang2022continual . TPT and TDA extended TTA to vision--language models through prompt updates and dynamic caching, respectively~ shu2022test,karmanov2024efficient . In embodied settings, fast and slow updates and feedback-driven reinforcement learning have been used for online vision--language navigation~ gao2023fast,kim2025test . TT-VLA, VANE, and PDF use task progress, future visual observations, and delayed feedback, respectively, to adapt VLA models~ liu2026fly,ji2026vane,zang2026test . Retrieve-then-Steer guides action generation by retrieving successful past experiences~ zhao2026retrieve . For methods that fine-tune the model at test time, limited on-device resources constrain the updates they can perform. Optimization methods for test-time adaptation. FOA, FOZO, and CAZO reduce the cost of TTA by avoiding backpropagation through evolutionary strategies, ZO prompt optimization, and curvature-aware perturbations, respectively~ niu2024test,wang2026fozo,zhang2026curvature . ZO-SVRG, MeZO-SVRG, and ZO-AdaMM explore variance reduction and the use of historical gradient information~ gautam2024variance,chen2019zo,liu2018zeroth . MeZO and Dust apply ZO optimization to language model fine-tuning and Transformer pretraining, respectively~ malladi2023fine,dahal2026backprop . In long-horizon VLA-TTA, perturbation noise can overwhelm the dominant error signal and weaken parameter updates. This motivates Dune's approach to the performance plateau problem: combining current ZO perturbation observations with regression predictions from historical statistics to obtain more reliable estimates of layerwise error signals. Motivation sec:motivation The preceding results demonstrate the memory advantage and early convergence potential of ZO optimization for VLA-TTA. Maintaining stable updates over long horizons of online adaptation remains an open challenge. Two questions guide the design of Dune: Why does ZO optimization degrade over long adaptation horizons in VLA-TTA? How can we mitigate this degradation without backpropagation? title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor

Our code is available at: Introduction World Action Models (WAMs) offer a new paradigm for embodied policy learning by integrating visual dynamics modeling with action generation, providing predictive representations for robotic control~ gr1-wu,dreamzero-ye,lingbotva-li,lingbotva2-zhang,fastwam-yuan,fasterwam-zhao,cosmos-kim,motus2-bi,zerowam-zhou . However, most existing WAMs generate actions via flow matching~ fm-lipman, rectified-liu , which uses predicted velocities to update noisy actions over multiple Euler steps, incurring substantial inference cost and limiting task efficiency. Speculative inference~ sd-leviathan provides a promising solution for accelerating flow-matching-based WAMs. It achieves this by generating draft denoising trajectories and leveraging parallel verification to advance multiple denoising steps in a single round, reducing inference latency while maintaining outputs close to those of the target model. Existing speculative inference methods for embodied policies~ waspecdec-wen,kerv-zheng,heisd-zheng,specvla-wang,realtimevlaflash-niu rely on lightweight draft models trained for specific tasks, which must be retrained whenever the robot or task changes, introducing additional training overhead. In parallel, recent work on image and video generation exploits velocity smoothness in flow matching by reusing a previously computed velocity as an anchor to approximate subsequent ones~ flowcast-jyoti,parastep-wang . This allows us to construct readily available drafts for speculative inference without additional training. However, as shown in , we revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and uncover a previously overlooked dual nonuniformity that breaks the smoothness assumption underlying prior velocity reuse. First, velocity smoothness is nonuniform along WAM denoising trajectories, with pronounced changes between adjacent velocities at the beginning and end of denoising. Second, nonuniform integration time steps translate comparable velocity residuals into different local state errors, which accumulate and propagate to the final action distribution. These observations make it necessary for us to fundamentally rethink and naturally reshape two key questions in WAM’s speculative inference: Which velocities in WAMs can serve as reliable anchors for reuse? What factors affect the final action distribution error induced by velocity reuse in WAMs? To answer these questions, we formulate speculative inference as a trajectory error tolerance problem. Concretely, we bound the discrepancy between speculative outputs and reference Euler outputs using a weighted sum of anchor velocity reuse residuals. Our analysis shows that unreliable anchors introduce larger velocity residuals, increasing the error bound as these residuals propagate through subsequent nonuniform integration steps and affect the final action distribution. Based on this analysis, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to this dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It is built on two mechanisms: First, we perform Reliable Anchor Velocity Selection by deferring drafting until after the first Euler update. Second, we design a Time-Step-Aware Verification rule based on the quadratic relationship between squared velocity residuals and integration time step size, tightening verification for larger steps and relaxing it for smaller ones while providing a trajectory error tolerance guarantee. We seamlessly integrate WAMotor into three representative WAMs, Joint-WAM~ fastwam-yuan (a controlled implementation representing Joint-WAMs~ fasterwam-zhao,dreamwam-yuan,4dwam-yang ), Fast-WAM~ fastwam-yuan and Faster-WAM~ fasterwam-zhao , replacing their standard flow matching denoising pipelines. Comprehensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate that our method achieves greater speedups with near-lossless task performance relative to vanilla models, outperforming cache-based and other speculative inference baselines. Our experiments show that WAMotor accelerates flow matching inference by 3.24 --6.62 , yielding overall speedups of 2.86 --4.28 over vanilla models. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. In this paper, we revisit WAM denoising dynamics and uncover a previously overlooked dual nonuniformity in velocity smoothness and integration time steps. We propose WAMotor, a training-free speculative inference method combining reliable anchor selection with time-step-aware verification. It achieves 2.86 --4.28 end-to-end speedups across three WAMs while maintaining comparable task success rates. We further derive trajectory error bounds linking velocity-reuse residuals and integration time steps to final action distribution error. This analysis provides a principled foundation for future WAM acceleration, paving the way for more efficient and reliable embodied control. Related Work Efficient World Action Models World Action Models predict future world states, providing policies with temporal information beyond the current observation~ dreamzero-ye,lingbotva-li,lingbotva2-zhang,fastwam-yuan,vpp-hu,vpp2-guo , but their video and action denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Models~ gigaworld-ye,selfwam-pan,internw0delta-miao exemplified by Fast-WAM~ fastwam-yuan argue that the benefits of future modeling arise primarily during training, making explicit future video prediction optional at inference time. However, Faster-WAM~ fasterwam-zhao and related approaches~ efficientwam-li,simplewam-zhou show that removing inference-time future modeling can compromise robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings. They retain future information as a conditioning signal for action generation while reducing its computational cost through mechanisms such as KV-Fusion and sparse video--action interaction. Our work is complementary to this line of research, exploiting the velocity smoothness characteristics of WAMs to accelerate action generation through velocity reuse. Speculative Inference for Embodied Policies Speculative inference reduces sequential model evaluations by generating candidate outputs and verifying them in parallel. It has been widely studied in large language models~ sd-leviathan,ss-chen,eagle-li,eagle2-li,eagle3-li,dflash-chen . Recent methods~ kerv-zheng,heisd-zheng,waspecdec-wen such as SpecVLA~ specvla-wang and FLASH~ realtimevlaflash-niu extend speculative inference to embodied policies by training lightweight draft models. However, these methods require separate draft models to be trained for different task domains, introducing additional training overhead and complicating their transfer to WAMs. Alternatively, FlowCast~ flowcast-jyoti exploits trajectory smoothness in flow matching to construct speculative drafts by reusing velocity predictions without additional training. However, such velocity-reuse methods implicitly assume uniform trajectory smoothness and overlook how integration time steps scale reuse errors into the final action distribution. In contrast, WAMotor addresses the dual nonuniformity by deferring drafting past abrupt velocity transitions and weighting verification by integration time step size We discuss caching methods that are orthogonal to ours in . . Observation and Motivation sec:motivation Not Every Velocity Is Suitable to Be an Anchor sec:motivation-1 Recent studies on speculative inference for flow matching construct draft trajectories by approximating the velocity field. To characterize the variation of velocities in WAMs, we analyze differences between consecutive velocity predictions along the denoising trajectories of several WAMs. As shown in , adjacent velocities remain close in both direction and magnitude throughout most intermediate denoising steps. This local smoothness provides a natural draft for predicting the subsequent velocity field, enabling velocity reuse without an auxiliary draft model. However, this local smoothness breaks down near the beginning and end of denoising, where consecutive velocities change sharply in direction and magnitude. These changes limit how well the preceding velocity represents subsequent updates. Speculation based on such anchor velocity may face early rejection or, even when the candidate is ultimately accepted, result in substantial deviations in the trajectory We provide further visualization and quantitative analysis in and , respectively. . Given this nonuniform velocity smoothness, WAMotor defers speculation until after the first standard Euler update, using the velocity at the updated state as the initial anchor. Velocity Residual Alone Does Not Determine Final Action Distribution Deviation sec:motivation-2 Having identified a more reliable anchor velocity for speculation, the second question is which drafted velocities should be accepted. Existing speculative inference methods for flow matching assess the residual between the reused velocity and the model prediction at each candidate state using a velocity-space MSE criterion. However, flow matching samplers often employ nonuniform integration time step sizes across denoising steps~ srft-esser,iddpm-quinn,edm-karras,dj-chen . As shown in , under such schedules, the same velocity discrepancy can have different effects on the action state update depending on the corresponding integration interval. Moreover, deviations introduced by accepted updates may accumulate and propagate along the denoising trajectory. A uniform velocity-MSE threshold therefore does not provide uniform control over the velocity residuals introduced by speculation. In the following analysis, WAMotor establishes a link between velocity residuals, integration time steps, and final action distribution, motivating a time-step-aware verification criterion. title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
summary: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

VLA models such as OpenVLA openvla2024 , pi05 , and GR00T groot_n1 integrate pretrained vision-language backbones with diverse action-generation modules, while world-action approaches such as Unified World Models uwm2025 , Cosmos Policy cosmos_policy2026 , and DreamZero dreamzero2026 couple action prediction with video generation or future-state modeling. Meanwhile, large-scale multi-robot datasets openx2023,droid2024 have substantially expanded the volume and diversity of embodied training data. Together, these developments give rise to heterogeneous training workloads with distinct computation graphs, memory footprints, communication patterns, and data-processing requirements. Consequently, efficiently scaling embodied foundation models requires training infrastructure capable of accommodating such diversity while delivering high performance. Efficient training of heterogeneous VLA and WAM models faces two closely related challenges. First, diverse model architectures and training objectives give rise to substantially different performance bottlenecks. Variations in attention structures, computation graphs, activation-memory requirements, and distributed execution patterns shift the dominant costs among computation, memory, execution overhead, data I/O, and communication. These bottlenecks also depend on hardware characteristics, making a fixed optimization strategy insufficient across models and hardware platforms. Second, the embodied learning ecosystem remains fragmented. Despite recent efforts toward unified robot learning frameworks lerobot2024,starvla2026 , many embodied foundation models still rely on independently developed training stacks, with customized distributed execution, data processing, and evaluation pipelines. Although broadly reusable system optimization mechanisms exist, including optimized attention flashattn2_2023,dong2024flex , graph compilation torch2_2023 , CUDA Graphs cudagraphs , and communication optimization zeropp2023 , their effective integration and configuration often depend on model architectures and hardware characteristics. Consequently, similar optimizations must be repeatedly integrated, tuned, and validated across separate training stacks, limiting cross-model optimization reuse and increasing engineering overhead. This raises a fundamental systems question: can heterogeneous embodied models share a common training infrastructure while still enabling model-specific, high-performance optimization? We address this question with LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous VLA and WAM models. The key design principle is to separate model-specific computation from reusable training infrastructure. Although these models differ substantially in architecture, learning objectives, and execution patterns, they share common system-level functionalities, including training orchestration, distributed execution, data processing, optimization, checkpoint management, and evaluation. To capture this commonality without imposing a fixed computational structure, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a unified abstraction layer built around configuration-driven model registration, a lightweight model interface, and an extensible training engine. These abstractions allow heterogeneous models to reuse shared training infrastructure while preserving their individual computation graphs and training requirements. More importantly, this separation provides a foundation for cross-model optimization reuse: shared optimization mechanisms can be integrated once at the framework level, while architecture-specific and hardware-aware optimization choices remain customizable. In this way, LoongForge-Embodied combines the benefits of unified training infrastructure with the flexibility required for model-specific, high-performance optimization. Building on this unified abstraction, LoongForge-Embodied provides a composable acceleration toolkit that combines reusable system-level optimization mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware strategies. Guided by the performance bottlenecks of individual workloads, the framework integrates efficient attention kernels flashattn2_2023,dong2024flex,flashattn3 , mixed-precision computation, and fused operators and optimizers to improve computational efficiency. Graph compilation torch2_2023 and configurable CUDA Graph capture cudagraphs reduce execution overhead, while activation checkpointing chen2016training and parameter-efficient adaptation address memory constraints. Precomputation, caching, and asynchronous checkpointing further mitigate data-processing and I/O overhead. For distributed training, LoongForge-Embodied supports both Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) and Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) with FP8-based communication optimizations, reducing gradient synchronization traffic in DDP and parameter AllGather traffic in FSDP, particularly in bandwidth-constrained environments. Beyond communication compression, configurable synchronization and prefetching strategies improve computation--communication overlap. Rather than imposing a uniform optimization recipe, LoongForge-Embodied enables heterogeneous models to reuse shared acceleration mechanisms while retaining the flexibility to select architecture-specific implementations and hardware-aware configurations. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied provides a unified data infrastructure and evaluation framework. The data infrastructure of LoongForge-Embodied accommodates heterogeneous dataset formats, model-specific processing requirements, and cross-embodiment data synthesis from egocentric vision to robot manipulation, while the evaluation framework enables composable model and benchmark integration through shared inference implementations. In addition, LoongForge-Embodied accelerates evaluation through concurrency, reduced per-episode overhead, and reuse of computation. We evaluate LoongForge-Embodied across representative VLA and WAM models with diverse architectures and training characteristics. Compared with their corresponding open-source implementations, the framework achieves 1.47 --4.38 improvements in end-to-end training throughput, demonstrating its effectiveness across heterogeneous embodied workloads. With the same protocols, the evaluation of LoongForge-Embodied achieves 4.1\( \)–23.2\( \) speedup over the baseline. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: A unified training framework. We introduce LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies the training of heterogeneous VLA and WAM architectures through a common abstraction layer, enabling reusable training infrastructure across models. System-level acceleration. We develop a composable acceleration stack spanning efficient attention, compilation, CUDA Graphs, operator and optimizer fusion, data loading, and FP8-based distributed communication for both FSDP and DDP. Evaluation acceleration. We accelerate the evaluation loop through concurrent episode execution, reduced per-episode inference and rendering cost, and reuse of policy-independent computation, reducing evaluation wall-clock time by 4.1 --23.2 under an unchanged benchmark protocol. Broad empirical validation. We evaluate LoongForge-Embodied across nine representative VLA/WAM models and widely used embodied benchmarks, achieving 1.47 --4.38 training speedups while maintaining task success rates comparable to official baselines. title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
summary: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
