Introduction sec:intro Humans become skilled in the physical world not by being shown every motion, but by practice: they act, observe the outcome, and adjust. Repeated over many attempts, this loop turns a clumsy first try into a reliable skill, and it continues long after instruction ends. Generalist robot policies now perform a wide range of manipulation tasks~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,oxe2024,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t , yet they rarely improve this way: when a policy fails, making it better typically means collecting new human demonstrations. Enabling a robot to improve from its own experience is the goal of self-improvement in physical AI~ luo2026rsi,bousmalis2023robocat , and it would scale robot learning beyond what human teleoperation can supply. The most direct form of self-improvement changes the policy itself: the robot acts, keeps its successful rollouts, and is fine-tuned on them. This recipe has two limitations. First, a policy acting alone stays within its own distribution, so its successes show it only what it can already do. Second, on the long-horizon tasks where improvement matters most, the policy fails often and has few successes to collect. Experience improves a policy when it contains successes the policy cannot yet produce, and self-collected experience contains few of them. Existing methods obtain such successes with supervision from outside the policy. Interactive imitation learning brings in a human operator who takes over when the robot errs and supplies corrective actions~ kelly2019hgdagger,amin2026pistar06 . Every correction costs operator time, so the supervision scales with human effort, the cost that self-improvement is meant to remove. Reinforcement learning replaces the operator with reward and value models that score the robot's own attempts~ ghasemipour2025selfimproving,chen2026sarm2 . These models must themselves be trained before they can supervise the policy. Hierarchical systems place a vision-language model above the policy to decompose the task into steps~ ahn2022saycan,shi2025hirobot . The policy itself is left unchanged, and the system depends on the high-level model at every deployment. To understand what keeps a policy from producing these successes on its own, we analyze rollouts of generalist policies on long-horizon tasks. We find that the missing successes are closer than they appear. The policies execute atomic skills reliably, yet fail when the same skills are composed into a long-horizon task~ mees2022calvin,liu2023libero,fan2025longvla,tao2026prism , and the failures take a specific form: partway through the task the policy stalls, and a stalled policy almost never recovers on its own. In a recurring case, the robot is already at the right object and holds the required skill, yet does not act. What the policy lacks in that moment is not a skill but the next step. What it needs is therefore far less than corrective actions or rewards: a single instruction. We introduce ( ), a self-improvement method guided by language alone. Its central component is a language coach: a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) that watches the robot and replaces the task instruction with the next step, phrased in the format of the policy's atomic instructions. The coach never outputs an action; every motion is produced by the policy's own skills. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction~ andrychowicz2017her and used to fine-tune the policy, which is then deployed on its own. On a World Action Model, fine-tuning updates only the video backbone and keeps the action backbone frozen. needs no human operator, no reward model, and no VLM at test time. We evaluate on RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 with a World Action Model (WAM)~ wang2026openwam and a Vision-Language-Action model (VLA)~ xiaomi2026robotics . On states where the two policies have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by over the unchanged task instruction, and a VLM coach that sees only the policy's camera images delivers 91 of the gain of an oracle that always names the correct step. With the coach, the policy completes more than a quarter of the episodes it fails on its own. After fine-tuning the WAM on coached experience, unassisted success on 18 long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4 to 59.3 , 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8 , above both baselines. The action backbone is frozen throughout, so the entire gain comes from what the policy predicts will happen next: the skills were already there. Our contributions are: We identify a class of stalls in long-horizon manipulation in which the policy has the skill but lacks the next step, and show that a single next-step instruction resolves them, for both a WAM and a VLA. We propose , a self-improvement method of language coaching, hindsight relabeling, and fine-tuning, guided only by a frozen VLM's next-step instruction. We show that turns coached experience into unassisted capability and outperforms both human demonstrations and self-collected experience at an equal data budget. Related Work sec:related Self-improving robot policies. A growing body of work improves robot policies with experience collected after pretraining~ luo2026rsi . Autonomous-improvement systems let the policy practice and train on its own rollouts after hindsight relabeling or success filtering~ bousmalis2023robocat,zhou2024soar . Reinforcement-learning methods learn reward or value functions and optimize the policy against them~ ghasemipour2025selfimproving,xiao2025pld,xu2025rldg,chen2026sarm2,amin2026pistar06,yang2026rise , with VLMs increasingly serving as the reward model~ ma2025gvl,lee2026roboreward . Interactive imitation learning queries an expert, typically a human teleoperator, for corrective actions on the states the policy visits~ ross2011dagger,kelly2019hgdagger,liu2023sirius,luo2024hilserl,amin2026pistar06 . Most recently, agents built on LLMs and world models improve the system around the policy: RoboRSI~ wen2026roborsi writes and repairs skill code, and RoboCoach~ liu2026robocoach selects which subtask demonstrations to collect next. In contrast to these works, improves the policy with a single signal, the next-step instruction of a frozen VLM. It trains no reward or value model, requires no action-level expert, and updates the policy itself. Language guidance at deployment. Language is the standard interface between high-level reasoning and low-level control. Hierarchical systems decompose a task into language steps at run time, with a separate LLM or VLM planner~ huang2022zeroshot,ahn2022saycan,huang2022inner,liang2023cap,shi2025hirobot,hu2026orchestrating or inside the policy~ belkhale2024rth,zawalski2024ecot,black2025pi05,yang2025lohovla . A second line corrects the policy in language during execution, with corrections issued by humans~ shi2024yell,liu2023olaf or by VLMs that detect and explain failures~ liu2023reflect,duan2024aha or choose among the policy's candidate action plans~ wu2025forewarn . RACER~ dai2024racer trains both a VLM supervisor and a language-conditioned policy on expert-corrected failure data and keeps the supervisor in the loop at deployment. These systems rely on a human or a high-level model at test time, and several train the policy to follow a new language interface. uses the VLM only during data collection: the coach is frozen and off-the-shelf, it reuses the instruction format of the policy's atomic skills, and the fine-tuned policy executes the task instruction on its own. Language as a training signal. Language also serves as a signal for training. Hindsight relabeling assigns to a trajectory the goal it reached~ andrychowicz2017her , and DIAL~ xiao2023dial and SOAR~ zhou2024soar use VLMs to produce such instruction labels for offline or autonomously collected data. BOSS~ zhang2023boss has an LLM propose which skills to chain during practice and learns the chains as new skills. Scaling Up and Distilling Down~ ha2023scalingup and Manipulate-Anything~ duan2024manipulate have an LLM or a VLM generate demonstrations and distill them into a policy. title: Communication-Aware UAV Spatio-Temporal Relay Cooperation and Planning in Complex Urban Environments
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in low-altitude urban airspace for delivery, emergency response, and other applications. However, UAV mobility across spatially heterogeneous urban communication environments can lead to time-varying communication outages, disrupting mission execution and compromising flight safety. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a Spatio-Temporal Relay Cooperation and Planning (ST-RCP) framework that leverages delivery UAVs as opportunistic communication relays for disconnected UAVs without requiring additional communication infrastructure. The framework predicts communication blind-spot events over a finite planning horizon, constructs a helper-event compatibility graph, and jointly optimizes relay selection, obstacle-aware trajectory replanning, and communication-aware scheduling. Multiple planners are evaluated to investigate the trade-offs among communication coverage, computational cost, and energy consumption. Experiments based on real-world traffic scenarios compare the performance of ST-RCP against baseline methods. In the peak scenario, ST-RCP improves descent-phase communication coverage by 29.93% compared with the base-station baseline and by 27.38%, 22.02%, and 15.20% compared with configurations using one, two, and three dedicated relay UAVs, respectively. Process flexibility analysis demonstrates that predictive task-aware relaying expands the pool of feasible relay resources and improves communication continuity while maintaining the feasibility of delivery missions. These findings demonstrate the potential of trajectory-enabled UAV coordination to enhance the safety and resilience of urban aerial operations.

Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are playing an increasingly important role in low-altitude urban air mobility, with growing applications in logistics delivery, emergency response, and search and rescue gao2024noise,10803914 . Reliable communication is essential for these operations, as command and control signals, traffic management information, and mission-related data must be exchanged between UAVs and ground infrastructure to ensure safe and efficient operations greenfeld2019uam,8470897 . Communication disruptions can pose significant risks to flight safety, as the loss of command and control connectivity may compromise UAV operations and increase the risk of accidents. Maintaining reliable connectivity, however, is particularly challenging in dense urban environments. High-rise buildings can obstruct line-of-sight (LoS) communication links and cause signal reflection, diffraction, and scattering, leading to substantial spatial variations in received signal strength and localized communication coverage gaps, particularly in urban canyons and areas obstructed by buildings 8709739,11162132 , as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:spatial_blindspot . Simply increasing base station density may not fully resolve these challenges. UAVs may establish strong propagation links with multiple neighboring base stations simultaneously, potentially exacerbating co-channel interference and limiting the coverage and throughput gains of network densification 8692749 . Furthermore, additional base stations may not eliminate coverage gaps caused by signal blockage from urban structures 11162132 . UAV connectivity is also inherently trajectory dependent, particularly when mission locations are uncertain. As a UAV moves through a spatially heterogeneous radio environment, its received signal quality varies over time, causing it to repeatedly enter and leave communication coverage regions d1d2325ba27041e9ab61322119b00720 . Therefore, reliable urban UAV communication depends not only on the spatial distribution of radio coverage but also on the spatiotemporal interaction between UAV trajectories and communication conditions. Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate intermittent UAV connectivity. One representative approach is to establish flying ad hoc networks (FANETs), in which neighboring UAVs exchange data through multi-hop communication links. However, the high mobility of UAVs leads to rapidly changing network topologies, making it difficult for conventional routing protocols to maintain reliable end-to-end communication paths ullah2025spectral . Moreover, network-wide flooding of routing messages can generate substantial redundant transmissions, increasing channel contention and routing overhead kilicarslan2025broadcast . An alternative approach is to deploy UAV-mounted base stations or dedicated relay UAVs to restore or extend communication coverage. Although such aerial relays can effectively improve connectivity, they require additional aerial resources and incur substantial deployment and operational costs cong2025multi,yang2025multiobjective . More recently, studies have explored the use of delivery UAVs as communication relays by adjusting their flight routes and introducing communication waypoints to support multi-hop connectivity soya2025flight . Such studies demonstrate the potential of leveraging the mobility of task-performing UAVs to support communication without relying exclusively on dedicated relay platforms. However, existing approaches largely plan communication topologies and delivery routes in advance, rather than dynamically adapting to time-varying communication outages arising from task uncertainty. This limitation motivates a more dynamic planning framework that treats future communication blind spots as time-dependent service events and predictively reserves and reroutes available task-performing UAVs to provide relay assistance while satisfying communication, flight safety, obstacle avoidance, energy, and delivery constraints. To address this research gap, this paper proposes a spatio-temporal relay cooperation and planning (ST-RCP) framework to enable self-organizing UAV communication in complex urban environments. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on dedicated relay platforms, ST-RCP leverages the mobility of UAVs already performing delivery missions, allowing available UAVs to temporarily serve as opportunistic communication relays while maintaining the feasibility of their original tasks. Furthermore, rather than optimizing communication locations along predetermined routes, ST-RCP models communication outages as time-varying service demands and coordinates relay resources based on both spatial reachability and temporal availability. Specifically, future communication blind-spot events and their associated attributes are predicted over a finite planning horizon. For each event, ST-RCP identifies candidate delivery UAVs capable of providing relay assistance while satisfying their original mission constraints. A helper–event compatibility graph is then constructed to capture spatial, temporal, and communication feasibility. This formulation transforms relay selection from a static waypoint placement problem into a constrained spatio-temporal resource allocation problem. Based on the selected helpers, smooth, obstacle-aware relay trajectories are subsequently generated using B\'ezier curves. The proposed framework is evaluated in terms of communication performance, operational efficiency, and computational cost. Beyond conventional coverage metrics, this study introduces a process flexibility perspective to characterize the structural adaptability of the task-performing UAV relay system. This analysis complements conventional performance evaluations by examining not only the effectiveness of relay strategies under given scenarios but also the system's ability to accommodate varying communication demands, resource contention, and fleet sizes. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: A spatio-temporal relay cooperation and planning (ST-RCP) framework is proposed to enable task-performing UAVs to opportunistically provide communication relay assistance without requiring additional infrastructure. Communication blind-spot recovery is formulated as a predictive helper–event assignment and constrained trajectory planning problem, enabling time-dependent, event-driven relay resource allocation. A process flexibility analysis framework is introduced to quantify the scalability and adaptability of UAV relay systems, characterizing their ability to maintain feasible relay options under increasing traffic demand and resource contention. Literature Review sec:lit UAV Communication and Relay Strategies FANETs establish connectivity through UAV-to-UAV multi-hop links, with recent studies using clustering, reinforcement learning, link-stability prediction, and selective forwarding to improve routing under high mobility. Ullah et al. ullah2025spectral combine spectral clustering with reinforcement learning, while Li and Sun li2025prediction adapt route discovery using predicted link stability. Kılıçarslan et al. kilicarslan2025broadcast show that unrestricted rebroadcast can cause redundant transmissions and channel contention, and He et al. he2025fanet jointly optimize UAV trajectories, topology, and transmit power to improve throughput. Despite these advances, FANETs remain sensitive to rapid topology changes and link instability, while frequent neighbor discovery and routing updates can introduce substantial communication overhead and limit scalability in dense or highly dynamic UAV networks. Dedicated UAV relays and UAV-mounted base stations offer another approach to improving aerial connectivity. Cong et al. cong2025multi jointly optimize scheduling, transmit power, and trajectories for multi-UAV relaying, while Yang et al. yang2025multiobjective optimize relay population, placement, communication performance, and propulsion energy. Although such dedicated aerial resources can enhance coverage and throughput, they introduce additional deployment, scheduling, and energy costs, which increase as the network scales. Tsai and Huang tsai2025implementation further demonstrate the practical feasibility of UAV-based relaying using a 3GPP-compatible onboard communication module. More recently, Soya et al. soya2025flight employ delivery UAVs as multi-hop communication nodes by introducing communication waypoints into predefined routes, showing that task-performing UAVs can also support communication. However, these methods remain largely route-oriented and do not explicitly model time-varying communication outages, temporal relay demand, or competition among limited relay resources. These limitations motivate predictive and event-driven relay coordination that jointly considers relay assignment, temporal availability, and trajectory feasibility. Communication- and Obstacle-Aware UAV Trajectory Planning in Urban Environments In urban low-altitude environments, UAV trajectory planning must jointly consider communication and mission constraints. Zhong et al. zhong2024joint combine radio and environmental maps with D3QN to reduce communication interruptions, mission time, and obstacle risk, while related work uses radio maps and deep reinforcement learning to maintain connectivity in three-dimensional flight space liu2024deep3d . These studies incorporate communication constraints into trajectory optimization but primarily focus on maintaining the connectivity of individual UAVs, with limited consideration of coordinating UAVs to provide time-bounded relay assistance to others. Urban buildings also require explicit geometric planning. Hu et al. zhang2025layered model buildings as cuboid obstacles in a layered visibility graph and add maneuvering protection spots to reduce collision risk. Banik et al. banik2025performance compare PRM, RRT*, and EST in Gazebo using a three-dimensional occupancy grid. Li et al. li2026energy jointly optimize NOMA power and a three-dimensional relay trajectory under several constraints. title: Trajectory-Calibrated Merging of Embodied Policies
summary: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $π_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.
full_text: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present ( ), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four specialists and achieves 77.83 success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively. We also find that continued training from a merged checkpoint improves peak success: TCR reaches 97.75 versus 94.00 when training from the common base. These results show that calibrating model merging around execution dynamics and evolving internal representations provides an effective path toward preserving diverse embodied skills in a unified policy. Introduction sec:introduction General-purpose robots need policies that can perform diverse physical tasks. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising foundation~ pmlr-v305-black25a,KimM1-RSS-25 , but demonstration data cover limited tasks and environments, making it difficult to acquire a broad skill set through a single training run. Training task specialists from a shared foundation model expands coverage, but leaves their capabilities in separate checkpoints. We seek to consolidate them into one policy. Model merging can do this without joint training or selecting an expert at inference. We focus on post-hoc consolidation of independently trained VLA specialists into one static policy, without redesigning the experts or adding a task router. Parameter-space methods combine weights or align task updates to reduce interference~ pmlr-v162-wortsman22a,yadav2023tiesmerging,stoica2025model . But the mapping from weights to actions is nonlinear: reducing conflicts between weights does not ensure that the merged policy preserves expert actions or closed-loop success. Regression-based methods instead fit merged weights to expert outputs on calibration inputs~ jin2023dataless,nguyen2026regmean . Such a fit is only as useful as the inputs it covers. An action error can change not only the current output but also what the policy sees next; matching a fixed set of expert observations may leave later inputs unconstrained and allow errors to accumulate. A slightly misplaced grasp, for example, can change both the camera observation and the robot state at the next decision. Even when the observation is held fixed, the input to an iterative action generator changes across calls as each intermediate prediction updates the action state passed to the next call. Calibration using only the final call can therefore miss states encountered earlier in generation. During merging, a further change occurs within the network. Updating an upstream block can alter the features passed to a downstream block, so a block fitted on the original expert’s features may receive different inputs in the merged policy. The regression fit thus depends on which states are sampled during execution and action generation, and on how the features used to fit each block are computed (see Figure fig:method_overview ). We introduce ( ), a gradient-free framework for merging compatible robot experts. TCR uses frozen experts as teachers and collects two kinds of inputs: observations, robot states, and instructions across expert rollouts, and intermediate call states from each expert's native action generator. The first covers stages reached after earlier expert actions; the second covers generator inputs, such as noisy actions and flow times, that an observation alone does not specify. TCR fits adapted perception, conditioning, and action modules to expert outputs on these inputs. Following blockwise feature replay~ nguyen2026regmean , it recomputes each block's inputs through the blocks already merged before fitting that block. Downstream regressions therefore use features produced by the merged prefix rather than relying only on the original expert features. TCR makes two passes over separate rollout caches: the first updates the parameter average, and the second uses that checkpoint as its prior while still matching the frozen experts. The second cache adds expert calls not used in the first fit, and the updated prior carries the first pass into the second. The result is one policy with the original inference graph, no expert router, and no gradient training. We evaluate TCR on LIBERO~ NEURIPS2023_8c3c6668 using four specialists trained for 10,000 steps each. Across 1,200 episodes, TCR achieves 77.83 success, the highest among the static post-hoc mergers evaluated in this -LIBERO setting. This is 9.50 points above FeatCal (68.33 ), 24.17 above RegMean (53.67 ), and 33.00 above direct weight averaging (44.83 ). The gains are strongest on Goal and Long, although FeatCal remains ahead on Spatial. All methods share the same experts and evaluation protocol, while retaining their own calibration budgets. Ablations test the calibration choices; real-robot and cross-benchmark evaluations test TCR beyond LIBERO. We also find that merged checkpoints are useful starts for joint training: all four attain higher peak success than common-base training, with TCR highest at 97.75 versus 94.00 for the base. Our contributions are: To our knowledge, we are the first to study calibration coverage across both task execution and iterative action generation in post-hoc VLA weight merging. Calibration on isolated observations can miss states reached later in a task, and even a recorded observation leaves unspecified the intermediate inputs used to generate its action. We introduce Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), a gradient-free method that merges VLA specialists into one router-free policy. In two passes over separate rollout caches, TCR replays recorded action-generation inputs through already merged blocks and fits each subsequent block to frozen expert outputs. Merging four specialists on LIBERO, TCR achieves 77.83 success over 1,200 episodes, 9.50 percentage points above FeatCal, the strongest of eight baselines. TCR also leads the evaluated mergers on LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin~2.0, and the physical robot (30/40 successes versus 23/40 for FeatCal). Related Work sec:related_work Combining Expert Parameters Some merging methods combine parameter updates without explicitly matching model outputs. Model Soups averages fine-tuned checkpoints; Task Arithmetic scales and combines updates from a common base; TIES and DARE address coordinate conflicts and redundancy~ pmlr-v162-wortsman22a,ilharco2023editing,yadav2023tiesmerging,yu2024language . Breadcrumbs, DELLA, and Selective Task Arithmetic refine coordinate selection, while TSV, Iso-CTS, Subspace Boosting, and DC-Merge operate on singular directions or update geometry~ 10.1007/978-3-031-73226-3_16,deep2024dellamergingreducinginterferencemodel,bowen2024taskvectorsselectivetask,11092448,marczak2025no,skorobogat2025subspaceboostedmodelmerging,zhang2026dcmergeimprovingmodelmerging . KnOTS aligns independently trained LoRA updates, and WUDI and its variants estimate useful input subspaces from weights~ stoica2025model,cheng2025whoever,wei2026closedformspectralregularizationmultitask . LoRA-specific and base-anchored methods further constrain update geometry~ Lee_2026_CVPR,ryum2026ctmergingconsensusdirectionstasklevel,zheng2025decoupleorthogonalizedatafreeframework,shi2026pactpreservinganchoredcores , while generative weight-space models such as Text2Weight synthesize task-specific weights from language and support text-guided fusion~ 10.1145/3746027.3755441 . Calibration-Guided Functional Merging RegMean and RegMean++ fit merged linear weights to expert outputs, with the latter recomputing features through already merged layers~ jin2023dataless,nguyen2026regmean . LOT Merging studies feature drift during model merging and introduces layer-wise task vector fusion to reduce representation mismatch~ NEURIPS2025_fbb4f226 . ESM uses task-induced layer-wise feature shifts to extract essential subspaces, while activation-guided coefficient methods optimize a more restricted merge parameterization~ Li_2026_CVPR,NEURIPS2025_b395e7bd . Fisher merging and AdaMerging additionally use gradient information or optimization on calibration data~ NEURIPS2022_70c26937,yang2024adamerging . FeatCal performs closed-form feature calibration in forward order, refreshing features after preceding layers are updated~ gu2026featcalfeaturecalibrationpostmerging . TCR builds on regression and sequential feature replay, focusing on calibration inputs collected across robot task execution and action generation. Robot Policies and Specialist Consolidation OpenVLA and the family connect pretrained visual-linguistic representations to robot actions~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,BlackK-RSS-25,pmlr-v305-black25a . Action chunking predicts several actions per policy request, while diffusion and flow policies, including language-conditioned humanoid controllers such as ECHO and DAJI, generate these chunks through repeated prediction steps~ Zhao-RSS-23,Chi-RSS-23,lipman2023flow,jia2026echoedgecloudhumanoidorchestration,jia2026bodymoveslearninganticipatory ; SmolVLA provides a smaller flow-based implementation~ shukor2025smolvlavisionlanguageactionmodelaffordable . OpenVLA-OFT instead decodes continuous actions in parallel~ KimM1-RSS-25 . Adapting calibration to a different policy architecture requires matching its actual inference computation. Combining robot skills. FLEET-MERGE studies policy merging for robot fleets by aligning separately trained policies under parameter permutation symmetries~ ICLR2024_e28b3369 . MergeVLA explores robot skill consolidation by modifying expert construction with sparse masks to encourage mergeability~ Fu_2026_CVPR . OSRM studies LoRA mergeability in language models through structured adapter subspaces~ zhang-zhou-2025-unraveling . TCR instead starts with existing compatible experts and fits merged weight matrices using inputs recorded during task execution. CapVector transfers capability vectors for subsequent adaptation, while VLA-Pro retrieves and dynamically fuses adapter memories at inference time~ song2026capvectorlearningtransferablecapability,si2026vlaprocrosstaskproceduralmemory . RETAIN interpolates generalist and fine-tuned VLA parameters and uses the merged checkpoint to initialize adaptation to a subsequent robot task~ yadav2026robust . Our continuation study instead jointly trains the original source tasks after merging four specialists under matched updates. ReVLA restores visual generalization after adaptation through representation recovery~ 11128823 . title: Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking: Memory-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Embodied Navigation
summary: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

title: GraF-VTA: Neuro-Symbolic Trajectory Generation from Vision and Temporal Logic via Graph-Based Fusion
summary: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@$K$ than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets $K\geq16$. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91\% without observation history to 62.50\% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06\% Success@1024, compared with 12.50\% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34\% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.

Introduction sec:intro Robotic tasks often combine goal achievement with deadlines, ordering, and obstacle avoidance. Signal temporal logic (STL) expresses these requirements precisely through spatial predicates and bounded temporal operators~ maler2004monitoring,belta2019formal,lindemann2019feedback . Trajectory generation and execution from visual observations, STL specifications, and robot state are therefore important for fulfilling these requirements. Visual input provides a practical interface between STL planning and robot sensing, with grounding mechanisms relating symbolic references to image regions~ Kamath_2021_ICCV,Li_2022_CVPR,liu2024grounding . Pretrained vision-language models have also been used to propose visual predicates and evaluate them from images, enabling the learning of symbolic world models for long-horizon planning~ athalye2026p2p . For STL-conditioned trajectory generation, TeLoGraF~ meng2025telograf conditions trajectory generation on syntax graphs containing exact object geometry, which must be supplied externally. End-to-end visuomotor learning~ levine2016endtoend,brohan2023rt,zitkovich2023rt2,li2024roboflamingo demonstrates that perception can instead be trained jointly with action prediction. Vision-TL-Action (VTA)~ liu2026visiontlaction brings visual grounding to STL-conditioned generation by connecting logic nodes to image tokens. This supports a learned observation-to-trajectory mapping without exact object geometry in the STL specifications. Executing trajectories planned by generative models is challenging because model mismatch, disturbances, and tracking errors can separate intended and realized motion. Receding-horizon STL control~ sadraddini2015robust,raman2015reactive,meng2023signal and Diffusion Policy~ chi2025diffusion motivate repeated planning from execution feedback. We therefore execute short action prefixes and refresh visual observations and robot state before generating subsequent actions, allowing plans to respond to observed deviations. Refreshed observations alone may not reveal the robot's recent interactions with the environment or the current task stage. MemoryVLA~ shi2026memoryvla demonstrates the value of historical perceptual and semantic information for temporally dependent manipulation. This motivates conditioning STL planning on causal observation history. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations while compressing older frames, providing recent execution context within a finite memory window. A complementary challenge is exposing task semantics to the generator. An STL syntax graph preserves composition, time bounds, and object references. Yet, as Xie et al.~ xie2021embedding observe for finite-trace LTL, equivalent formulas can have different syntax trees, complicating semantic learning. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) makes the accepted event sequences explicit through transitions and accepting states. This motivates combining timed, visually groundable syntax with a semantic view. We introduce GraF-VTA, a unified visual temporal-logic planning framework supporting STL syntax graph and DFA graph conditioning (Fig.~ fig:dvta_overview ). It also combines bidirectional logic--vision fusion, causal observation memory, and action-prefix replanning within a conditional flow-matching generator. The optional dual-graph configuration adds a frozen RADE embedding~ yalcinkaya2024compositional after pooling and base-condition encoding. Our main empirical analysis concerns the single-graph configuration; dual-graph conditioning is a complementary representation extension. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We present a unified framework for end-to-end trajectory generation from visual observations, STL specifications, and robot state. Building on TeLoGraF's graph-conditioned flow matching and VTA's visual grounding, bidirectional logic--vision fusion connects object references to scene evidence while retaining temporal constraints. Conditioning uses the STL syntax tree alone or adds a DFA embedding for complementary task-transition structure. (2) To address execution errors, we interleave action-prefix execution with replanning from updated visual observations and robot state. A causal temporal pyramid retains detailed current observations while compressing older frames, providing recent execution context for multi-stage tasks. This feedback-driven design responds to observed deviations, aiming to improve robustness to execution errors. (3) We evaluate open-loop trajectory generation and dynamics-executed rollouts across five simulation environments, complemented by comparisons with related planners and observation-memory ablations. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Related Work Temporal-logic-conditioned robot planning. Temporal-logic planners incorporate specifications through constrained optimization~ dawson2022robust , sampling guidance~ vasile2017sampling , or learned conditioning~ guo2024specification . Differentiable STL robustness supports optimization~ leung2023backpropagation,kapoor2025stlcg ; generative planners use STL-constrained diffusion~ meng2024diverse,zhong2023guided , hierarchical options~ feng2025diffusion , or trajectory composition~ liu2026zeroshotstl . Robust STL model predictive control~ sadraddini2015robust uses mixed-integer optimization under linear dynamics and bounded disturbances, whereas LTLDoG~ feng2024ltldog guides diffusion sampling with finite-trace LTL satisfaction at inference time. TeLoGraF~ meng2025telograf instead learns a flow-matching generator conditioned on an STL syntax graph with exact object geometry. VTA~ liu2026visiontlaction replaces that geometric input with node-level graph--vision cross-attention and training-time predicate-to-region supervision. Among other visual STL planners, S-MSP~ ye2026smsp combines images, STL structure, and pose--region context in a mixture-of-experts waypoint decoder, with RRT-based local trajectory repair. Logic-VLA~ wang2026logicvla pretrains an STL encoder using robustness supervision and adapts a pretrained VLA through supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Our framework retains VTA's visual--symbolic interface and flow-matching formulation, extending its conditioning with causal observation history and optional automaton features with closed-loop replanning. LTL2Action~ vaezipoor2021ltl2action combines structured LTL instructions with environment-agnostic pretraining for multi-task reinforcement learning. T-LEAF~ xie2021embedding embeds DFAs derived from finite-trace LTL using a hierarchical graph encoder trained with satisfying and violating traces; distances in this space define a logic loss for sequential prediction and imitation learning. RADE~ yalcinkaya2024compositional pretrains graph embeddings on reach--avoid-derived automata for reinforcement learning conditioned on compositional DFAs. We reuse frozen RADE features to condition trajectory generation alongside the visually grounded STL representation. Its embedding represents the original component initial states, fixed throughout execution rather than tracking observed task progress. The STL representation retains time bounds and object references, and the original timed specification remains the evaluation criterion. Visual generative policies and observation memory. Generative planners represent multiple possible behaviors through distributions over trajectories or action sequences~ black2024pi0,ghosh2024octo,bjorck2025groot . Diffuser~ janner2022planning plans by denoising trajectories, while Diffusion Policy~ chi2025diffusion conditions action-sequence denoising on visual observations and executes predictions in a receding horizon; FlowPolicy~ zhang2025flowpolicy uses consistency flow matching. VLA research also explores multimodal prompts~ jiang2023vima , cross-embodiment learning~ openx2024,kim2025openvla , spatial representations~ zhen2024threedvla,qu2025spatialvla , open-world generalization~ pi2025pi05 , and simplified architectures~ ye2026starvlaalpha . Recent VLA models retain history in different ways, with MemoryVLA~ shi2026memoryvla retrieving and consolidating perceptual and semantic features, HAMLET~ koo2026hamlet aggregating compressed moment tokens across time, and MEM~ torne2026mem combining short-term video memory with long-term textual memory. Our planner uses a finite window of visual observations with an explicit allocation of spatial tokens such that current frames retain fine detail, while older frames receive coarser representations. title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
summary: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.

Introduction An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) searching for a regional target must decide where to move, when to observe and which predictions to compute. Overhead imagery narrows the search region; current camera observations establish local target evidence. Cross-view benchmarks connect these perspectives~ dai2024denseuav,zhu2023sues200 . Closing the sensing loop adds an operational question: which prediction is worth computing before the vehicle commits its next movement? Two uncertainties shape that decision. Positive and negative observations update an uncertain overhead prior. Future-view scores are uncertain too. A move may leave the target occluded but enable a useful view one step later. We score reachable views over a short horizon, execute the first move, and replan. A cheap proposer scores candidates before selective WM queries. Several paths may start north. Once north is verified as the best first action, their ranking cannot change it. Figure~ fig:motivation isolates the roles of context, feedback and confirmation. Over 4,320 noisy-sensor tasks, likelihood-based belief updating confirms 84.00 of targets, versus 32.78 without context and 2.57 with negative feedback frozen. Qualified stopping reduces false confirmation from 30.42 to 0.67 with more observations. A global-mass controller reaches 86.34 , motivating strong planning baselines alongside evidence-handling controls for information-gain (IG) planning. Information-driven trajectory and next-best-view planning connect informative views to motion~ charrow2015information,bircher2016nbv . A receding-horizon controller executes the first motion before observing again. AeroBelief makes this execution unit the verification unit: it groups viewpoints sharing a first motion and queries contenders that can change the winning group. A group's lower score bound exceeding every rival group's upper bound certifies the next action without resolving its best continuation. Figure~ fig:system shows the resulting loop. Qualified observations update belief (a); a cheap proposer and selective reference queries allocate prediction work (b); action bounds or controller acceptance rules determine the first movement (c). The strict verifier commits on separated bounds. The three-dimensional AeroBelief controller with (D6) combines selective prediction with Guard, progress handling and a belief-guided geometric fallback (NoWorld). Evidence epochs invalidate obsolete predictions, and a ledger accounts separately for prediction, sensing, motion and time. The next observation then revises the belief for replanning. This design places selective evaluation at two sensing interfaces. Before motion, the system admits reference predictions that can resolve an action comparison. Along a recorded flight route, it admits images whose footprints and observations can advance target confirmation. Both decisions use the current belief, with separate budgets for prediction and sensing. Evidence epochs connect new observations to prediction reuse, while capture and processing timestamps connect image admission to result readiness. Table~ tab:evidence maps the evaluation populations and endpoints. Matched controls isolate grouping, query refinement and evidence feedback; common-input timing separates reference work from complete-decision latency. On simultaneous score coverage, separated group bounds identify the first movement of every exhaustive reference optimum. Charged reference anchors and proposer-derived scaling increase resolution within the query budget. Prediction and sensing in one control loop. Selective WM access, belief updates, Guard and progress handling connect the prediction budget to three-dimensional execution. Evidence epochs prevent reuse across changed beliefs, and a resource ledger distinguishes prediction, observation, motion and result readiness. Matched control and self-collected sensing evidence. title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
summary: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $π_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $π_{0.5}$.

Refined extraction skills annotate the demonstrations with affordance features for VLA training. For an unseen tool, uses validated skills to extract its affordance, verifies it in simulation, and supplies the encoded functional-region features to guide VLA execution. fig:overview Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. Introduction sec:introduction People can often reuse a familiar manipulation skill with an unfamiliar tool after inspecting it and attempting to interact with the environment using it. A differently shaped implement may still provide functional regions similar to those of a familiar tool, such as an edge for cutting or a tip for hooking, even though its appearance and required wrist motion differ substantially from those of the original tool. What transfers is therefore neither the tool's identity nor a fixed end-effector trajectory, but an understanding of the properties that make the intended interaction possible. Enabling robots to acquire and reuse this understanding from limited tool experience would reduce the need to collect demonstrations for every new tool--grasp combination. Toward this goal, we study how to enable a robot system to adapt to new tools that can perform the same task, starting from teleoperated demonstrations using a small set of source tools. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies already possess some tool-manipulation capabilities~ openvla,pi0,pi05 , but adapting them to entirely new tools still requires repeated rollout collection and fine-tuning to maintain performance. Predefined functional representations of tools have shown useful structure for transfer: MimicFunc establishes functional correspondences through keypoints and function frames~ mimicfunc , and FuncBridge learns functional trajectories separately from their grounding into actions~ funcbridge . Meanwhile, improvements in the embodied manipulation capabilities of general-purpose large vision-language models (VLMs) make autonomous analysis of tool function possible. Our focus is how an agent system can autonomously identify task-relevant functional regions and determine their key geometric features, capturing functional commonality across tools to guide a VLA policy in adapting to new tools. We treat task-relevant affordance features as experimentally testable hypotheses. Although hierarchical robot systems already connect reasoning by general-purpose VLMs to low-level policy execution through language or spatial guidance~ hirobot,hamster,steerable , language or keypoints alone cannot fully represent the geometric details of tools. Cross-tool adaptation additionally requires deciding which tool properties should be represented for a specific task and testing whether these properties can guide the policy to complete it correctly. We introduce , in which the agent starts from a few real-robot teleoperated demonstrations, reconstructs the demonstrated scenes and tools in simulation, and conducts experiments within them. The agent analyzes how different source tools accomplish the task, determines task-relevant affordance features, develops affordance-extraction skills, and applies them to other tools to attempt task execution. Based on experimental feedback, it analyzes unsuccessful interactions and refines the selected functional regions, geometric features, or extraction skills. Successful skills and their applicability conditions accumulate during this process in a reusable skill library. When faced with an unseen tool, the agent can therefore reuse previously validated skills to identify corresponding functional regions and extract the same features. We condition the low-level VLA execution policy on agent-encoded functional-region features through a low-dimensional affordance interface. While analyzing the source tools, the agent determines task-relevant affordance features, which are encoded under a unified protocol as conditioning inputs for VLA training. Unseen tools' affordances are described through the same protocol: their specific affordance parameters are extracted while the coordinate representation and feature semantics remain unchanged. This gives the agent freedom to select functional regions and geometric features while maintaining a consistent policy input format. Encoded features serve as conditioning inputs when training a policy with an auxiliary affordance prediction head. During deployment, the agent reconstructs the unseen tool in simulation, extracts and tests candidate affordances, and refines their parameters from simulation feedback before encoding them under the same protocol for the VLA policy. At execution time, the VLA conditions each action chunk on the updated affordance features and current observations. Our evaluation examines the reliability and reusability of autonomously discovered affordances and their effectiveness in cross-tool transfer. Simulation tests compare our affordance discovery and validation process with other tool-adaptation methods, including task success when using affordances to retarget trajectories in reconstructed scenes. Three real-robot tool-use tasks test the robustness of cross-tool transfer. Human Oracle uses human-provided affordances for both VLA policy training and inference to distinguish failures caused by poor affordance features from those caused by the VLA's execution capability. Our main contributions are: An agentic tool-adaptation framework that starts from teleoperated demonstrations using a small set of source tools and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features. The agent reconstructs the demonstrated scenes in simulation, tests and refines these features through autonomous experiments, and retains refined affordance-extraction procedures as reusable skills across tools. An affordance-guided VLA model that integrates the resulting low-dimensional feature vectors into action generation. Affordance conditioning and auxiliary affordance-trajectory supervision train the policy to faithfully follow the supplied affordance information while using current observations and robot state to complete tool-use tasks. Related Work sec:related_work Tool adaptation. Tool adaptation requires understanding how a tool itself functions in a specific task. KETO~ keto and GIFT~ gift learn sparse grasp and functional keypoints, while FuncBridge~ funcbridge predicts 2D functional keypoint trajectories to guide action generation. However, functional points alone may not capture more complex manipulation characteristics. Other work, such as MimicFunc~ mimicfunc , automatically extracts keypoints and constructs function frames for cross-tool transfer. Its affordance schema and frame-construction rules are predefined, however, so adaptation remains organized around interactions expressible within that abstraction rather than autonomously determining which functional features a task requires. MAGIC~ magic matches DINOv2 visual features and local curvature to transfer a demonstrated contact strategy, with physical simulation checking candidate motions. Its candidate generation relies on visual--geometric analogies and struggles with substantially different tools. Other work uses simulation environments to discover and validate reliable tool geometries, including GeT-USE~ getuse and ToolAnalogy~ toolanalogy , thereby improving the ability to select suitable tools. Vision-language-action models. VLAs learn observation-conditioned manipulation from multimodal pretraining and robot demonstrations. Representative models include OpenVLA~ openvla , the flow-matching policy ~ pi0 , and ~ pi05 . However, their manipulation knowledge remains dependent on the behaviors and interactions covered by training data. Unfamiliar tool geometries and contact patterns can expose gaps in this coverage, limiting cross-tool generalization. Hierarchical architectures decouple high-level task-related information from low-level policies, allowing task reasoning and action control to be modeled separately. Hi Robot uses language subgoals and HAMSTER uses 2D paths; these intermediate interfaces guide low-level execution with task goals or spatial plans~ hirobot,hamster,steerable . Existing work also adds functional guidance to VLAs and related visuomotor policies, grounding task intent in spatial interaction structure. RT-Affordance~ rtaffordance uses key-stage end-effector poses, FuncBridge~ funcbridge predicts functional keypoint trajectories, and AFI~ afi uses 3D affordance fields to guide waypoints and select trajectories. These representations provide explicit cues about where and how to interact, connecting semantic goals to geometrically grounded action generation. Embodied agents. Embodied agents use general knowledge to analyze tool functions and formulate execution strategies. ReKep~ rekep generates relational keypoint constraints, and ToolAnalogy~ toolanalogy proposes functional features. Meanwhile, agentic real-to-sim systems, such as WorldMirror and SceneRig, reconstruct interactive environments for trajectory replay and policy testing~ worldmirror,scenerig,agenticrsr , allowing agents to test their understanding of manipulation through interaction. For reusable skill development, ASPIRE~ aspire uses execution feedback to repair control programs and distill reusable skills. applies real-to-sim interaction testing and reusable skill development to tool adaptation. The agent autonomously identifies task-relevant functional regions and determines their key geometric features, then refines these features and extraction skills through simulation feedback to guide VLA execution with unseen tools. title: CauSyncVLA: Causal Latent World Modeling for Asynchronous Robot Control
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.

On LIBERO-10, reaches 93.8 success at inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness. Introduction Vision--Language--Action (VLA) policies transfer pretrained multimodal knowledge to robotic manipulation~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024 . They pair foundation backbones with generative action heads to synthesize continuous motion~ chi2023diffusion,black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . During physical deployment, however, the environment does not pause for model inference. Approaching, grasping, and placing continuously alter the robot--scene configuration and demand timely closed-loop decisions grounded in the evolving physical state. Meeting this requirement is difficult because heavy visual encoding cannot match the rate of fast physical execution, stalling synchronous closed-loop feedback. Action chunking~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion and asynchronous execution~ black2025rtc,shukor2025smolvla amortize this latency by overlapping inference with ongoing motion, yet leave perception and action temporally misaligned because replaying open-loop tails or stitching boundaries keeps intermediate queries conditioned on delayed perceptual memory when contacts shift mid-chunk. Existing methods address stitching or latent extrapolation~ black2025rtc,liu2026latentbridge,yang2026eaglevla , motivating a common execution reference for perceptual conditioning and action refinement. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser , asynchronous control must reconcile reactivity, perceptual freshness, and trajectory continuity across mismatched sensing and control timescales. To resolve this misalignment, we observe that actual robot execution supplies a shared temporal reference to align perception and action. Observed state transitions and applied commands record physical evolution since the latest visual frame, while the unexecuted tail of the preceding plan provides a structured motion prior. Rather than predicting pixels or physical states independently of control, we formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction under one physical clock, updating prefix key--value (KV) memory from execution history before refining remaining actions. We instantiate this principle in , an asynchronous dual-system controller~ kahneman2011thinking . A slow visual stream periodically publishes KV memory anchors from observed images, while a fast control stream predicts current perceptual memory and refines subsequent actions. Specifically, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current KV memory from the latest delayed anchor and executed state--action history under action-sensitive distillation. Conditioned on this predicted memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon to the current step and refines it in one flow step. Training only the lightweight predictor keeps the backbone and action expert frozen, retaining pretrained competence while supporting rapid closed-loop replanning between visual updates. On LIBERO-10, raises task success from 91.2 to 93.8 over the ten-step synchronous policy while delivering higher model replanning capacity on a shared GPU. Ablations, perturbation tests, and physical trials isolate the complementary roles of causal perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction. Our principal technical contributions are organized around three axes. =1.0pt =0pt Execution-grounded asynchronous control. We formulate asynchronous control as coupled perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction, evaluating execution-aligned replanning across simulation and physical trials, reducing feedback latency with frozen VLAs. We propagate delayed KV anchors along realized state--action history in latent prefix space, supervising residual updates via action-sensitive distillation, which recovers control-relevant perceptual conditioning. title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose , a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, reaches 76.4 and 83.3 average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8 , reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3 , and runs 1.66 faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0 average success over three tasks, against 52.0 for the 16-bit model and 30.0 higher than QuaRot. Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) jointly predict how a scene will evolve and how to act~ yuan2026fastwam,kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero . Trained together with a video generator, they condition their actions on a predicted future and inherit the visual priors of large video backbones, and also their size. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam has 6B parameters, and its BF16 weights alone occupy 12\,GB of the 16\,GB that an onboard computer such as the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX shares with the rest of the robot stack. Post-training quantization removes most of this cost without retraining: a fully 4-bit pipeline stores the weights, the activations and the key--value caches of attention at 4 bits (W4A4KV4)~ ashkboos2024quarot,liu2025spinquant . These savings matter only if the quantized policy still acts reliably in closed loop. Existing quantizers, whether built for language and diffusion models~ xiao2023smoothquant,ashkboos2024quarot,liu2025spinquant,frantar2023gptq,zhao2025viditq,li2025svdquant or recently for WAMs~ zhou2026quantwams,akbari2026qwam,wang2026steerquant , preserve each layer's output or the final action one denoising step at a time; none protects the predicted future on which the action depends, or the caches through which it is read at every denoising step. We find that this omission is costly: existing quantizers fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future, and the loss reaches the action. We call reader the part of a WAM that maps the predicted future to the action, and ask what a 4-bit WAM still loses once its action pathway is protected. Three observations on Fast-WAM answer it ( ). First, protecting the action is not enough: restoring the predicted future to full precision removes 71.2 of the remaining action error ( ). Second, the future is damaged where it is written, and most by errors that are read many times: an error frozen in a weight, a cache or an unchanging token damages the future two to three times more than an error of the same energy that is redrawn at each denoising step. Third, the reader depends on a narrow part of the future, stable in location but not in direction: the tokens it depends on agree across contexts while the directions do not. A 4-bit WAM must therefore treat the predicted future, as the reader sees it, as a quantization target in its own right. Building on this diagnosis, we propose , a latent-aware quantization framework for W4A4KV4 world action models ( ). estimates a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and assigns every source of rounding error a read count, the number of denoising steps over which one realization of the error is read, so that errors frozen in caches and unchanging tokens are weighted by their accumulated effect. With both, the allocation of precision over activations and caches has a closed-form solution: a single threshold that decides which tokens deserve more precision in the denoising loop and in the cache. Gaze-guided refinement then gives those tokens a second 4-bit pass, and selects them at run time from the attention of the action tokens. The quantized model stores every weight at 4 bits, has no high-precision branch, and needs no training and no recalibration for a new task. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We identify future-latent fidelity as a key quantization target for WAMs: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error of a 4-bit WAM enters through a degraded predicted future, which is damaged most by errors that are written once and read at every denoising step. We propose , a latent-aware quantization framework for W4A4KV4 WAMs. A reader metric and a read count give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution, and gaze-guided refinement protects the tokens the reader depends on with a second 4-bit pass. We evaluate on two WAMs in simulation and on a real AgileX PiPER arm. On LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus , it reaches 76.4 average success on Fast-WAM, within 1.2 points of BF16 and 3.4 points above the strongest baseline with 16-bit caches, and 83.3 on Cosmos-Policy (BF16: 83.5 ), while compressing the model by 3.8 . On three real-world tasks, it reaches an average success of 47.0 (BF16: 52.0 ), compared with 17.0 for QuaRot. Related Work sec:related action models. World action models train a video generator jointly with an action model and condition actions on a predicted future~ yuan2026fastwam,kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero , which extends vision-language-action policies~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 with the visual priors, and the size, of video backbones. -training quantization. Second-order rounding compensates the error of each layer with the inverse Hessian of a layer-wise reconstruction objective~ frantar2022obc,frantar2023gptq , and activation-aware scaling~ xiao2023smoothquant,lin2024awq and rotations~ ashkboos2024quarot,liu2025spinquant,chen2026prismquant remove activation outliers, which brings language models to 4-bit weights, activations and key--value caches. Mixed-precision methods allocate bit widths across layers~ wang2019haq,malinovskii2025higgs , and GuidedQuant weights the layer objective with gradients of the end loss~ kim2025guidedquant . For diffusion and video generators, post-training methods correct errors that accumulate over the denoising loop~ he2023ptqd , handle timestep-dependent activations~ zhao2025viditq and absorb outliers into a 16-bit low-rank branch~ li2025svdquant ; quantization-aware training reaches 4 bits and below for these generators~ huang2026qvgen,li2026dsaquant and for vision-language models~ chen2026grace . Cache quantizers compress the key--value caches of video-language models~ tao2025vidkv,tao2026windowquant and of video generators and world models~ xi2026qvg,zhao2026quantwm , down to 2 bits and below. These methods preserve layer outputs or generation quality; builds on rotation and second-order rounding, and changes what the quantizer preserves: the predicted future as the reader sees it. of robot policies and WAMs. QuantVLA and BitVLA compress vision-language-action policies with calibrated scales and 1-bit weights~ zhang2026quantvla,wang2025bitvla . For WAMs, QuantWAMs~ zhou2026quantwams , Q-WAM~ akbari2026qwam and SteerQuant~ wang2026steerquant decide which channels, activation directions, token streams and denoising steps to protect by their impact on the action, and PreDE predicts the task degradation of a quantization configuration from offline action deviations~ xu2026prede . They measure sensitivity to the final action or the training loss, one denoising step at a time. instead targets the predicted future that the action is read from, counts how often each rounding error is read, and quantizes the caches. -level precision. Squat keeps the tokens with the highest attention at 8 bits~ shen2024squat , STaMP concentrates the activation energy in a few tokens that receive higher precision~ federici2026stamp , SemanticDialect re-quantizes the residual of salient tokens in video diffusion transformers~ jang2026semanticdialect , and ZipCache assigns cache precision by token saliency~ he2024zipcache . In all of these token-level quantizers, a model's own attention or activation energy decides which tokens matter. In a WAM, the predicted future is consumed by a different part of the model, and lets this reader decide: tokens are selected by their effect on the action and tracked at run time through the attention of the action tokens. Motivation sec:motivation Quantizing a WAM sec:prelim action models. A WAM maps an observation and an instruction to a predicted future latent and an action chunk , and the action is conditioned on : where collects all weights and both are produced by iterative denoising over steps. We call the reader, the computation that turns the predicted future into an action; it is well defined whether and are generated one after the other or denoised jointly ( ). We write for the outputs of the full-precision model and for those of a quantized one. 4-bit quantization. A -bit quantizer maps a tensor onto a scaled integer grid, , with one scale per group of entries. Weights are quantized once offline and activations per token at run time, so that a linear layer with weight and input computes . Post-training quantizers choose the rounded weight by minimizing the layer-wise reconstruction error , where collects the layer inputs on calibration data~ frantar2023gptq . A WAM also caches keys and values: tokens that are computed once per control step, such as those of the observation or of the finished future, are read by attention at every denoising step that follows, and W4A4KV4 stores their keys and values at 4 bits as well~ ashkboos2024quarot,liu2025spinquant . and frozen errors. Rounding errors differ in how they recur over the denoising steps. An error is fresh if every step draws a new realization, as for the activations of tokens that are being denoised. It is frozen if one realization is reused at every step, as for a weight, a cached key or value, or a token that does not change across steps. and the future share. A rounding error can change the action directly, or by degrading the predicted future on which the action is conditioned. We measure the second path with the future share the fraction of the action error that disappears when the quantized reader is given the full-precision future.
