title: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Code and checkpoints: https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role.
  However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full
  history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past
  experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that
  decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native
  video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this
  inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets
  the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation
  across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena,
  surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared
  methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above
  the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and
  https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate ActMem on simulated memory benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks to answer four questions: (1) How does ActMem compare with existing VLA policies on memory-dependent manipulation benchmarks? (2) Can it handle different forms of historical dependence that require knowing task progress beyond the current observation? (3) Where do its gains come from: the long interaction history, Latent Memory CoT, or Perception Attention? (4) Does conditioning on a long history remain practical at inference time? To answer these questions, we evaluate ActMem on RoboMemArena and MIKASA-Robo, run real-world experiments covering exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory, and conduct controlled ablations and diagnostic analyses on RoboMemArena, together with a latency study under increasing history length. Experimental Setup sec:setup . We evaluate ActMem on two memory-dependent simulation benchmarks and four real-world manipulation tasks. RoboMemArena~ robomemarena comprises 26 tasks in four categories (transferring, occlusion, counting, and sequence execution), in all of which the correct action depends on events that are no longer visible in the current observation. MIKASA-Robo~ mikasa evaluates history-dependent manipulation on five tasks: ShellGame, Intercept, and RememberColor-3/5/9 (RC-3/5/9). Following each benchmark's protocol, we run 51 trials per task on RoboMemArena and 100 trials per task on MIKASA-Robo, and evaluate a single trained model per benchmark. On RoboMemArena we report task success rate (TSR), the fraction of episodes in which every subtask stage is completed, and completion success rate (CSR), the average fraction of stages completed per episode; on MIKASA-Robo we report the average task success rate. The four real-world tasks span exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory and are described in Sec.~ sec:exp_real . . For simulation, we compare against representative vision-language-action models and memory-augmented policies, reporting numbers from the corresponding publications or our own reproductions. For the real-world experiments, we compare against MemoryVLA~ memoryvla , MEM- ~ mem , and SimpleMemVLA~ simplememvla . Details. ActMem is built upon the pretrained starVLA~ starvla framework, comprising a Qwen3-VL backbone and a flow-matching action expert. We jointly fine-tune the vision-language backbone and action expert, conditioning action generation on history-dependent subtask representations and contextualized visual features through Perception Attention, which is incorporated at layers 3, 7, 11, and 15 of the 16-layer action expert. We follow the optimizer and learning-rate schedule of starVLA. Historical observations are sampled at 1\,fps over 126\,s for RoboMemArena and 20\,fps over 3\,s for MIKASA-Robo. Training is conducted on 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with a global batch size of 64 for 60k iterations, and we evaluate the final checkpoint. During inference, the policy predicts 16-step action chunks using 10 flow-matching integration steps and executes the first 10 actions before replanning. Further model and training hyperparameters are provided in the supplementary material. Memory-Dependent Simulation sec:exp_memory . As shown in Table~ tab:robomemarena , ActMem achieves 71.1 task success rate (TSR) and 80.8 completion success rate (CSR), outperforming SimpleMemVLA by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, respectively. Gains are largest in Occlusion and Sequence (+9.7 and +9.3 TSR over the best baseline), which depend most on earlier interactions. ActMem trails FrameSamp+Modul on Transferring (42.6 vs.\ 63.8 ), which relies more on fine-grained manipulation; we attribute this to visual detail competing with history, a weakness also seen in SimpleMemVLA, where Perception Attention already lifts Transferring from 35.8 to 42.6 . -Robo. ActMem achieves an average success rate of 73.8 on MIKASA-Robo (Table~ tab:mikasa ), surpassing SimpleMemVLA by 2.4 percentage points. Gains are largest on Intercept (85 vs.\ 76 ) and RememberColor-9 (67 vs.\ 62 ), where the action depends on a cue that is no longer visible, while ShellGame remains comparable to SimpleMemVLA (95 vs.\ 97 ). The same pattern appears on RoboMemArena: the advantage is largest when the current observation conceals the information needed to act. Real-Robot Manipulation sec:exp_real We evaluate ActMem on four real-world manipulation tasks spanning three forms of memory dependence: exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory (Fig.~ fig:realworld ). Exogenous-memory tasks require recalling events introduced by external agents: in Cup-and-Block, the robot must identify the cup containing a previously hidden block, while in Scissor Retrieval, it must locate scissors that are no longer visible. Endogenous memory is evaluated through Cabinet Search, where the robot must track previously inspected drawers to avoid redundant searches. Finally, Tissue Counting tests traceless memory, requiring the robot to count completed pulls despite nearly identical observations after each action. -World Results. Each task is evaluated over 40 trials. As shown in Fig.~ fig:realworld , ActMem achieves an average success rate of 68.8 , outperforming SimpleMemVLA (58.8 ) by 10.0 percentage points, MemoryVLA (55.0 ) by 13.8 points, and MEM- (48.8 ) by 20.0 points, and is the best method on all four tasks. ActMem reaches 75 on both Cup-and-Block and Scissor Retrieval, where the required information was introduced by an external agent and is no longer visible, and 65 on Tissue Counting, where the observations after each pull are nearly identical. Performance is lowest on Cabinet Search (60 ), which requires the policy to track the drawers it has already inspected. These results demonstrate that ActMem handles different forms of historical dependence, while tracking self-generated task progress remains the most challenging. Ablation Studies sec:ablation We conduct ablation studies on RoboMemArena to examine whether each design of ActMem is necessary: the long interaction history, the Latent Memory CoT that conveys it, and Perception Attention. All variants, including the full model, are trained for 40k iterations with the same data and schedule and evaluated on the 26 tasks with 10 trials per task, so absolute numbers are lower than in Table~ tab:robomemarena . History. As shown in Table~ tab:ablation , removing historical observations reduces TSR from 52.3 to 17.7 , and keeping only the most recent 10\,s recovers just 31.2 . This indicates that the required information lies far back in the episode and that a short context cannot substitute for the full history. Memory CoT. Given the same history, how it reaches the action expert matters. Conditioning on the text embeddings of the generated subtask alone yields 40.4 TSR, and letting the action expert read all history tokens directly yields 38.8 , both below the 52.3 of Latent Memory CoT. Subtask text is therefore an incomplete memory signal: the action expert does not recover this progress from the raw history. Attention. Removing Perception Attention reduces TSR from 52.3 to 47.7 and CSR from 68.5 to 64.2 . This indicates that subtask-level guidance alone does not capture the visual information useful for continuous action generation. The two conditions are complementary: Memory CoT selects what to do from experience, and Perception Attention supplies the current geometry with which to do it. Analysis sec:analysis Evidence. Fig.~ fig:attnvis visualizes attention over historical frames in a representative RoboMemArena task. At the decision step, ActMem attends most to the frame containing the task-relevant event, although this event is no longer visible in the current observation. Latent Memory CoT Encodes. To test whether Memory CoT carries information beyond its text, we take the counting task Pour wine into the mug twice and extract representations at the end of the first and the second pour for all 100 demonstrations (Fig.~ fig:pca ). The two moments are nearly indistinguishable in current visual features encoded before the history, whose class means have a cosine similarity of 0.99, whereas Memory CoT places them far apart (0.22; Fig.~ fig:pca ). The gap persists (0.25) when the same text ``pour the wine into the mug'' is forced for every sample, so the count is carried by the hidden states, not only by the words of the subtask. In Fig.~ fig:pca , visual features of both moments collapse into a single cluster, whereas Memory CoT splits them into two groups along the count direction. Thus, subtask inference does more than emit text: its hidden states keep a compact record of task progress that the action expert reads directly. Inference Efficiency sec:exp_latency As shown in Fig.~ fig:latency , the per-decision latency of standard inference grows from 0.87\,s to 1.42\,s as the history lengthens from under 30 to over 90 frames, close to that of SimpleMemVLA (0.70\,s to 1.25\,s). Efficient Memory CoT Inference (Sec.~ sec:learning ) reduces it to 0.33--0.52\,s, to faster than standard inference and about to faster than SimpleMemVLA at every history length. The gain comes from exactly reusing the history cache and the previous subtask (Sec.~ sec:learning ), which leaves the output unchanged. Since the history is only appended, the cost of each decision depends mainly on the new chunk rather than on the full history, so efficient latency rises by only 0.19\,s over the history range, versus 0.55\,s for standard inference. -family policies with a fixed-size memory run at 0.08--0.09\,s, so ActMem trades part of this speed for access to the full history.

title: TuringPAI: A Foundation for On-Device Physical AI
summary: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

Left: TensorRT~8.6 FP16 timings with model-specific inputs (not accuracy-matched). Right: On the same TuringPAI-VL backbone, XNRT BF16+INT8 is faster than TensorRT FP32+INT8 (both with QAT). fig:vla_overview Introduction sec:intro Physical AI systems must understand changing environments and translate observations into decisions and actions under real-world computational and latency constraints~ shukor2025smolvla, black2026real, zhang2026turingllm . Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a reusable foundation by connecting visual perception with language instructions and reasoning~ liu2023visual, wang2024qwen2vl, bai2025qwen3vl . Autonomous driving, a mature and practically important application of Physical AI, serves as a major setting for developing and evaluating such models~ team2026xcot, tian2024drivevlm . It requires spatial understanding, reasoning over observations across cameras and time, and timely responses within limited onboard resources. Robotic manipulation presents complementary demands on object geometry, interaction state, and instruction following~ black2024pi0 . Visual inputs in Physical AI applications often consist of high-resolution observations collected across multiple cameras and time steps~ caesar2020nuscenes, khazatsky2024droid . These observations contain substantial redundancy, yet local geometry and small temporal changes can affect downstream actions. VLM pipelines that encode each observation as a dense patch sequence can spend substantial computation on spatially correlated content~ bolya2023tome, shang2025llava . Forwarding separate visual sequences for successive frames further expands the language-model context with overlapping scene information~ huang2025prunevid, shen2026fastvid . Under limited onboard compute and strict latency constraints, this redundancy increases the cost of using rich observation histories. These requirements motivate VLM designs that aggregate local evidence before global modeling and integrate complementary information across spatial scales and time, while retaining the cues needed for downstream action. Architecture alone, however, does not ensure that a VLM learns the physical information required by these tasks. General image--text alignment and instruction learning support broad semantic understanding, but do not necessarily provide explicit supervision for metric geometry or temporal changes. For example, a caption may identify a vehicle ahead without specifying its distance or whether the gap is closing, although both quantities matter for driving decisions. Prior work shows that explicit spatial and temporal training tasks can strengthen the corresponding capabilities of VLMs~ chen2024spatialvlm, ren2024timechat . Architecture and training data thus play complementary roles: the architecture organizes observations efficiently, while the data guide the learning of information relevant to physical interaction. To address these challenges, we present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI built around a shared vision-language foundation. At its core, TuringPAI-VL combines HybridViT-MLQ with a training mixture tailored to Physical AI. TuringPAI-VL provides the pretrained foundation for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied, which adapt it to autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, respectively. HybridViT-MLQ organizes local features, scene context, and observation history into a multi-scale representation of the current observation. HybridViT first uses a convolutional front end to form locally condensed patch tokens, over which the visual Transformer models global relationships. We then introduce Multi-scale Latent Queries (MLQ), a hierarchy of feature-conditioned queries that aggregates visual evidence within the same Transformer. The queries occupy spatial grids at multiple resolutions and share a spatiotemporal positional encoding with patch tokens. For video, one query hierarchy is initialized from the current frame and aggregates evidence from both current and preceding frames. Only the updated query features are passed to the language model. For a fixed query layout, this interface incorporates observation history without increasing the output sequence length. HybridViT thus reduces the sequence length used for visual encoding, while MLQ organizes multi-scale and temporal evidence within a controlled language-model input budget. MLQ can also be adapted to other ViT backbones with compatible feature, positional, and attention interfaces. As an additional deployment benefit, the convolutional front end supports heterogeneous execution on NVIDIA Orin-X hardware~ nvidiaDriveAGXOrin , including DLA and GPU overlap in our implementation. To train TuringPAI-VL, we complement general vision--language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal tasks. Following the data-construction approach of VLM3~ cai2026vlm3 , we use pixel-depth questions and camera-conditioned 3D object localization to supervise distance, position, size, and orientation, providing geometric cues for driving clearance and object placement. Cross-view correspondence and relative camera-pose data support associations across observations, while multi-frame driving and manipulation examples provide signals about motion and state changes. We evaluate TuringPAI-VL on general multimodal benchmarks and spatial and geometric understanding tasks relevant to Physical AI. Driving evaluations of TuringPAI-Drive cover open-loop trajectory prediction and XPeng's in-house simulation. For deployment, we use XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT), our in-house inference runtime that combines mixed-precision execution with hardware-aware optimization, enabling 12~Hz trajectory generation on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC. TuringPAI-Drive is scheduled for rollout to XPeng vehicles equipped with NVIDIA Orin-X as part of the VLA~2.0 system. Beyond driving, TuringPAI-Embodied, initialized from TuringPAI-VL, achieves a 96.8 average success rate across the four LIBERO~ liu2023libero suites. These results support TuringPAI-VL as a shared vision-language foundation for driving and manipulation under practical deployment constraints. Methodology sec:arch TuringPAI-VL is the shared vision-language foundation of the TuringPAI family. Its design centers on three elements: HybridViT, Multi-scale Latent Queries (MLQ), and training data for Physical AI. First, HybridViT combines convolutional aggregation of local image structure with Transformer-based global modeling over condensed patch tokens (Section~ sec:hybridvit ). Second, MLQ aggregates multi-scale spatial features and observation history into a structured visual interface for the language model within the same visual Transformer (Section~ sec:mlq ). Third, we supplement general vision--language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal tasks to develop capabilities relevant to physical interaction (Section~ sec:training-data ). Together, these elements support spatial and temporal understanding while enabling efficient visual processing for downstream Physical AI tasks. Figure~ fig:orinvlm-main-architecture presents the overall architecture, downstream adaptation, and representative training examples. Figure~ fig:mlq-architecture details the MLQ mechanism. HybridViT: Local Aggregation and Global Modeling sec:hybridvit HybridViT combines convolutional local feature extraction with Transformer-based global modeling. The convolutional front end in Figure~ fig:orinvlm-main-architecture (a) aggregates local image content into locally condensed patch tokens. The encoder supports dynamic-resolution inputs by adjusting image height and width to multiples of . The resized image is partitioned into computation regions. With a total spatial stride of along each axis, the convolutional front end produces a feature grid for each region. These regional features are reassembled into a full-image feature map , where and for a resized input of dimensions . We flatten this grid and project its features to the Transformer embedding dimension: Here, and are the CNN and Transformer feature dimensions, respectively. The input projection applies the same linear map from to dimensions to each feature vector. At the same input resolution, a patch-size-16 ViT~ faghri2025mobileclip2, tschannen2025siglip produces tokens. HybridViT therefore supplies one quarter as many patch tokens to the Transformer. The Transformer component follows the mixed-attention design of TuringViT~ wu2026turingvit , combining efficient and standard self-attention. It models relationships across the condensed patch sequence to incorporate global scene context. MLQ operates within this same Transformer, as described next. Multi-scale Latent Queries sec:mlq Backbone reuse and query construction. Multi-scale Latent Queries (MLQ) provide a query-based plug-in that aggregates visual features within a pretrained Transformer. MLQ reuses the backbone's attention and feed-forward weights without adding a separate Transformer stack. It can be incorporated during VLM training without an additional visual pretraining stage. The design is not specific to HybridViT; adaptation to another ViT requires compatible feature, positional, and attention interfaces. In HybridViT-MLQ, multi-scale pooling and linear projection of convolutional features initialize latent query grids at different spatial resolutions, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:mlq-architecture . The grid sizes adapt to the spatial dimensions of the input feature map. The grids are flattened and concatenated in coarse-to-fine order, forming a feature-conditioned query hierarchy spanning global, regional, and local spatial scales. Unified spatiotemporal positioning. We organize video inputs into four-frame observation windows, taking the last frame in each window as the current observation. Each window uses one latent-query hierarchy initialized from the current frame's features. A single image is treated as a one-frame window, with queries initialized from its own features. title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.

It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45 versus 97.5--100 for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies combine visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to perform manipulation tasks~ vaswani2017attention,dosovitskiy2021image,ichter2023do,brohan2023rt1,driess2023palme,jiang2023vima,shridhar2023perceiver,chi2023diffusion,brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer . Because these policies repeatedly use visual feedback to choose actions, a persistent texture can affect observations throughout task execution. Evaluating such attacks therefore requires measuring their effects on closed-loop task completion. Existing texture and patch attacks demonstrate the vulnerability of learned perception and control to visual perturbations~ goodfellow2015explaining,carlini2017towards,madry2018towards,brown2018adversarialpatch,eykholt2018robust,athalye2018synthesizing,karmon2018lavan,thys2019fooling,wang2025exploringadversarialvulnerabilitiesvisionlanguageaction,lu2026robotsobeypatchuniversal . However, optimized patterns can appear conspicuous against their surroundings~ hu2021naturalistic . Such visual contrast can make the attack easier for an observer to notice, exposing the modified object as suspicious and prompting its inspection or removal. This motivates searching for textures that disrupt task execution while remaining visually compatible with the scene. To address this limitation, our key insight is that the structured image distributions learned by diffusion models can guide the search toward natural-looking textures, while rollout feedback identifies candidates that disrupt task execution~ sohldickstein2015deep,ho2020denoisingdiffusionprobabilisticmodels,nichol2021improved,song2021score,rombach2022highresolutionimagesynthesislatent,karras2022elucidating,meng2022sdedit . We use a diffusion prior to generate textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths, allowing the attack carrier to blend into the workspace. Based on this idea, we propose , a diffusion-prior texture attack that searches the latent space of a frozen text-conditioned diffusion model to generate candidate textures. Inspired by the eight harmonic templates used in color harmonization~ cohenor2006color , we use an eight-expert proposal network whose experts learn diverse latent proposals. The network is initialized by matching previously evaluated teacher latents and refined using closed-loop rollout feedback. An appearance filter screens decoded textures before simulation, while replay and random exploration expand the candidate pool. This gradient-free gray-box search uses source-policy attention and behavioral diagnostics while keeping the VLA policy, diffusion model, and renderer frozen. Together, these components turn naturally generated textures into persistent, task-disruptive scene content through closed-loop feedback. We evaluate task disruption and visual compatibility using paired task-completion outcomes, CLIP/DINO feature comparisons, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and a feature detector calibrated on clean scenes~ radford2021learning,caron2021emerging,gretton2012kernel,liang2023advdm,chen2023diffattack,luo2024visual,gong2023figstep,bailey2024imagehijacks . Selected textures are tested on held-out initial states. Across ~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld and OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodels on LIBERO-Object, Spatial, Goal, and Long~ liu2023liberobenchmarkingknowledgetransfer , achieves a macro-averaged clean-conditioned attack success rate ( ) of 57.9 , compared with 44.7 for UPA-RFAS. It attains the highest cASR in all eight policy--suite cells. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce , a diffusion-prior texture attack on closed-loop VLA policies that combines a frozen image generator with a learned multi-expert latent proposal network and rollout feedback. We present an evaluation protocol that assesses task disruption and visual compatibility, with paired task outcomes and testing on initial states excluded from candidate selection. We evaluate the method across two policies and four LIBERO suites, and examine task-isolated selection, cross-suite transfer, scene appearance, and search-budget effects. Related Work sec:related Visual attacks on embodied policies. Adversarial examples and patch attacks established threat models for learned visual systems~ goodfellow2015explaining,carlini2017towards,madry2018towards,brown2018adversarialpatch . Studies of physical transformations and localized perturbations extend these attacks to varied observation conditions and restricted image regions~ eykholt2018robust,athalye2018synthesizing,karmon2018lavan,thys2019fooling,zhang2022adversarialpatchmultiscale . Naturalistic patch generation uses natural-image priors to address visual conspicuousness~ hu2021naturalistic . In VLA robotics, recent work examines physical vulnerabilities, action deviation, representation misalignment, model-agnostic transfer, and universal patches~ cheng2025manipulationfacingthreatsevaluating,wang2025exploringadversarialvulnerabilitiesvisionlanguageaction,xu2025modelagnosticadversarialattackdefense,lu2026robotsobeypatchuniversal . Other attacks target reasoning pathways, visual proprioception, and partial observability~ huang2026traphijackingvlacotreasoning,fu2026vlahijacktransferablepatchattack,wang2026partiallyobservableadversarialpatch . Our focus is the joint evaluation of task disruption and visual compatibility: searches a diffusion-generated texture family and compares the resulting textures with optimized patch baselines under both criteria. Diffusion priors and proposal learning. Denoising, score-based, and latent diffusion models provide structured image generators with controllable sampling trajectories~ sohldickstein2015deep,ho2020denoisingdiffusionprobabilisticmodels,nichol2021improved,song2021score,rombach2022highresolutionimagesynthesislatent,karras2022elucidating,meng2022sdedit . Adversarial research also studies generative models as attack targets and purification defenses~ liang2023advdm,chen2023diffattack . uses a frozen diffusion model to define a texture search space and learns a multi-expert proposal from rollout feedback. This formulation combines a generative image prior with optimization against closed-loop task outcomes. VLA foundations and embodied benchmarks. Transformer attention and vision transformers underpin modern multimodal policies~ vaswani2017attention,dosovitskiy2021image . Embodied models such as RT-1, PaLM-E, VIMA, Perceiver-Actor, and Diffusion Policy connect visual or multimodal observations to robot actions~ brohan2023rt1,driess2023palme,jiang2023vima,shridhar2023perceiver,chi2023diffusion,ichter2023do . LIBERO benchmarks knowledge transfer across manipulation tasks~ liu2023liberobenchmarkingknowledgetransfer . We use its task-completion predicates to evaluate persistent texture attacks. Appearance-aware evaluation. CLIP and DINO provide feature spaces for image comparison~ radford2021learning,caron2021emerging , while MMD summarizes differences between image collections~ gretton2012kernel . Natural-image benchmarks and imperceptible-attack studies provide context for evaluating appearance alongside attack strength~ hendrycks2019benchmarking,chen2023imperceptible,croce2020reliable,hendrycks2021natural . Related visual-generation and image-hijacking work examines how image content can alter model behavior~ luo2024visual,gong2023figstep,bailey2024imagehijacks . We report feature similarity and anomaly-detector flag rates alongside overall task success and failures among paired clean-successful episodes. Diffusion-prior Texture Search sec:method Threat model and objective Let a frozen policy produce actions from observations and a benign instruction . The attacker controls one static texture. The attack uses an ordinary scene object, such as a tablecloth, as its carrier. The generated natural texture blends the carrier into the workspace while persistently influencing the policy's visual observations throughout an episode. The instruction, controller, and task-completion objective remain unchanged. Search uses paired clean/patched behavioral traces and attention-derived diagnostics from the source policy. This gradient-free gray-box search updates proposal-side parameters through rollout rewards while keeping the VLA, diffusion model, and renderer frozen. Once selected, the texture remains fixed on the scene carrier during policy execution. Algorithm~ alg:dmt summarizes the complete search pipeline. Phase I transfers evaluated high-gap latents into the multi-expert proposal family. Phase II alternates candidate generation, appearance screening, closed-loop feedback, and proposal updates; the final texture is selected only after online refinement and then locked for held-out evaluation. For episode , let indicate clean and attacked task success. The attacked task success rate ( ) and clean-conditioned attack success rate are Higher indicates greater disruption of episodes the clean policy solves, while measures overall attacked execution performance. Reporting both metrics distinguishes disruption of clean-successful episodes from overall task performance, which also includes clean-failed episodes that succeed under the changed texture. Text-conditioned multi-expert proposals shows the two-stage learning framework. Its ``Soft Gate'' routes expert proposals, and the appearance filter screens decoded textures. Dashed feedback paths carry rollout rewards to the trainable proposal and optimization modules. The frozen Stable Diffusion 2.1 text encoder supplies 77 token embeddings and a pooled 1024-dimensional end-of-sequence representation. A shared backbone uses LayerNorm and SiLU. Eight independent heads produce 128-dimensional bottlenecks; a text-conditioned decoder maps each into . Its upsampling blocks use token cross-attention and pooled-conditioning modulation. A soft routing network produces expert weights , and a separate score head chooses a preferred proposal with two companion heads for exploration. We compute all latent heads and decode the candidates selected for evaluation. Each initial diffusion latent is projected to a fixed radius, This controls the latent norm near the typical Gaussian radius. The frozen diffusion model maps to a texture using 30 sampling steps and classifier-free guidance 7.5. Search optimizes the initial diffusion latent with fixed reverse-process parameters. title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
summary: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We show that PRIO combines generalizable configuration priors with real-time physical interaction. Pre-trained solely on simulated 4D trajectories and evaluated without per-object training, its predicted spaces capture the deformations of unseen shapes, improve with pre-training scale and transfer zero-shot to real captures ( ), and enable real-time physical responses on meshes, point clouds and 3D Gaussians ( ). Against 4D generation methods, PRIO follows user actions more faithfully in a fraction of their time ( ). We also ablate key designs in ; details of the pre-training data, additional results and comparisons are provided in the supplementary material. Representation Quality sec:exp_statespace A pre-trained configuration space is useful only if it can express how an unseen object deforms. Following CANOR~ canor and NeuROK~ neurok , we test this through inverse kinematics on unseen objects: each method builds an object's representation from its rest shape, and we fit deformed targets within it, measuring Chamfer and distances~ psgn and volumetric IoU. We compare with five learned object representations that span the common alternatives: skeletons with skinning weights, predicted by UniRig~ unirig , Puppeteer~ puppeteer and SkinTokens~ skintokens ; neural skinning fields, predicted by PhysSkin~ physskin ; and the nonlinear latent kinematic space that NeuROK~ neurok predicts with a conditional VAE. PRIO fits the targets most closely on all three metrics ( ): the space predicted from the rest shape alone captures the deformations of objects unseen in pre-training. Skinning-based representations blend the motion of a few handles, which can bend limbs but not express the local deformation of soft regions. NeuROK is trained largely on articulated objects, which explains its weaker fit on these deformable ones; we further compare with it on articulated objects, using the articulated extension of PRIO, in the supplementary material. Effect of Training Data sec:exp_pretrain A pre-trained space should improve as it sees more objects deform. To test this, we pre-train PRIO with the same budget of about 100k steps on nested subsets of the pre-training set, from 266 to 2,142 objects, and evaluate each model on the unseen shapes of , measuring the reconstruction error as the relative distance between the fitted and the observed deformation. The error decreases steadily as the pre-training set grows ( ): more diverse 4D trajectories yield configuration spaces that better express how unseen objects deform. The benefit of pre-training extends to real objects. On Deform360~ deform360 , which captures real-world objects deforming under user interaction, PRIO recovers the captured deformations zero-shot through inverse kinematics, and the error again falls with pre-training scale ( ). In , a robot arm further manipulates these objects with PRIO: ropes bend and plush toys deform in response to its actions. Fast Interaction on Any 3D Input sec:exp_input The same linearity that lets PRIO learn from 4D data also makes interaction fast. The matrices the dynamics require are cached once per object, and each step solves a dense system in a few hundred coordinates before mapping the motion back to the full geometry, without further network inference ( ). On the same apple mesh, simulation setting, and GPU, PRIO runs faster than VBD~ vbd run to convergence (10 iterations per substep), while producing nearly identical surface deformations ( ). Because the configuration map is spatially continuous, it can be evaluated at arbitrary points, so PRIO can also drive point clouds and 3D Gaussians. In , a user steers a robot arm through two objects unseen in pre-training, a ficus represented by 3D Gaussians and flowers represented by point clouds; both bend, sway, and recover in real time as the arm passes through their foliage. PRIO thus delivers real-time physical responses regardless of how the object is represented. Interactive 4D Dynamics Generation sec:exp_4d_generation Because PRIO generates dynamics by physics rather than by a generative model, it should follow user actions faithfully and at low cost. We give all methods the same three objects and actions: a cloth pulled at a corner, a plush toy lifted by its ear, and a flower pulled at its head. PhysDreamer~ physdreamer estimates physical properties from video priors, PhysCtrl~ physctrl generates force-conditioned point trajectories, RealWonder~ realwonder guides video generation with simulation previews, and NeuROK~ neurok evolves the motion in a nonlinear configuration space. A shape and an action do not determine a unique motion, so following PhysCtrl, a VLM scores semantic adherence (SA), physical commonsense (PC), and video quality (VQ) from 1 to 5. We also report the average end-to-end generation time. Details are in the supplementary material. PRIO scores highest and generates fastest ( ). PhysCtrl moves the whole object rigidly, and the other generative baselines respond weakly, tear or collapse. NeuROK follows the actions more closely but is much slower, since its network runs throughout the motion. PRIO follows the action and keeps each object intact. Ablations sec:exp_ablation We ablate the shape tokens ( ) and ( ) in on the same unseen shapes, also reporting a sparse IK error, for which the coordinates are fitted to a sparse set of 256 random surface points and the error is measured over the whole surface. Both designs help the space fill in unobserved regions (details in the supplementary material). Applications Both applications below place objects in a loop with live actions, which requires a configuration space without per-object training and dynamics fast enough to keep up. Interactive Real-World Objects sec:exp_real A photograph of an object becomes an object that responds to touch ( ). PRIO predicts the configuration space of each reconstructed object without per-object training; the workflow is detailed in the supplementary material. None of these objects is in the pre-training set, yet each responds to user actions at interactive rates. Robot Interaction sec:exp_robot Robot manipulation requires deformable objects that respond to contact at the robot's pace, often many at once. Given the robot's motion, PRIO simulates the pillow in (a), with a 145k-triangle surface, at 7.6\,ms per step on a single GPU, and the eight plush toys grasped by a humanoid robot in (b), nearly 1M triangles in total, together at 25\,ms per step on average. At this cost, the pre-trained prior still captures natural responses: folds form around the gripper on the pillow, and the plush toys deform where they are grasped.

title: AGE-Capture: Autonomous, General, and Efficient UAV Capture for High-Fidelity Scene Reconstruction
summary: High-fidelity scene reconstruction with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) requires more than identifying valuable viewpoints: the system must autonomously acquire informative observations and determine task completion under different sensing configurations and limited flight resources. We present AGE-Capture, an autonomous, sensor-adaptive, and efficient active-capture framework for real UAVs. Building on renderability, the framework uses a lightweight online state to evaluate the utility of candidate views, assess task progress, and guide flight execution. By decoupling geometric exploration from reconstruction observations and establishing a unified camera-ray interface, the framework allows different range sensors and RGB camera models to share a reconstruction-driven acquisition pipeline. Reconstruction-frontier viewpoints characterize residual acquisition value for region screening and autonomous termination; dynamics-aware hierarchical planning combined with asynchronous event-driven capture reduces unnecessary inter-region motion, time spent waiting for plans, and repeated observations. Across ten indoor and outdoor simulation scenes, AGE-Capture achieves a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) $3.30$--$3.53\,\mathrm{dB}$ higher than that of the online baselines while using $58.2\%$ of the common mission-time budget on average. Its mean peak GPU memory usage is $91.0\%$--$93.3\%$ lower than that of the same baselines. Experiments with different sensor configurations validate the adaptability of the shared acquisition pipeline, while flights in nine real-world scenes further demonstrate onboard closed-loop operation under practical computational and motion constraints.

[Video] High-fidelity scene reconstruction with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) requires more than identifying valuable viewpoints: the system must autonomously acquire informative observations and determine task completion under different sensing configurations and limited flight resources. We present AGE-Capture, an autonomous, sensor-adaptive, and efficient active-capture framework for real UAVs. Building on renderability, the framework uses a lightweight online state to evaluate the utility of candidate views, assess task progress, and guide flight execution. Reconstruction-frontier viewpoints characterize residual acquisition value for region screening and autonomous termination; dynamics-aware hierarchical planning combined with asynchronous event-driven capture reduces unnecessary inter-region motion, time spent waiting for plans, and repeated observations. Its mean peak GPU memory usage is -- lower than that of the same baselines. Experiments with different sensor configurations validate the adaptability of the shared acquisition pipeline, while flights in nine real-world scenes further demonstrate onboard closed-loop operation under practical computational and motion constraints. Introduction sec:introduction Neural rendering and Gaussian Splatting have advanced high-fidelity 3D reconstruction and novel-view synthesis~ mildenhall2020nerf,kerbl20233dgaussians . Yet reconstruction quality remains strongly dependent on the spatial and angular coverage of the acquired observations. Active reconstruction addresses this dependence by selecting observation positions and viewing directions that improve the current scene representation under limited acquisition resources. For large-scale real-world scenes, UAVs provide a practical platform because they can reach viewpoints at different elevations and headings (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Existing active-capture methods primarily address where to observe next. Traditional next-best-view (NBV) methods evaluate candidate viewpoints using geometric uncertainty, information gain, coverage, or visibility~ bircher2016receding . More recent approaches estimate the potential value of candidate observations through neural-field uncertainty, radiance-field feedback, or related reconstruction-aware signals, thereby relating observation utility more directly to the reconstruction objective~ lee2022uncertainty,jin2023neunbv,nvf2024 . Identifying valuable candidate viewpoints, however, is only one part of a deployable UAV active-reconstruction system. The system must also accommodate heterogeneous sensing configurations and coordinate acquisition decisions with execution under limited flight resources. Existing methods commonly evaluate reconstruction under a fixed view count or time budget. These limits constrain capture but do not indicate whether further observations would improve the reconstruction. The system must therefore assess residual reconstruction value online and terminate capture when further acquisition is no longer warranted. Renderability-based reconstruction gain provides a state representation suitable for this online decision process. R3CON represents the value of candidate observations through a lightweight renderability state that is decoupled from a particular reconstruction backend, avoiding repeated optimization of a complete neural radiance field during planning~ r3con . Its computation and storage requirements support frequent online queries and updates. We build a closed-loop UAV capture process around this state: heterogeneous RGB observations are converted to a common camera-ray representation and update the state; the state guides region scheduling and local NBV selection; and the UAV acquires the next observation at the selected viewpoint. The main contributions of this work are as follows: A unified active reconstruction architecture for heterogeneous sensing configurations. We decouple geometric sensing from reconstruction observations and construct a common observation interface using camera rays, allowing RGB camera models with calibrated ray mappings to share the same reconstruction-aware active capture pipeline, while the geometric exploration module handles depth-map and LiDAR inputs. A reconstruction-frontier mechanism for autonomous task completion. We define reconstruction-frontier viewpoints at the position level and use seed-based region screening to assess task progress and residual acquisition value, allowing the system to determine whether to continue capture under the defined reconstruction-value threshold. An efficient active capture system under limited flight resources. Hierarchical planning coordinates region scheduling with local view selection. Asynchronous perception, state updates, planning, and execution reduce the time spent waiting for plans. Related Work sec:related-work Viewpoint Utility for Active Reconstruction sec:related-geometric-to-reconstruction-aware Early active perception and NBV planning primarily focused on geometric mapping and exploration of unknown space. Frontier-based methods prioritize the boundary between known and unknown space, whereas information-driven methods rank candidate viewpoints using criteria such as expected entropy reduction, voxel visibility, or surface coverage~ yamauchi1997frontier,bourgault2002information,stachniss2005information,isler2016information,bircher2016receding . These works established the basic active-observation paradigm: estimating the utility of candidate observations from the current scene state and selecting the view with the highest expected return. With high-fidelity scene representations such as neural radiance fields and Gaussian Splatting entering online mapping, the focus has further shifted from geometric coverage to observation value that is more directly associated with final rendering or reconstruction quality. ActiveNeRF and NeurAR use neural-field uncertainty to assess the utility of candidate observations~ activenerf2022,neurar2023 , while FisherRF uses Fisher information to characterize the potential contribution of new observations to radiance-field parameter estimation~ fisherrf2024 . NVF and NARUTO further combine visibility, uncertainty, and target observation quality for active mapping and reconstruction~ nvf2024,naruto2024 . Subsequent Gaussian Splatting methods construct reconstruction-aware gains from Gaussian statistics, rendering feedback, localization--exploration coupling, and multi-level information value to improve geometric and appearance reconstruction quality~ agslam2024,activegs2025,gaussmi2025,activesplat2025,activegamer2025,active3d2026,activepolicy2026 . Motion and Mission Planning sec:related-embodied-mission Beyond candidate-view valuation, active reconstruction must plan feasible motions to reach observation goals and acquire the corresponding measurements. NeurAR integrates uncertainty-driven view selection with online reconstruction, while EVPP combines implicit and volumetric representations with graph-search-based view-path planning~ neurar2023,zeng2023efficient . Other work incorporates frontier exploration into task progression for implicit reconstruction~ zeng2024autonomous . Together, these methods move reconstruction-aware planning beyond candidate-view ranking toward embodied acquisition coupled with motion, paths, and online reconstruction. For large-scale tasks, making an individual viewpoint executable is insufficient; the system must also organize continuous observations and mission progress. TARE combines detailed local planning with sparse global planning~ cao2021tare . Informative UAV path planning combines information value, topology, and path cost~ efficientipp2022 , while kinodynamic exploration incorporates vehicle constraints into target and trajectory evaluation~ mendes2026kinodynamic . TRACE directly optimizes sensor-footprint-aware trajectories in a dynamic information field~ zheng2026trace , extending discrete NBV selection to trajectory-level active reconstruction. Their tasks are commonly bounded by a prescribed view count, path length, time budget, or exploration condition. Requirements for Autonomous UAV Capture sec:related-gap Reconstruction-aware methods determine which observations can improve reconstruction, but their scores are often tied to a particular representation. Embodied planners organize visits to candidate viewpoints, but commonly optimize paths or trajectories under a given sensing setup and mission boundary. Autonomous UAV active reconstruction additionally requires a common reconstruction-oriented state that accepts heterogeneous RGB camera rays and supports observation-value queries, regional task progress, and completion decisions. Planning must also coordinate online state updates with trajectory execution to maintain continuous acquisition. R3CON represents online reconstruction value with a lightweight, explicit renderability state that supports efficient queries and updates~ r3con . We use this state as feedback for closed-loop UAV capture. Method Overview sec:method-overview We formulate active reconstruction as a closed-loop capture process for a UAV. The system centers on a persistent renderability state that summarizes reconstruction support from acquired observations and provides residual observation value for subsequent capture. The active-reconstruction node queries this state to select an executable next-best view (NBV); executing the NBV produces the observation that updates the state and closes the loop. Figure~ fig:method-framework shows the data flow. The exploration module maintains a geometric map, provides candidate positions and motion information, and supports region partitioning. Timestamp-matched RGB--pose observations are represented by world-space camera rays and update the persistent renderability state. During planning, the node queries this state for the gain of candidate positions and directions, and returns an NBV with its region and execution information. The system organizes this loop into observation and planning layers. The sensor-adaptive observation interface maps RGB observations from pinhole, fisheye, and panoramic cameras to a common world-space ray representation for renderability operations. Depth maps and LiDAR provide the geometric information used for free-space reasoning, candidate generation, and motion feasibility. The hierarchical active capture planner organizes decisions from scene-level task management to regional NBV selection and trajectory execution. Based on task progress, global region management selects a region for planning. Within that region, Regional NBV Planning combines renderability gain, free-space reachability, and motion cost to select a position and direction. Continuous event-driven capture registers the target observation time for the selected NBV and matches it to streaming synchronized RGB--pose data; the matched observation updates the persistent state while the next decision is prepared during execution. Renderability Preliminaries sec:preliminaries We adopt R3CON's online renderab

title: Multi-View Relighting with Mergeable Radiance Fields
summary: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.
full_text: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations. Introduction sec:intro Radiance field methods, including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) mildenhall2021nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233d , enable realistic novel-view synthesis, but they bake the illumination present at capture time into the appearance of the scene. Changing that illumination, a process known as relighting, therefore requires additional machinery. Existing relighting methods generally follow two directions. Model-based inverse rendering approaches explicitly estimate scene properties such as geometry, materials, and illumination, and shade them under the new lighting boss2021nerd,engelhardt2024shinobi,zhang2021nerfactor,jin2023tensoir . More recent learning-based approaches use generative models or learned appearance representations to synthesize relit images and construct relightable 3D scenes zhao2024illuminerf,jin2024neural,zhang2025relitlrm,tang2026rogr . These ideas have also been extended to 3D Gaussian Splatting, where lighting is incorporated through precomputed light transport, explicit shading models, or lighting-conditioned neural representations zhang2024prtgaussian,li2025recap,fan2025rng,poirier2024diffusion . Although effective, these methods rely on material and shading models, on representations designed specifically for relighting, or on large generative priors. In this paper, we take a simpler route: we keep the radiance field and its renderer essentially unchanged, and obtain the relit scene by linearly combining network parameters. Our approach combines two well-known ideas. The first is the linearity of light transport with respect to illumination nimeroff1995efficient,debevec2000acquiring : since light contributions add, the image under a target illumination can be approximated by a weighted sum of images under individual basis lights. This holds in linear radiance, when pixel values are proportional to the light reaching the camera, before any tone mapping, sRGB encoding or clipping. The second is model merging singh2020model,ainsworth2022git,stoica2024zipit : under certain conditions, the parameters of neural networks can themselves be combined linearly, and simple weight averaging is effective when the models remain in compatible regions of the loss landscape wortsman2022model . These two forms of linearity do not combine for free. A radiance field is nonlinear in its parameters, so combining the parameters of fields trained under different lights does not, in general, produce the corresponding combination of their images; for independently trained models, we find that it fails entirely. Our key idea is to train parameter combinations of nonlinear appearance networks to reproduce the corresponding combinations of basis-light images. We introduce ``Mergeable Radiance Fields'' (MergeableRF), a framework that trains radiance fields for direct parameter-space merging ( ). MergeableRF takes multi-view images of a scene captured under a set of basis lights ( , with a light stage) and represents the scene with two components. A single illumination-independent radiance field, either a NeRF or a set of 3D Gaussians, stores the geometry and a feature for every scene point or primitive. One small appearance MLP per basis light decodes this feature and the viewing direction into radiance; for 3DGS, these MLPs replace the conventional spherical harmonics (SH) colors. Training jointly updates the shared geometry and features together with the illumination-specific appearance networks. Since the geometry is shared, only the appearance MLPs need to be merged, and two ingredients make this possible. First, for both NeRF and 3DGS, the basis appearance networks start from identical randomly initialized parameters, which keeps them compatible throughout training ilharco2022editing,ortiz2023task . Second, we introduce a merge-aware training strategy: in addition to the usual reconstruction under each basis light, every training step renders random convex combinations of the MLPs and supervises them with the same combinations of the basis-light images. By the linearity of light transport, these are the true images under the mixed lights, so no additional data is needed. To relight the scene under a target environment map, we express that map as a non-negative combination of the basis lights and combine the appearance MLPs with the same coefficients. Instead of evaluating every basis network and blending the results, MergeableRF renders the merged model directly: once the appearance networks are merged, rendering uses the shared geometry and a fixed number of appearance-network evaluations, independent of the number of basis lights. Changing the target illumination requires no optimization of the scene model. We evaluate MergeableRF, with both NeRF and 3DGS, under complex high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps on synthetic objects from the Neural Gaffer benchmark jin2024neural and on real light-stage captures from OLATverse zhou2026olatverse , against relighting methods trained on the same basis-lit images. Our analysis separates the error of the lighting basis, of the fitted model, and of merging. With independently initialized networks, the merged render is 14.6\,dB below the blend of the per-light renders; a shared initialization reduces this gap to 8.5\,dB, and merge-aware training to 1.4\,dB. On the synthetic objects, our NeRF model has the second-highest PSNR among the compared methods, and on real captures our 3DGS model is the most accurate. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We propose MergeableRF, a relighting framework for NeRF and 3DGS that constructs the radiance field for a target illumination by linearly combining the parameters of basis-light appearance networks over a shared scene representation. We introduce merge-aware supervision, which trains linear combinations of appearance-network parameters to reproduce the corresponding combinations of basis-light images, at no additional data cost. We demonstrate multi-view relighting under HDR illumination on synthetic and real objects with both NeRF and 3DGS, and analyze how the lighting basis, the initialization, and the mixture supervision each contribute to the final error. Related work sec:related Relighting from basis illuminations. For a fixed scene, light transport is linear in illumination. Images under new lighting can therefore be synthesized by blending basis-light images in linear radiance~ nimeroff1995efficient,debevec2000acquiring . Precomputed radiance transfer (PRT) encodes this relationship in compact bases~ sloan2023precomputed,ng2003all , while learned transport reduces the observations required for relighting~ xu2018deep,zhang2021neural . Recent Gaussian methods extend relighting to multi-view light-stage captures~ bi2024gs3,saito2024relightable . Relightable NeRFs. NeRV~ srinivasan2021nerv , NeRFactor~ zhang2021nerfactor , and NeRD~ boss2021nerd recover scene properties for physically based relighting. TensoIR~ jin2023tensoir uses tensor factorization to jointly estimate geometry, reflectance, and illumination, with support for shadows and indirect lighting. NeRF-OSR~ rudnev2022nerf addresses outdoor relighting, while NeRF-W~ martin2021nerf captures appearance variation without explicit illumination control. Generative approaches, including IllumiNeRF~ zhao2024illuminerf and Neural Gaffer~ jin2024neural , use diffusion-based relighting to produce observations for reconstruction under a target illumination. Relightable 3DGS. Gaussian inverse rendering extends these ideas through explicit material and shading models~ liang2024gs,gao2024relightable,jiang2024gaussianshader . ReCap~ li2025recap jointly models observations across lighting conditions with shared material properties. SVG-IR~ sun2025svg introduces spatially varying material and normal attributes within each Gaussian, together with physically based indirect lighting. Other approaches learn light transport more directly. PRTGaussian~ zhang2024prtgaussian learns per-Gaussian transfer coefficients from multi-view OLAT captures for environment-map relighting. RNG~ fan2025rng predicts Gaussian radiance conditioned on viewing and lighting directions. OLAT Gaussians~ kuang2024olat uses learned Gaussian features and neural illumination and scattering functions to model appearance under point lights. MergeableRF places illumination dependence in basis appearance networks and combines their parameters according to the target lighting. Model merging. Parameter averaging can combine networks with compatible weights~ wortsman2022model,frankle2020linear . Further work addresses parameter alignment, importance weighting, and conflicts during merging~ singh2020model,ainsworth2022git,matena2022merging,yadav2023ties,stoica2024zipit . Task arithmetic~ ilharco2022editing and tangent-space analyses~ ortiz2023task motivate combinations of adaptations around a shared initialization. Closest to our training, Wortsman~ ~ wortsman2021learning learn simplexes of networks whose every point is accurate on one task. We also supervise random points of a simplex, but each has its own target: the image under the corresponding mixture of basis lights. These findings support our initialization strategy, but parameter combinations do not generally preserve output combinations. We therefore train merged appearance networks to reproduce the corresponding blends of basis-light images, with scene geometry shared across illuminations. Relighting datasets. Relighting datasets cover human subjects~ nestmeyer2020learning,sun2021nelf,sun2020light,zhou2019deep and general objects~ ren2015image,xu2018deep . Object benchmarks include controlled multi-view captures~ bi2020neural,toschi2023relight,liu2023openillumination and natural environment lighting~ kuang2023stanford . Neural Gaffer~ jin2024neural provides synthetic object renderings under diverse HDR environment maps. OLATverse~ zhou2026olatverse provides multi-view captures of real objects under one-light-at-a-time illumination. We evaluate MergeableRF on these two complementary datasets to assess relighting on synthetic scenes and real captures. Method sec:method Overview sec:overview MergeableRF uses a shared scene representation and appearance networks, one per basis light , whose parameters are linearly combined for relighting ( ). For a fixed scene, light transport is linear in the illumination when images are represented in linear radiance, where pixel values are proportional to the light reaching the camera, before tone mapping, gamma encoding

title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
summary: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.
