We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36 success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96 ). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1 . Project page Codebase fig:teaser - - - - [c] + > Introduction sec:introduction Generative robot policies can produce rich, continuous action sequences, but they must do so quickly enough for closed-loop control. Modern vision-language-action (VLA) policies and world-action models (WAMs) commonly use flow matching to transform Gaussian noise into executable action chunks~ black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t,yuan2026fastwam,yang2026lila . Each refinement step requires another network evaluation, creating a trade-off between action quality and control latency. While much effort has gone into reducing sampling steps~ wang2024onedp,prasad2024consistencypolicy,zhang2025flowpolicy , we revisit a more basic question: Most flow-based policies predict the velocity that transports a noisy action toward the data. An alternative is to predict the clean action endpoint directly. Although these two predictions are analytically interchangeable along a linear noise-to-data path~ lipman2023flowmatching,liu2023rectifiedflow,albergo2023interpolants , they pose different learning problems. Endpoint prediction seeks a structured action, whereas velocity prediction must also account for the injected noise. Moreover, generation itself changes character over time: the model first needs to recover an action from heavy noise, then make increasingly precise corrections as the sample approaches a valid trajectory. There is little reason to expect one prediction target to be equally effective at both stages, from early recovery to final refinement. We investigate this question by comparing three objectives: velocity prediction (V), direct endpoint prediction (X), and endpoint prediction with a velocity-weighted loss (X--V), as explored in action-manifold learning~ yang2026abot,xiao2026multiviewaml . Our study covers three policy architectures---StarVLA, FastWAM, and LiLa-WAM~ starvla2026,yuan2026fastwam,yang2026lila ---on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0~ liu2023libero,fei25libero-plus,chen2025robotwin . Within each policy, we keep the architecture, training data, and update budget fixed while varying inference from one to sixteen network evaluations. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V performs particularly well with one or two evaluations, while V benefits substantially from additional steps. Direct X, in contrast, improves little as the budget grows. The best prediction objective therefore depends not only on the policy, but also on how many refinement steps it can afford. Why does this ranking change? We examine the structure of the targets and the behavior of their predictions along the noise-to-action path. Clean action chunks have far more concentrated sample covariance spectra than velocity targets or Gaussian noise. At high noise, endpoint predictions remain substantially more stable across different noise initializations. Near a clean action, velocity-based updates produce lower recovery error: they correct the current estimate rather than predicting the entire action again. These results point to a natural division of labor ( ): Guided by this finding, we introduce UniVEP (Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction). UniVEP trains both prediction modes within a shared action network, using a consistency objective to align the clean actions implied by each mode. A velocity-weighted endpoint loss further strengthens endpoint supervision. During sampling, UniVEP first predicts endpoints at high noise and then switches to velocity prediction for low-noise refinement. Each step evaluates only the selected mode, retaining the inference cost of a single-target policy. Joint training also strengthens the endpoint predictor, allowing the policy to generate effective action~chunks~with~a~single~network~evaluation. The resulting gains extend across simulated and real-robot manipulation. On RoboTwin Clean, UniVEP with StarVLA achieves 61.36 success in one evaluation, exceeding the strongest single-target baseline at sixteen evaluations (59.96 ). On LiLa-WAM, two evaluations achieve 85.96 success, surpassing the best sixteen-step single-target result (82.60 ) while cutting action-generation latency by 77.1 . On three real dual-arm tasks, mean success increases from 49.33 to 58.67 . Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,nosep,topsep=2pt] Comprehensive comparison of prediction targets. We systematically study V, X, and X--V across multiple VLA and WAM architectures, manipulation benchmarks, and inference budgets, revealing distinct performance trends as the sampling-step budget changes. Understanding their complementary strengths. Through action-space statistics and noise-conditioned prediction probes, we find that endpoint prediction is more stable at high noise, whereas velocity prediction is more effective for near-clean refinement. UniVEP for efficient robot manipulation. We unify endpoint and velocity prediction through joint supervision and noise-dependent switching. Across the policies we evaluate, UniVEP achieves strong manipulation performance with one or two network evaluations. At the same number of sampling steps, it matches Related Work sec:related_work Prediction targets in generative models sec:rw_visual_generation Diffusion and flow models predict noise, velocity, or clean data. Although algebraically related, these targets impose different learning objectives on finite networks~ ho2020ddpm,lipman2023flowmatching,karras2022edm,ma2024sit,gagneux2026training,kumar2025loss,kim2026analyzinglearningdynamicslossprediction . Recent studies connect target selection to data structure: JiT favors clean-image prediction~ li2025jit , AsymFlow uses full-rank data and low-rank noise~ chen2026asymflow , and MFlow blends targets along principal directions~ mukhopadhyay2026mflow . The influence of data dimensionality has also been investigated~ jin2026dimension . SC-Flow is the closest methodological precedent~ han2026scflow . It jointly predicts velocity and endpoints within a shared network, enforces consistency between them, and switches from endpoint to velocity updates during sampling. Building on this formulation, UniVEP investigates observation-conditioned robot actions, where prediction quality must translate into closed-loop task success. We systematically examine prediction objectives across inference budgets and noise levels, together with velocity-weighted supervision and its interaction with pretrained action heads. Prediction objectives for robot actions sec:rw_action_manifolds Diffusion policies generate action chunks via iterative denoising~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,reuss2023beso,ze20243d,team2024octo,liu2025rdt , while flow-based policies learn velocity fields~ black2024pi0,braun2024rfmp,bjorck2025gr00t,shukor2025smolvla,pi2025pi05 . World-action models further couple actions with future visual features or video~ yuan2026fastwam,yang2026lila,zhu2025uwm,shen2026videovla,ye2026world,song2026uniwam,liu2026cswam . For dexterous video prediction, DexAC-WM~ yuan2026not preserves dimension-level action structure through per-dimension tokenization. Alternatively, ABot-M0 and multi-view Action Manifold Learning predict clean actions under velocity-space supervision~ yang2026abot,xiao2026multiviewaml , matching our X--V baseline except its bounded weighting. MM-ABC also reports gains from clean-action prediction~ liang2026mmabc . We distinguish prediction targets from their training losses by comparing V, X, and X--V under matched training setups on StarVLA, FastWAM, and LiLa-WAM~ starvla2026,yuan2026fastwam,yang2026lila . Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~ liu2023libero,fei25libero-plus,chen2025robotwin cover different inference budgets, perturbations, and scene randomization. We further investigate how velocity-oriented pretraining influences target selection in world-action models tied to a video backbone. Few-step generative control sec:rw_fast_action Consistency Policy, ManiCM, and FlowPolicy accelerate robot action generation through consistency learning or distillation~ prasad2024consistencypolicy,gao2024manicm,zhang2025flowpolicy . One-Step Diffusion Policy and One-Step Flow Policy pursue single-evaluation control~ wang2024onedp,li2026onestepflow . Much Ado About Noising analyzes intermediate supervision, stochasticity, and iterative computation in generative robot control~ pan2025noising . Rather than distilling a separate student, we study prediction objectives within existing policies, distinguishing gains from joint training at one or two evaluations from those due to endpoint-to-velocity switching at larger budgets on both StarVLA and LiLa-WAM. Prediction Targets sec:prediction_background A Common Noise-to-Action Path sec:targets Let denote a clean action chunk with action steps and dimensions per step. title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
summary: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.

Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast--slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0 relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1 . Introduction sec:intro Determining whether a vehicle ran a red light may seem simple, but it requires several linked visual judgments: identifying the vehicle and traffic signal, locating the stop line, tracking the vehicle, and checking whether it crossed while the signal was red. An error in any step can change the final answer. Recent studies~ zhou2025tumtraf,parikh2025roadsocial, guan2026roadscenevqa,wei2025driveqa,ma2026drivecombo show that traffic understanding requires both fine-grained perception and reasoning over spatial relationships, temporal events, and traffic rules. Beyond recognizing objects, an agent must decide what evidence to collect, which tools to use, and whether the evidence supports its answer. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) combine general reasoning with specialized perception tools~ zhang2026vital,lu2026vistagym, chen2026videochatm1,ke2025dwim . Recent work such as TAU-Agent~ lin2026tauagent has brought this approach to traffic understanding. However, using expert tools introduces a series of linked decisions, from planning and expert selection to argument generation and evidence checking. The agent must also recognize failed tool calls and correct earlier decisions when needed. Learning these behaviors is difficult with terminal rewards alone, which provide little guidance on where an interaction succeeds or fails. Recent studies explore finer-grained feedback for agent training~ cheng2026graphgpo,wang2026beacon, zhang2026qevolve , but effective tool collaboration also calls for supervision that reflects each decision's role. Teacher demonstrations can provide successful examples~ li2026guidedopd , yet their value depends on whether they address the student's actual weaknesses. More importantly, real-world traffic monitoring systems demand timely responses, while many traffic questions share reusable tool-use patterns. However, their target objects, arguments, and evidence dependencies may differ. For example, two red-light questions may follow the same detection and tracking steps but involve different vehicles and traffic signals. Reusing a workflow therefore requires adapting its inputs rather than copying past arguments. Moreover, the agent must decide which workflows are worth reusing and updating. Recent work on agent memory and experience ~ jiang2026xskill,feng2026expweaver, cai2026memopilot motivates learning from past interactions, but efficient reuse also requires simple selection and feedback from actual execution. These challenges suggest a natural division: a slow reasoning path for tasks requiring adaptive tool planning, and a fast execution path for tasks with reusable tool-use patterns. To address these challenges, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning and experience evolution for reliable and efficient generalist--specialist collaboration. Built on a shared VLM policy and frozen expert tools, StarTV-Agent supports complementary slow and fast paths: the former uses ReAct-based orchestration for adaptive reasoning, while the latter directly executes suitable parameterized workflows. Execution feedback further connects the two paths by turning useful tool-use patterns into reusable experience. For policy learning, we introduce Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) and Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL). RSPO combines terminal advantages with process advantages that compare decisions by their roles in the interaction, providing feedback for tool use and error recovery. WDL identifies questions the student struggles with and uses an independent teacher to generate successful tool interactions. Demonstration trajectories are then used to fine-tune the trained policy. Together, RSPO and WDL improve learning from both intermediate feedback and complete examples, strengthening the agent's slow reasoning path. For experience evolution, we propose Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR). It enables the fast path through lightweight hybrid search and parameterized workflow execution. The selected workflow keeps its tool sequence but sets new arguments for the current task. When no suitable workflow exists, the agent uses the slow ReAct-based reasoning path. After execution, the agent updates its workflow memory using our label-free feedback signals based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings. This allows useful execution patterns to be reused and refined over time, reducing the need for repeated planning. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce RSPO and WDL, combining role-sensitive process advantages with targeted teacher demonstrations to improve multi-step tool orchestration. We propose LAWR, connecting slow reasoning with fast workflow execution through task-adaptive reuse and label-free experience evolution. We conduct extensive experiments on three traffic scenario understanding benchmarks, validating the effectiveness and efficiency of StarTV-Agent. Related Work sec:related_work Traffic Scenario Understanding sec:related_traffic_agents Traffic scenario understanding requires more than detecting road objects. It also involves reasoning about their spatial relationships, motion, and traffic rules. Driving benchmarks study scene reasoning, rare events, and traffic-rule knowledge~ sima2024drivelm, chen2025codalm,wei2025driveqa,ma2026drivecombo , while roadside benchmarks focus on traffic events and interactions among road users~ zhou2025tumtraf, parikh2025roadsocial,guan2026roadscenevqa . Recent multimodal benchmarks further include audio and thermal inputs~ xing2025echotraffic, zhang2026trafficvqa . Together, these tasks require agents to combine evidence across objects, frames, and input types rather than relying on single visual observations. Following ReAct~ yao2023react , visual agents combine reasoning with tool use to solve complex tasks. General frameworks such as OctoTools~ lu2026octotools support planning and execution across different tools. Other studies improve visual evidence collection through frame selection and temporal navigation~ zhang2026vital,li2026lenswalk, qiu2026longvideor1,tan2026msjoe,tang2026tspo . Recent methods also explore multi-step tool use, workflow generation, and RL for visual reasoning~ yin2025toolvqa, ke2025dwim,lu2026vistagym,guo2026codevision, chen2026videochatm1,li2026agentflow . Structured visual representations provide another way to support reasoning~ janjua2026perceptionprograms, li2026geoanchor,gao2026motto , while TAU-Agent~ lin2026tauagent applies tool-based collaboration to traffic anomaly understanding. These studies show the value of specialized tools, but effective collaboration also requires knowing when to reason carefully through tool interactions and when familiar tool-use patterns can be reused without repeated planning. Policy Learning and Experience Evolution sec:related_learning_evolution Policy learning. Reinforcement Learning~(RL) has improved planning and tool use in visual agents~ li2026agentflow, zhang2026vital . However, rewards based on final outcomes provide limited guidance for individual decisions in multi-step interactions. Beyond sequence-level methods such as Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO)~ zheng2025gspo , recent studies improve intermediate feedback through state grouping, transition modeling, and milestone-based rewards~ feng2025gigpo,cheng2026graphgpo, wang2026beacon . Others explore process supervision, step-level optimization, and tool-based reward models~ guo2026codevision,chen2026videochatm1, zhang2026qevolve,liu2026mlagent,ding2026armthinker,gao2026sapo . Teacher guidance and experience-based learning provide additional ways to train agents ~ zhang2026earlyexperience,li2026guidedopd,huang2026calibrl . In generalist--specialist collaboration, errors in expert selection, tool arguments, or evidence checking can lead to the same wrong answer, making it difficult to identify which decisions need improvement. Moreover, process feedback alone may not teach the agent how to solve tasks beyond its current ability. To strengthen the slow reasoning path, StarTV-Agent combines RSPO for role-sensitive process feedback with WDL for targeted demonstrations on difficult tasks. Experience evolution. Prior work shows that agents can improve their decisions by learning from past interactions~ shinn2023reflexion, zhao2024expel,wu2026evolver . Recent methods retrieve and update stored experience~ feng2026expweaver,cai2026memopilot or turn past executions into reusable procedures~ mi2026skillpro,shao2026nsi,wei2026evoc2f . FlowEvo~ ren2026flowevo distills successful workflows into skills that can be executed directly or used to guide later planning. Multimodal agents also learn reusable tools and skills from visual experience~ huang2026meta,jiang2026xskill . In traffic scenario understanding, similar questions can concern different road users or require different visual evidence. A past workflow may therefore miss evidence needed for the current question, while planning from scratch for every question adds unnecessary cost. LAWR addresses this trade-off by reusing workflows that fit the current task and using adaptive planning for the remaining tasks. Execution feedback guides which workflows to reuse or update over time. Methodology sec:method Framework Overview sec:method_overview Given a traffic input (images or video frames) and a question , StarTV-Agent uses a vision-language policy to coordinate frozen domain-specific experts , including detection, segmentation, and attribute recognition (Appendix~ app:tool_inventory ). As shown in Fig.~ fig:framework , the framework combines ReAct-based tool orchestration, policy learning, and experience evolution to support complementary slow and fast execution paths. Detailed prompts for StarTV-Agent are provided in Appendix~ app:training_prompts . (A) ReAct-based Tool Orchestration. The slow path uses ReAct-based tool orchestration~ yao2023react for adaptive planning and error recovery. The policy makes decisions based on the current state and decision role: where is the interaction history, stores the collected evidence, and is the remaining budget. The role takes five values: Planner (initial task planning), Tool Selector (expert tool selection and sub-goal decision), Executor (tool argument and resource-reference generation), Verifier (continuation decision), and Summary (evidence-based answering). title: One View, One Action: Spatially Generalizable VLAs through Observation-Aligned Experts and Cross Graph Consistency
summary: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $π_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.

These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1 and 85.7 on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from 's 28.3 to 58.3 across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transfer visual and semantic knowledge from large-scale pretrained vision-language models to robotic control, achieving substantial progress in language-conditioned manipulation~ brohan2023rt, GR00T2025Johan, intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, kim2024openvla, pi0-BlackK-RSS-25, pertsch2025pi0fast,shukor2025smolvla . However, reliable manipulation also requires spatial generalization: the ability to generate appropriate actions across changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. Viewpoint shifts alter the visual appearance of scenes and robot motion~ li2024simpler , whereas variations in the robot’s state may require different motion trajectories to accomplish the same task. Yet existing benchmarks reveal substantial performance degradation under both types of shifts, highlighting the persistent challenge of spatial generalization~ fei25libero-plus,zhang2026world,RADAR2026chen, colosseumv22026Jeremy, colosseum2024Wilbert . Action representation provides a useful perspective on this spatial generalization challenge. The same physical robot motion can have different numerical representations across coordinate frames~ zhang2025-ocvla,zhang2026ocvlaplus, li2026fixedfreecamerascalibrationfree . Figure~ fig:teaser (a) illustrates this for a single end-effector movement: its displacement components differ when expressed in the robot base coordinates and in each camera's coordinates. Yet multi-view VLAs typically combine observations from multiple cameras while receiving action supervision only in the robot base frame~ kim2025finetuning , requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions~ zhang2025-ocvla, jang2026axisguide . Consequently, the learned correspondence may become tied to spatial configurations encountered during training, limiting generalization to unseen camera viewpoints and robot initial states~ pmlr-v305-xing25a, tang2026movingeyeenhancingvla, gerigk2026listeningeasierscrubbingvisual . Prior work has explored camera-frame action prediction~ zhang2025-ocvla,li2026fixedfreecamerascalibrationfree and explicit camera-geometry conditioning~ jiang2026viewinvariant to improve this spatial correspondence. These studies highlight the importance of reference-frame choice and camera geometry in action learning. This motivates jointly leveraging action supervision from all available views to improve the spatial generalization of the base-frame policy. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (b), we introduce camera-frame action supervision for each view while retaining the original base-frame supervision. We introduce One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), a framework for learning observation-aligned actions. Its organizing principle is to predict actions expressed in the corresponding camera frame for each view. Specifically, we transform demonstration actions and robot states into each camera frame using known coordinate transformations. For each view, the model predicts actions in the corresponding frame, conditioned on the associated image and robot state expressed in that frame. In this way, the same physical motion provides diverse, observation-aligned action supervision across views, allowing each view to contribute to learning the base-frame policy not only through visual observations but also through its corresponding action prediction task. This encourages the policy to rely less on observation--action correspondences specific to the training configurations. We instantiate OVOA-VLA with a Mixture of Transformers~ liang2024mixture , comprising a view-specific action expert for each input view and a base-frame expert. Each view-specific expert directly attends to visual tokens from its corresponding view, receives robot state expressed in that camera frame, and predicts actions in the same frame. The base expert uses all visual inputs and the base-frame robot state, while retaining the original base-frame action supervision. We jointly train these experts under two complementary directed attention graphs. In the base-to-reference graph, the view-specific experts attend to action features from the base expert; in the reference-to-base graph, the base expert attends to action features from the view-specific experts. During training, we perform a forward pass under each graph for the same sample, with both passes sharing model parameters and receiving demonstrated-action supervision. Since both base-frame predictions correspond to the same action target, we introduce Cross Graph Consistency (CGC) to encourage agreement between them. Our model supports two inference modes: full inference uses the reference-to-base graph, while base-only inference uses the base-to-reference graph, where the base expert does not attend to the view-specific experts and thus permits their removal. OVOA-VLA demonstrates strong performance across multiple simulation benchmarks~ liu2023libero,fei25libero-plus,mandlekar2023mimicgen,Zhang_2025_ICCV . Full inference achieves average success rates of 98.7 and 88.1 on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves success rates from 66.2 to 75.4 under camera viewpoint perturbations and from 67.2 to 88.4 under robot initialization perturbations, compared with . Base-only inference achieves 85.7 on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating that the gains persist without view-specific experts. In real-world evaluations on a Franka Research 3 robot, base-only inference outperforms by 5.0 percentage points in average success rate across six in-distribution tasks and raises the average success rate from 28.3 to 58.3 across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts. Our main contributions are as follows: Observation-aligned action learning. We introduce OVOA-VLA, which jointly learns camera-frame actions from diverse, observation-aligned supervision derived from the same demonstration, improving base-frame policy generalization. Complementary expert training. We design two complementary directed attention graphs to model both interaction directions between the base and view-specific experts, with CGC encouraging consistent base-frame predictions across graphs for the same sample. Two inference modes. Our model supports full inference with the reference-to-base graph and base-only inference with the base-to-reference graph, where the base expert is independent of the view-specific experts. Experimental validation. Experiments across four simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization shifts. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language models to robotic control by training on large-scale robot demonstrations for direct action prediction~ pertsch2025pi0fast,kim2024openvla,brohan2023rt,pi0-BlackK-RSS-25 . These models have demonstrated strong performance in language-conditioned manipulation and generalization across objects, scenes, and robot embodiments~ o2024open,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025pi0fast . A major design choice in VLAs lies in how actions are encoded and generated, ranging from autoregressive prediction of discretized action tokens~ kim2024openvla,brohan2023rt,pertsch2025pi0fast to continuous action generation with diffusion~ li2024cogact or flow-matching objectives~ pi0-BlackK-RSS-25 . Another important consideration is the reference frame in which actions are expressed. Many VLAs predict joint-space actions or Cartesian actions expressed in robot-base or world frames rather than the input camera frames~ zhang2025-ocvla , leaving the geometric correspondence between camera-centered visual observations and action targets to be learned implicitly. Spatial Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models Existing approaches to spatial generalization can be broadly grouped by their focus on observations, spatial perception, or action prediction. VISTA augments demonstrations with synthesized camera views, while Cai et al. study multi-view demonstrations and generate additional views using RoboNVS~ tian2024view,cai2026viewpointgeneralizationmultiviewdemonstrations . AnyCamVLA instead adapts test-time observations toward the training camera configuration without policy retraining~ heo2026anycamvla . For spatial perception, Spatial Forcing aligns visual features with pretrained 3D representations, QDepth-VLA introduces quantized depth prediction as auxiliary supervision, and ActiveVLA actively selects viewpoints and zooms into critical regions~ li2025spatialforcingimplicitspatial,li2026qdepthvlaquantizeddepthprediction,liu2026activevla . For action prediction, OC-VLA predicts camera-frame actions using camera extrinsics, whereas CamVLA jointly predicts camera-frame actions and hand-eye transformations for calibration-free control~ zhang2025-ocvla,li2026fixedfreecamerascalibrationfree . OC-VLA++ introduces geometry-guided cross-view action equivariance, while Huang et al. enforce consistency between flow velocity predictions from action-equivalent views~ huang2026cross . Qwen-RobotManip further adopts camera-frame EEF deltas with camera positional encoding~ yuan2026qwen . Our work is most closely related to action-level approaches, introducing observation-aligned action supervision as auxiliary prediction tasks for individual views while retaining the original base-frame action supervision. title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
comment: A two-stage pipeline that teaches VLAs to stop prohibited tasks safely while preserving permitted skills
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

Code is available at franciscoliu/SAFI . Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,qu2025spatialvla , building on robot demonstration learning~ brohan2023rt1 and multimodal task grounding~ driess2023palme,jiang2023vima . Generalist policies extend these capabilities across robot platforms and unfamiliar environments~ ghosh2024octo,black2025pi0,black2025pi05 , while action-sequence prediction and efficient fine-tuning improve manipulation performance~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,kim2025oft, cui2026learning . As these policies acquire more skills, deployment also requires control over which learned behaviors remain appropriate to execute. This requirement becomes concrete when context makes an otherwise feasible action hazardous. Risk can emerge as a multimodal interaction develops~ liu2026mtmcs , and changed semantic conditions can similarly make successful robot execution unsafe~ chen2026hazardarena . VLAs may also act without meaningful instructions~ jang2026nonstart , while adversarial prompts and poisoned training data can induce harmful or attacker-chosen behaviors~ robey2025robopair,zhou2025goba,xu2025dropvla . Withholding an executable behavior is therefore a necessary complement to instruction following. Planning methods support this control through robot affordances~ ichter2023saycan , uncertainty-based requests for help~ ren2023knowno , and contextual safety specifications~ ravichandran2026roboguard . At the policy level, constrained learning~ zhang2025safevla and refusal demonstrations~ chen2026hazardarena teach safer responses. Selective unlearning offers another route by reducing unwanted behavior while preserving useful capabilities in language models~ yao2024unlearning,liu2024sku and VLAs~ ranjan2026vlaforget,wang2026suppression . Since earlier actions determine later observations in sequential control~ ross2011dagger , evaluation from initial states can leave intermediate states untested when an edited policy stops before reaching them. We examine these states by transferring control from the original policy during execution. This reveals a failure to stop ongoing tasks, as several policies that suppress completion from initial states still complete the prohibited task after takeover. Even when it remains unfinished, unsafe alternative responses arise, including dropping a held bottle (Figure~ fig:task-failure-example ). Dropping and holding both prevent placement but have different physical consequences. These observations, developed in Section~ sec:motivation , motivate the following research question. [colback=gray!5!white,colframe=black!75!black,title style= font= ,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=4pt] How can VLAs stop ongoing prohibited tasks while maintaining an appropriate physical response? Addressing this requires models to suppress prohibited behavior across execution states and produce an alternative response suited to the robot's current state. To meet these requirements, we propose State-Aware Fallback Imitation ( ) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative. Its two-stage design combines Fallback Target Construction, which assigns holding targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, with Joint Policy Adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. By learning an explicit fallback across execution states, enables the robot to stop prohibited tasks with a holding response while preserving its other skills. Our main contributions are as follows. [itemsep=0.1em,topsep=0.3em,leftmargin=*] We identify failures to stop ongoing tasks and unsafe alternative responses in VLAs through an intermediate-state takeover evaluation that jointly examines prohibited execution and physical events. We propose , a two-stage framework that constructs fallback targets from prohibited-task demonstrations and jointly optimizes fallback and retained-task imitation to suppress prohibited behavior and learn an appropriate alternative response while preserving permitted skills. We evaluate across multiple LIBERO task suites and a BadLIBERO backdoor setting. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, achieves low prohibited-task completion rates after takeover with no recorded drops or falls, while preserving performance on retained tasks. Motivations sec:motivation Failure to Stop Ongoing Tasks. Our first motivation is inspired by findings that safety-aligned language models can continue harmful responses when given their opening text, despite normally refusing such requests~ qi2025safety . This raises a related question for VLAs about whether suppressing a prohibited task also prevents its continuation once execution is underway. To examine this, we let the original policy begin a task and then transfer control to a policy trained to suppress it. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation (a), some evaluated policies prevent prohibited stove activation from the initial state, yet activate the stove in nearly all episodes after early takeover and all episodes after mid-task takeover. These results show that suppression from initial states does not reliably prevent continuation of the same prohibited task once execution is underway. Unsafe Alternative Responses. A second challenge is about what a robot does when a forbidden task remains unfinished. Prior work distinguishes execution failure from deliberate refusal, showing why low task success alone is an incomplete safety signal~ chen2026hazardarena . Similarly, for a robot already holding an object, this distinction also involves the consequences of its alternative actions. In the example shown in Figure~ fig:motivation (b), some evaluated policies leave the prohibited task unfinished but drop the held bottle. Both dropping the bottle and keeping it held satisfy the non-completion criterion, although their physical consequences differ. These findings reveal two challenges in enforcing behavioral prohibitions in VLAs: (1) suppression observed from initial states may fail after takeover, and (2) preventing task completion does not ensure an acceptable physical response. Addressing both challenges calls for an approach that suppresses the prohibited behavior across execution states and guides the robot toward an appropriate alternative response. Method sec:method In this section, we present , a two-stage framework for adapting VLAs to behavioral prohibitions. title: FastRoverVLA: Fast Vision-Language-Action Execution for Off-Road Autonomous Driving
summary: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.

Introduction Off-road driving requires motion decisions in environments without fixed lane structure, where surface conditions, visibility, and feasible routes can change within a journey~ rellis3d2020,orfd2022,orad3d2025 . Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language-based reasoning to numerical actions or trajectories~ lmdrive2024,drivelm2024,drivevlm2024,emma2024 . Their outputs must also accommodate the vehicle motion that follows prediction. A scene-conditioned plan can remain relevant across several trajectory updates, while its speed and curvature commands require continued adjustment to the measured state. Coupling every trajectory update to a new prediction repeatedly invokes multimodal inference~ autovla2026,orion2026,drivemoe2026,recogdrive2026 . Efficient encoders and inference pipelines reduce the cost of individual calls~ fastvlm2025,flashdrive2026 , while slow--fast systems combine expensive reasoning with a faster planning path~ drivevlm2024,adadrive2025 . Action-chunk methods address continuity between predicted sequences through temporal aggregation, constrained generation, or learned correction~ act2023,rtc2025,remac2026iclr . These developments leave a specific execution problem at the decoded-action interface: retaining the motion corrections accumulated after a plan has been generated, without another learned planner or access to the generative sampler. A retained plan must account for two changes during reuse: commands are consumed as time advances, and measured motion changes the state to which the remaining commands must be matched. Direct replay advances the sequence without resolving this state mismatch. Realigning the original plan at each update incorporates current motion but discards previous corrections. Carrying the corrected remainder into the next update preserves both the unconsumed actions and the motion corrections retained in them (Fig.~ fig:motivation ). FastRoverVLA decouples visual plan generation from recurrent execution around a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and a deterministic action adapter. The name combines ``Fast'' for reduced VLM inference demand, ``Rover'' for off-road driving, and ``VLA'' for vision-language-action planning. Visual inference refreshes the action buffer, while recurrent execution maintains motion-conditioned trajectories between refreshes. Each update aligns the retained speed--curvature actions with measured ego motion, generates a local trajectory, consumes the current action, and writes the corrected remainder back to the buffer. A bounded rule uses variation within the refreshed plan to assign its reuse budget. The resulting interface separates visual plan generation from motion-conditioned trajectory updates without modifying the backbone or training an auxiliary driving policy. Evaluation on ORAD-3D~ orad3d2025 and RELLIS-3D~ rellis3d2020 separates three questions: whether decoded plans benefit from persistent correction, whether visual initialization adds information beyond motion history, and whether sparse refresh reduces measured inference demand. Shared-prediction controls isolate the maintenance operations; motion-only and matched-image controls examine initialization. Backbone transfer, disjoint-sequence evaluation, and a past-only heading check test the stability of the execution effect. Independent real-request runs measure its computational consequence under serial replay. The main contributions are: FastRoverVLA introduces an action-level execution interface for off-road VLA planning. Maintaining a decoded plan as a recurrent state separates visual prediction from motion adaptation, allowing local trajectory updates between model requests without an additional learned driving policy. The interface combines state alignment, action consumption, and correction write-back to preserve measured-motion updates in the retained plan. A bounded refresh rule assigns reuse budgets from normalized action variation, controlling inference demand through the same decoded-action representation. Controlled replay and independent real-request evaluation cover two datasets and four backbones. In real-request evaluation, Qwen3-VL reduces 3~s FDE by 18.0 and 36.7 relative to every-update execution, while serial request-processing cost falls by factors of 16.6 and 20.8, respectively. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Planning Robotic VLA models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA~ rt2_2023,openvla2025 connect vision-language representations to actions. Driving planners UniAD and VAD~ uniad2023,vad2023 emphasize planning-oriented scene representations. LMDrive, DriveLM, DriveVLM, and EMMA~ lmdrive2024,drivelm2024,drivevlm2024,emma2024 incorporate language instructions, structured understanding, or hierarchical reasoning. AutoVLA, ORION, ReCogDrive, and SimLingo~ autovla2026,orion2026,recogdrive2026,renz2025simlingo connect language or reasoning with numerical driving actions; DriveMoE~ drivemoe2026 specializes vision and action experts. ColaVLA, WAM-Flow, and Latent-CoT-Drive~ colavla2026,wamflow2026,latentcot2026 explore latent reasoning, parallel decoding, or world-model-based planning. Complementary work improves the information and constraints used for planning: FocalAD~ sun2026focalad models decision-critical local interactions, and GraphBEV++~ song2026graphbevplusplus aligns camera--LiDAR features. GraphWorld and DriveFuture~ song2026graphworld,hong2026drivefuture use latent world-state or future-aware conditioning. DriveWorld-VLA~ jia2026driveworldvla integrates world modeling with VLA planning, while MindDrive~ sun2025minddrive evaluates world-model-generated candidates with a VLM. GuideFlow~ liu2026guideflow constrains flow matching, and DIVER~ song2026diver applies reward-guided diffusion to multimodal planning. These advances improve scene-conditioned plan generation, whereas decoded actions must also remain consistent with the changing execution state. FastRoverVLA addresses this execution stage through deterministic measured-motion updates to speed--curvature actions. Its frozen planner supplies new visual plans, while a retained action buffer preserves corrections between predictions, separating plan maintenance from encoder, reasoning, and decoding design. Terrain-Aware Off-Road Planning Off-road planning couples geometric clearance with physical traversability. BADGR and STEP~ badgr2020,step2021 learn navigation affordances or combine stochastic traversability with risk-aware planning. How Does It Feel?, V-STRONG, and RoadRunner~ hdif2023,vstrong2024,roadrunner2024 learn terrain costs or traversability from visual, proprioceptive, or LiDAR observations. TRAIL~ trail2026 supports joint path and speed optimization through continuous terrain representations; terrain-adaptive MPC~ yu2025terrainadaptive incorporates vehicle--terrain interactions and online parameter estimates. OFF-EMMA~ offemma2026 uses visual prompts and self-consistent reasoning for off-road trajectory generation. RELLIS-3D, ORFD, and ORAD-3D~ rellis3d2020,orfd2022,orad3d2025 provide evaluation settings with rugged terrain and varied visibility. These approaches determine where and how to move, but measured vehicle motion can require adjustment without changing the selected route or terrain assessment. FastRoverVLA complements terrain interpretation by updating decoded actions between visual predictions, maintaining motion consistency without requiring new terrain labels or traversability estimates at every update. Efficient and State-Consistent Execution Temporal planners exploit cross-frame information: MomAD~ song2025momad carries trajectory and perception momentum, MomADv2~ song2026momadv2 retains command-consistent memory and uses flow refinement, and MomWorld~ song2026momworld propagates latent future scene states. Efficiency methods improve visual encoding or model size~ fastvlm2025,vldrive2025 , reduce reasoning~ autovla2026,nord2026,cfvla2026 , or accelerate action generation and inference~ linkvla2026,flashdrive2026 . Slow--fast systems combine infrequent VLM planning with trajectory refinement~ drivevlm2024 , learn adaptive activation and fusion~ adadrive2025 , or schedule query, cache, and drop decisions~ asscg2026 . These mechanisms determine when guidance arrives, while action maintenance determines how decoded sequences evolve during execution. ACT~ act2023 ensembles overlapping predictions, and Diffusion Policy~ diffusionpolicy2023 generates receding-horizon action sequences. RTC~ rtc2025 asynchronously generates chunks while preserving committed actions and constraining overlap through inpainting; REMAC~ remac2026iclr learns within-chunk corrections and preserves prefixes across chunks. FastRoverVLA instead deterministically aligns a retained speed--curvature sequence with measured motion and writes corrections back for subsequent updates. Its bounded refresh rule admits new visual plans, while intermediate updates require neither sampler access nor an auxiliary learned planner. The focus is persistent state correction after decoding, distinct from learned temporal planning, query scheduling, or new-chunk generation. title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
summary: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

Introduction sec:intro A practical robot policy must satisfy two competing demands: producing accurate actions from visual observations and language instructions, while operating within the GPU memory and latency constraints of closed-loop control. Recent world action models (WAMs) have made remarkable progress on the former by leveraging pretrained video diffusion models to learn robotic actions, often through jointly training video and action experts~ bi2026motus, kim2026cosmos, li2026causal, ye2026world, yuan2026fast . Drawing on physical priors from web-scale video pretraining, WAMs have achieved competitive performance with vision-language-action models (VLAs) on benchmarks such as LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , often without robot pretraining. However, these gains come at a cost that conflicts with the latter demand. Most current WAMs carry 2B to 14B parameters and repeatedly execute a deep action expert across multiple denoising steps, whereas closed-loop control calls for a small memory footprint, low latency, and the flexibility to trade accuracy for speed without retraining. Two natural approaches address different aspects of this challenge, but neither is sufficient on its own. Sharing weights across depth reduces the number of stored parameters without reducing the sequential computation required at a fixed execution depth. Conversely, reducing the number of sampling steps lowers latency but may degrade action quality when the policy is not trained for fewer steps. A practical compact WAM must therefore answer two questions: how much capacity must it store, and how much computation must it execute to produce useful actions? Answering these questions starts from where a WAM spends its computation. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast showed that a WAM need not generate future video at test time: the benefit of video modeling comes from joint training, allowing the video expert to encode the current observation once while the action expert generates an action chunk over sampling steps. A query therefore requires one video-expert pass and action-expert passes. At batch size one, for comparable block architectures, latency is primarily determined by the number of sequentially executed transformer blocks rather than parameter count alone ( , c). These observations suggest two complementary opportunities: reducing parameter storage through weight sharing and reducing execution cost by allocating computation differently between the two experts. ~For the first question, we turn to looped, or weight-shared, transformers~ bae2025relaxed, dehghani2018universal, geiping2026scaling, giannou2023looped , which reach the depth of a deep network with the parameters of a shallow one by repeatedly applying a shared group of blocks. We bring this idea to world action models with ( a). Each expert stores 12 blocks organized into a 3-block prelude, a 6-block shared core, and a 3-block coda. Repeating the shared core four times recovers the 30-layer depth of its Wan2.1 donor~ wan2025wan . The resulting policy has 0.58B parameters, fewer than an equally deep dense model built from the same donor. Importantly, this makes execution depth a potential test-time choice without changing the stored parameters. ~For the second question, the asymmetric inference costs of the two experts suggest that their execution depths can be controlled independently. Given this asymmetry, allows the two experts to use different loop counts, with late alignment enabling even a single action loop to access the deepest visual features. However, adjustable execution depth does not guarantee reliable inference at reduced depth: without elastic training, reducing the action expert to a single loop drops LIBERO success to 12.3 under our ablation training schedule ( a). To address this, we introduce elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint, , to operate across action-loop counts and sampling steps , while keeping the video expert at full depth. By matching a frozen full-depth teacher starting from the student's own intermediate states, the student learns to correct errors introduced by reduced computation. With only 0.58B parameters and no robot pretraining, is competitive with WAMs about ten times larger ( b). It reaches 91.9 on RoboTwin~2.0, on par with Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast and the best below 2B parameters, 96.1 on LIBERO, 0.5 points below Fast-WAM under the same protocol, and 52.2 on RoboCasa-GR1, ahead of StarVLA~ community2026starvla and DiT4DiT~ ma2026dit4dit , with less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM. A single checkpoint offers nine operating points over a latency range ( c): with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of on all three benchmarks, and with two action loops, it reaches 96.0 on LIBERO in 27.6\,ms per query on one H100, faster than Fast-WAM at its default ten steps. On a real robot arm, matches the success of Fast-WAM with less memory ( ). Our contributions are threefold: , a parameter-efficient two-expert WAM that decouples stored parameters from executed depth through weight-shared recurrence, with independently controlled video and action depths and late alignment. Elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint across action-depth and sampling-step budgets by distilling a frozen full-depth teacher from the student's own intermediate states. A systematic evaluation with dense baselines matched in parameter count or execution depth, controlled ablations, and real-robot experiments, demonstrating the importance of preserving video depth and explicitly training for reduced-depth execution. Related Work sec:related World action models Early video-based policies predicted future frames and inferred actions from them~ du2023learning,wu2024unleashing,hu2024video or diffused video and actions jointly~ Li2025UnifiedVA,zhu2025unified . Recent WAMs adapt large pretrained video diffusion transformers~ wan2025wan : Genie Envisioner~ liao2026genie and Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos fine-tune a video model to produce actions, DreamZero~ ye2026world scales a 14B WAM, Motus~ bi2026motus and LingBot-VA~ li2026causal couple video and action experts in a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT)~ liang2024mixture , DiT4DiT~ ma2026dit4dit conditions an action transformer on intermediate video features, and MemoryWAM~ yang2026memorywam adds persistent memory. Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast showed that the benefit of a WAM comes from video co-training rather than from imagining the future at test time, and several works now cut its cost: Light-WAM~ li2026light freezes a 1.3B video backbone, LiLa-WAM~ yang2026lila and LaWAM~ chen2026lawam predict compact latent dynamics instead of pixels, Efficient-WAM~ li2026efficient and Faster-WAM~ zhao2026faster make future conditioning cheaper, AHA-WAM~ cai2026aha runs video and action models at different rates, GigaWorld-Policy-0.5~ team2026gigaworld and SelfWAM~ pan2026selfwam decode only actions at inference, and Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flash distills LingBot-VA to one denoising step per modality. These works shrink or remove components of the model. keeps the full interface, a generative action expert as deep as the video expert, and instead shares depth across loops, which reduces stored parameters and makes the executed depth a test-time choice. Looped World Models~ Lu2026LoopedWM refine latent states with one shared block, and RD-VLA~ tur2026recurrent iterates a weight-tied action head until convergence. Closest to us, ELT~ goyal2026elt distills intermediate loops from the full loop count for visual generation, and LoopFormer~ jeddi2026loopformer conditions loops on their step size for elastic-depth language modeling. All of these loop a single network, and the elastic ones vary only its depth. loops both experts of a video--action policy with separate loop counts, since the video expert runs once per query and the action expert once per sampler step. Late alignment lets any number of action loops read the last video loop, the shared cores start from a non-looped video model, and action depth is elastic jointly with the sampler steps. Slimmable and once-for-all networks~ Yu2019UniversallySN,Cai2019OnceFA,cai2024flextron train one set of weights for many widths or depths, and early-exit and adaptive-computation models stop early~ Elbayad2019DepthAdaptiveT,Elhoushi2024LayerSkipEE,Graves2016AdaptiveCT,Banino2021PonderNetLT . Both the video and action experts reuse a compact weight-shared transformer core across depth while decoupling their recurrence counts to match their asymmetric inference rates. Elastic self-distillation then trains a single checkpoint, , across joint action-depth and sampling-step budgets. title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.

Introduction sec:intro Long-horizon robot manipulation requires both reliable execution and effective planning. A robot must carry out individual subtasks, assess their outcomes, and determine which goal to pursue next. Visuomotor policies, such as VLAs~ pmlr-v305-black25a and WAMs~ ye2026world , provide action execution capability, but successful long-horizon manipulation also requires coordinating these actions with task-level decisions. Recently, agentic robot control approaches such as GPT-as-Policy~ su2026astra and Harness VLA~ zhang2026harnessvla introduce multimodal reasoning agents to interpret task context, coordinate subtasks, and guide recovery. However, repeated agent calls incur substantial token costs and inference latency~ sun2026call,li2026spotter . These costs accumulate as the agent repeatedly processes visual observations and execution history. When execution must wait for its decisions, agent intervention becomes a bottleneck even during routine behavior that the policy can handle independently. The challenge is therefore to determine when agent intervention is needed and how it should guide execution repair and plan revision, without repeatedly querying the agent itself. To address this challenge, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor integrates stage-aware visual context with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate active subtask progress, predict transition requests, and propose next goals. Progress anomalies, transition requests, and critical contact events in candidate actions selectively trigger agent review. Using shared task and execution context, the agent can authorize continued policy execution, shorten or refine candidate actions, take over subtask execution, or revise the proposed next goal. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions. This design allows routine execution to remain with the policy while directing agent reasoning toward decisions that require further assessment or correction. We evaluate RoC on both simulated and real-world tasks, assessing task success and token consumption. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3 compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Three long-horizon tasks on the SO-ARM101 platform further demonstrate the effectiveness of RoC in real-world settings. To summarize, our main contributions are twofold: We propose RoC, an efficient agentic robot control framework for long-horizon manipulation that couples monitor-triggered agent review with coordinated execution repair and plan revision. We develop an online task-state monitor that serves as a plug-in module to guide selective agent intervention, reducing redundant agent calls and reasoning overhead. Related Work sec:related Long-Horizon Manipulation Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to execute interdependent subtasks while retaining historical observations and interaction outcomes. Policy-based approaches address this by incorporating task history into action generation and subtask selection. MEM~ torne2026memmultiscaleembodiedmemory and MemoryWAM~ yang2026memorywamefficientworldaction equip policies with short- and long-term memory, while MemER~ sridhar2025memerscalingmemoryrobot and PAL~ liu2026planfirstactlater use learned hierarchical policies to retrieve historical observations or organize them into executable subtasks. These methods improve memory-conditioned decisions, but recovery still depends on the learned policies' ability to correct failed interactions and inappropriate subtask choices. RoC complements these policies with selective agent intervention for execution repair and plan revision, expanding recovery capabilities while preserving efficient routine execution. Agentic Robot Control Recent advances in general-purpose multimodal models have enabled agentic robot control through visual understanding and semantic reasoning. Specifically, RoboICL~ liu2026roboiclembodiedincontextlearning generates actions using demonstrations and interaction memory, while CaP-X~ fu2026capx synthesizes executable robot-control programs. GPT-as-Policy~ su2026astra explores both direct agent control and a hybrid mode in which the agent reviews and corrects actions proposed by . Harness VLA~ zhang2026harnessvla combines agent reasoning with learned manipulation skills by composing VLA and analytic primitives for task orchestration and recovery. However, frequent agent calls introduce latency and token costs. Cocurrent work reduces this overhead through selective assistance~ sun2026call,li2026spotter , feedback-driven replanning~ lei2026longhorizonembodiedagentstoolaligned,chen2026astrarobomme , and learned monitors for progress, failures, and task transitions~ huang2026stageguard,ajith2026robomonitor,bhardwaj2026progressprobes . Detecting a problem or predicting a task transition does not, by itself, determine whether recovery requires correcting execution, revising the plan, or both. RoC makes this coordination explicit: the agent jointly reviews the current execution and proposed next goal, allowing execution repair and plan revision within the same intervention. Reward and Progress Models in Robotics Reward and progress models provide intermediate feedback for evaluating robot execution and improving policies~ zhang2025rewind . For multi-stage tasks, VICtoR~ hung2025victor identifies task stages and evaluates progress within each stage. SARM~ chen2026sarm jointly predicts task stage and fine-grained progress, using estimated rewards to filter and reweight demonstrations for behavior cloning. Robometer~ liang2026robometer combines within-trajectory progress supervision with cross-trajectory preference learning, leveraging successful and failed executions for reward modeling, policy optimization, and failure detection. Building on Robometer, RoC's online task-state monitor jointly estimates subtask progress, predicts transition requests, and proposes next goals, guiding selective agent intervention for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Method sec:method RoC follows a monitoring--execution--review loop. At initialization, the online task-state monitor proposes the first subtask from the task instruction and initial observation, using empty subtask and interaction-memory inputs. The reasoning agent confirms this proposal before policy execution begins. During execution, the monitor estimates the active subtask progress and predicts transition requests and next goals. Transition requests, progress anomalies, and critical contact events trigger agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes and approved transitions govern memory updates and task progression. title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.
