Introduction sec:introduction and have demonstrated broad generalization across language, image, and video tasks~ brown2020language,alayrac2022flamingo . Natural language and images provide a unified interface for representing information and specifying tasks across domains. Aligning heterogeneous data through this shared interface supports training at scale on diverse sources, allowing models to acquire knowledge that extends to new concepts, instructions, and reasoning tasks~ chung2024scaling,grattafiori2024llama3 . At inference, the same interface enables zero-shot transfer to new tasks without task-specific examples or parameter updates~ wei2022finetuned,sanh2022multitask,li2023blip2 . However, comparable generalization in robotics remains challenging. One of the main reasons is heterogeneity (Figure~ fig:overview (a)). Robot embodiments differ in their kinematics, observation spaces, and action representations; even the same numerical action can produce different physical effects depending on the robot and its controller~ openx2023,yuan2026qwenrobotmanip . These embodiment differences also shape how interaction experience is collected and represented, while datasets introduce further differences in coordinate conventions and annotation practices~ kim2025openvla,yuan2026qwenrobotmanip . These differences fragment experience across platforms, making it costly to collect and difficult to transfer to new environments and embodiments. These challenges also affect models, which extend pretrained to robot control by learning to predict actions from task-specific demonstrations~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,black2025pi0,black2025pi05,zheng2025xvla . Their improvements on manipulation benchmarks do not consistently translate into generalization beyond training conditions: changes in scenes, instructions, or embodiments can cause sharp performance drops~ fei2025liberoplus,yuan2026qwenrobotmanip,zhou2025liberopro . Qwen-RobotManip advocates aligning heterogeneous manipulation data in representation, motion, and behavior before training~ yuan2026qwenrobotmanip . Another line of work learns and evolves robot control policies through iterative interaction with the environment, reducing reliance on task-specific trajectory demonstrations~ chen2026gap,he2026skill2real,liang2026robofoundry,lu2026aspire,zhang2026playful . In this setting, or write executable policy code and continually revise it using interaction feedback~ liang2023code,lu2026aspire,zhang2026playful . Successful executions and validated repairs are distilled into programmatic skills, accumulating cross-task knowledge and enabling agents to solve diverse tasks through skill composition.~ he2026skill2real,lu2026aspire,zhang2026playful . This line of work represents a pragmatic middle ground between learning from demonstrations in predefined settings and open-ended continual learning. Its demonstrated scope, however, remains bounded by task definitions, hardware configurations, and benchmark suites. For example, GaP formulates policy evolution for variational automation tasks, where a specified task is repeated within a fixed workcell with bounded shape and pose variations~ chen2026gap . SHAPER evaluates evolved skills under fixed execution interfaces, leaving cross-embodiment transfer underexplored~ wang2026shaper . Skill2Real learns programmatic skills separately on LIBERO-90 and robosuite~ he2026skill2real . These boundaries and misalignments constrain the experience generalization across tasks, scenarios and embodiments. Naturally, they motivate three research questions. (i) Can alignment enable unified learning of manipulation skills from interaction across heterogeneous tasks, benchmarks, and embodiments? (ii) If so, does such learning improve generalization to unseen tasks and scenarios? (iii) Can the learned skills also transfer to unseen benchmarks and new embodiments? Inspired by the alignment first, then scale principle~ yuan2026qwenrobotmanip , we present , a unified framework designed to align heterogeneous settings (e.g., embodiments, environments, and benchmark cases) for learning robot manipulation skills through iterative interactions without trajectory demonstrations or updates to model weights. We realize this principle by introducing (i) a unified environment representation that describes observed scene entities as typed Objects and exposes robot and camera capabilities through a shared Python package; (ii) composable skills that use reusable library functions and declare the action interfaces required for execution, with adapters providing their hardware-specific implementations; (iii) a learnable orchestration policy that guides the agent model to write and execute programs in response to observations and rollout outcomes; and (iv) a canonical case representation that consistently specifies task instructions and success conditions, embodiments, scenes, and initial states across various benchmarks. During the skill learning stage, mixed rollouts of these cases provide aggregated feedback for jointly optimizing the shared programmatic components and the orchestration policy. This alignment enables each agent model to learn one shared repository from 180 tasks across LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, covering six robot embodiments. Learning interleaves these tasks and embodiments, yielding 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model (Figure~ fig:overview (b)). UniCraft demonstrates improved generalization across 66 unseen-scenario cases and 36 held-out tasks with continued refinement, as well as zero-shot transfer capability to four new robot embodiments and the unseen robosuite~ zhu2020robosuite and RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo benchmarks. Our main contributions are: [leftmargin=*,labelindent=0pt] Methodology. We introduce , which aligns execution interfaces and learning cases, enabling joint learning and refinement of one shared skillset and its orchestration policy across benchmarks and embodiments. Interleaved training. We interleave interaction experience from 300 task--embodiment pairs spanning 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments to learn one shared skillset per agent model for reuse across heterogeneous settings. Generalization. We demonstrate improved generalization across 3 agent models over 3 consecutive training epochs. From the first to the third epoch, pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks increases by percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8--13.3 on RoboTwin, and 3.1--14.4 on RoboCasa365. Zero-shot transfer. We show that can transfer zero-shot across 4 new robot embodiments, 2 unseen benchmarks, and 5 additional agent models. Cross-embodiment training combines demonstrations across robotic platforms. Open X-Embodiment pools data from 22 robot embodiments and demonstrates positive transfer across robots~ openx2023 . X-VLA uses source-specific soft prompts to accommodate heterogeneous datasets~ zheng2025xvla . Qwen-RobotManip further aligns state-action representations, motion, and behavior for large-scale training~ yuan2026qwenrobotmanip . These approaches address heterogeneity within shared action-prediction models. Our work examines alignment at the level of interfaces for reusable manipulation skills. -generated robot policies. turns language instructions into Python policies that call APIs for perception and control, allowing explicit branches and feedback loops~ liang2023code . Instruct2Act grounds generated programs with visual foundation models~ huang2023instruct2act , while VoxPoser writes code that composes 3D value maps for motion planning~ huang2023voxposer . RoboScript improves deployability through a simulation-to-real interface, syntax checks, and Gazebo validation~ chen2024roboscript . These helpers provide reusable components for subsequent program generation. RECENT extends reuse across embodiments by preserving skill semantics while adapting execution bindings through code refactoring~ choi2026recent . manipulation skill learning. Interaction-based skill learning retains executable procedures and validated repairs for reuse across tasks~ chen2026gap,lu2026aspire,zhang2026playful,liang2026robofoundry,he2026skill2real . GaP refines computation graphs built from modular skills through simulation rehearsal for variational automation in fixed workcells~ chen2026gap . ASPIRE transfers guidance distilled from validated repairs to support further debugging on a target robot~ lu2026aspire . Skill2Real learns hierarchical skills in simulation and transfers the frozen skills through a shared API, while its LIBERO-90 and robosuite skill collections are trained independently~ he2026skill2real . These studies differ in how experience is retained and what adaptation is needed in a new setting. Our focus is on how aligned interfaces let experience from heterogeneous tasks, benchmarks, and embodiments jointly refine one shared skillset. title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
summary: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points. The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0, +19.4]) and +6.0 points ([+0.2, +11.8]). Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3-4%. High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.

High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does. Introduction sec:intro Flow-based vision-language-action policies denoise a chunk of continuous actions~ black2025pi0,black2025pi05 . In the action expert of \( _ 0.5 \), each action query attends, at each denoising step, to a multimodal prefix and to all action tokens. Wang et al.~ wang2026vla observe that the first and last action tokens receive high incoming attention, call them radial action sinks, propose that they anchor temporal consistency across chunks, and use them to set an adaptive execution horizon. The word sink carries a specific profile from language models: one token receives much of the attention, its value is small, and reading it changes the output little~ gu2025attention,barbero2025overmixing . If the endpoints had that profile, attention on them would park probability mass rather than carry action information. Wang et al.\ make no small-value claim; the name alone invites this reading. We therefore ask three questions about the endpoints and the tokens around them. Where does the endpoint mass come from? Do the endpoint values behave like a sink's? If not, which token does, and what keeps the action tokens distinct from each other? We do not test the horizon rule of~ wang2026vla ; our results bear on how its anchors should be described, not on whether the rule works. We answer these questions with paired interventions in the action expert of \( _ 0.5 \) on RoboCasa~ robocasa2024 . Each intervention and its baseline share the observation and the initial noise, and every closed-loop comparison is paired with the baseline of the same execution. fig:teaser We find: Endpoint mass is positional. Current-layer RoPE produces it in shallow layers and upstream action-token RoPE in deeper layers; removing the relevant rotations returns it to the uniform reference at high and mid noise (Section~ sec:radial ). Endpoint values are not a null sink, and success is far less sensitive to them than to interior values. Their norms and gated outputs are typical or larger. Masking or zeroing them changes closed-loop success by less than 4 points and replacing them by 3 to 7 points, while replacing two executed non-endpoint tokens lowers it by 25 to 28 points (Section~ sec:sink ). The sink-like token is the prefix BOS. It has high mass and a small, shared value; on this checkpoint, zeroing that value raises success by \(+13.2\) and \(+6.0\) points in two runs (Section~ sec:sink ). Action routing follows a relative-offset profile. A shared profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75 of action-token spread and keeps success on three held-out tasks, while routings that break the offset structure drop success to 3--4 (Section~ sec:mixing ). Background and Related Work sec:background Action Expert sec:action-expert The action expert of ~ black2025pi05 has 18 layers in the network we measure. Each input is a multimodal prefix followed by a chunk of 50 action tokens, denoised jointly by flow matching. The prefix begins with a <bos> token and then contains image tokens and language tokens. Prefix queries read only the prefix, and do not read the action tokens. Action queries read the prefix and every action key, so attention inside the action chunk is bidirectional. Figure~ fig:architecture shows that head-averaged map at layer 2, with columns running from the prefix BOS through image and language into the action keys. Queries and keys use rotary position embeddings~ su2021roformer , so changing a token's position changes its attention logits even when its content is held fixed. Each layer scales the attention residual by an adaptive RMSNorm gate \(g\), conditioned on the flow-matching timestep, written \(g W_O(AV)\). Head-averaged attention of action queries at layer 2. Columns are grouped into BOS, image, language, and action keys. The color scale stops at the brightest action-key entry. fig:architecture Related Work sec:related Gu et al.~ gu2025attention treat an attention sink as a key-side bias on one early token: the sink key stores extra attention score, its value has a small \( _2\) norm, and the attended token contributes little to the attention output. Softmax ties the pattern to a competition among key scores that must sum to one~ gu2025attention . A different internal token role appears in vision transformers. Darcet et al.~ darcet2024registers find that low-information image tokens can be repurposed for internal computation, producing high-norm artifacts in low-information regions that are removed by adding register tokens. This provides a distinct example of a token function beyond the low-contribution sink account. Barbero et al.~ barbero2025overmixing argue that dumping attention onto the first token makes some heads nearly inactive, which slows over-mixing in deep, long-context language-model stacks. They call the resulting update an approximate no-op: attention on the low-norm value keeps the attention output small, so the residual stream changes less. These results describe one fixed early token in a causal language model. RoPE encodes relative position through position-dependent rotations of the queries and the keys~ su2021roformer . Chen et al.~ chen2025hope show that learned components inside RoPE can produce a global U-shaped pattern of attention. These findings motivate separating positional concentration from the functional role of the attended token. Diffusion transformers attend bidirectionally over the whole sequence, so high incoming mass is no longer tied to one early causal position. Wu and Summa~ wu2026attention show that editing sink scores or sink values in text-to-image diffusion transformers changes the generated image. Wang et al.~ wang2026vla observe the same kind of endpoint concentration on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA, and use those tokens as anchors for the execution horizon. We test the language-model sink profile on those endpoints: whether they have the small value norm and near-zero output contribution of a sink, and whether closed-loop control depends on reading them. We do not run or evaluate their horizon rule. Action chunking and diffusion policies generate action sequences~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy , and other VLA studies intervene on directions in feedforward activations~ brohan2023rt2,kim2025openvla,haon2025steering . Our measurements stay on attention inside the action expert: where the endpoint mass comes from, whether the attended values are null, and which routing keeps the action tokens distinct. Interventions and baselines share the same observations and the same initial noise. title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://tacinno.github.io
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce , which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, , learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. achieves average success rates of 87.5 across six simulation tasks and 70.5 across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robotic manipulation~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . Building on pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLA models learn to predict robot actions from visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive states through imitation learning~ intelligence2025pi05 . Nevertheless, contact-rich manipulation remains challenging, as critical contact events, such as incipient slip and jamming during insertion, are often difficult to infer from external visual observations. To capture contact events, recent efforts augment VLA models with tactile observations~ yuan2026ftp1,huang2025tactilevla,simpletouch2026,zhang2026restacvla,neoteai2026n0vtla,zhang2025vtla,cheng2026omnivtla,bi2026vlatouch,li2026atvla , typically acquired by vision-based tactile sensors such as GelSight~ yuan2017gelsight and DIGIT~ lambeta2020digit , which capture the deformation of a soft gel. Existing visuo-tactile policies incorporate tactile observations as additional inputs~ huang2025tactilevla,tapvla2026,yuan2026ftp1,tacvla2026,tacforcing2026 , predict future tactile signals~ chen2026ratg,fu2026decal,wang2026tacdynwam,simpletouch2026,zhang2026contactworld , or emphasize tactile changes during training~ tau2026vla,dreamtac2026,tactilewam2026,hitacwam2026,medex2026 ( c). However, incorporating tactile inputs yields inconsistent gains and can even reduce the success rate relative to the same VLA without tactile inputs~ yuan2026ftp1,zhang2026restacvla . Moreover, we apply a tactile-off test, which removes tactile input at test time, and find that the success rates of some existing policies change little, indicating limited reliance on tactile information ( ). We attribute the inconsistent gains and the limited reliance to the nature of the tactile signal, since a tactile sensor measures how the contact responds to the robot's own actions. Consequently, given the initial tactile observation, a substantial portion of the subsequent tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions ( , a). As an input, the predictable portion is largely redundant, and adding an input modality can even degrade performance~ wang2020multimodal . When future tactile signals are the prediction target, the predictable portion makes up most of the target, so the prediction loss is dominated by changes that vision and executed actions already explain. Weighting the loss by the magnitude of tactile change does not help, since the largest changes are often the predictable ones ( ). A central question arises: How can the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain be isolated and used to guide VLA policy learning? To answer this question, we propose , which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain as the supervision signal for VLA training. Inspired by the notion of innovation in estimation theory~ kalman1960filtering,kailath1968innovations , we define tactile innovation as the residual tactile change after accounting for the initial tactile observation, visual observations, and executed actions. Three properties of tactile innovation determine the design of . First, tactile innovation is conditional on visual observations and executed actions. We therefore introduce the TacInno tokenizer, which learns a compact discrete code as a proxy for tactile innovation and conditions both its encoder and decoder on the corresponding visual observations and executed actions, so that the code retains the contact dynamics that the two conditions cannot explain ( b). Second, tactile innovation is dynamic, arising from transient contact events, such as incipient slip, that span several control steps. The tokenizer therefore encodes a short sequence of tactile observations with causal temporal attention rather than a single pair of frames. Third, tactile innovation lies in the future and is unavailable when the policy acts. We therefore train to predict the code from current observations as an auxiliary objective, supervising the tactile representations used for action prediction. The code serves only as a training target, and the tokenizer and auxiliary prediction heads are removed at deployment. We evaluate on six contact-rich tasks from the UniVTAC benchmark~ univtac2026 and four real-world tasks using a Franka FR3 robot equipped with a vision-based tactile sensor. achieves average success rates of 87.5 in simulation and 70.5 in the real world, the highest among the evaluated visuo-tactile policies. Ablation studies verify the contribution of each design, and the tactile-off test confirms that relies on tactile input. Our contributions are summarized as follows: With the tactile-off test, we show that some existing visuo-tactile policies rely little on tactile input, attribute the limited reliance to the redundancy of the tactile signal, and propose to separate the tactile change that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation. We propose , which encodes tactile innovation into a discrete code with a conditional multi-frame tokenizer and uses the code solely as an auxiliary training target, adding no module for the code at deployment. outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points in average success rate in simulation and the real world, respectively. The success rate of drops from 88 to 0 on under the tactile-off test and by 21 percentage points on the lifting tasks when the code encodes the entire tactile change. Related Work sec:related Visuo-tactile policy learning. Earlier visuo-tactile policies fuse tactile images~ lee2019making,huang20243dvitac,liu2025vitamin or pretrained tactile representations~ higuera2024sparsh,zhao2024t3 with visual features in imitation-learning policies such as ACT~ zhao2023act and Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusion . Recent methods extend tactile sensing to VLA models in three progressive directions ( c). The first incorporates tactile observations as additional inputs and relies on the action loss alone to determine how the tactile inputs are used~ yuan2026ftp1,huang2025tactilevla,tacvla2026,tapvla2026,tacforcing2026,neoteai2026n0vtla,zhang2025vtla,cheng2026omnivtla,bi2026vlatouch,li2026atvla . Because the action loss rewards only what improves the imitated actions, the policy is not required to use the tactile inputs, and the gains are modest and occasionally negative~ yuan2026ftp1,zhang2026restacvla . FACT~ fact2026vla further replaces the tactile input with noise to examine how much of the reported gain originates from tactile information. The second direction therefore assigns the tactile signal an objective of its own and predicts future tactile signals, either within the policy~ simpletouch2026,chen2026ratg,fu2026decal,liu2026physword or through tactile world models~ wang2026tacdynwam,zhang2026contactworld . Since predicting every future tactile signal spends much of the supervision on periods in which the contact hardly changes, the third direction emphasizes tactile changes during training by weighting or gating the tactile signal according to the magnitude of its change~ tau2026vla,medex2026,dreamtac2026,tactilewam2026,hitacwam2026 . However, the second and third directions still supervise the tactile representation with the entire future tactile change, including the component that vision and executed actions already explain. Our method extends this progression by supervising only the component that vision and executed actions cannot explain. The closest work, ResTacVLA~ zhang2026restacvla , uses the quantized residual between visually predicted and observed tactile representations as a policy input, whereas our code encodes the future tactile change that vision and executed actions cannot explain and serves only as a training target. Discrete latent dynamics learning. Vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs)~ oord2017vqvae learn compact discrete representations by mapping continuous features to entries in a learned codebook and reconstructing observations from the quantized codes. Vector quantization has been extended to temporal modeling, where discrete latent variables capture transitions between observations. Genie~ bruce2024genie learns latent actions from unlabeled videos to enable controllable video generation. LAPA~ ye2025lapa employs a VQ-VAE-based action tokenizer to extract discrete latent actions from video transitions, which serve as supervision for VLA pretraining. UniVLA~ bu2025univla further incorporates language conditioning into inverse- and forward-dynamics learning to obtain task-centric latent actions. Building on discrete latent dynamics learning, our method applies vector quantization to tactile observations. The encoder compresses a sequence of tactile observations into discrete codes, while the decoder reconstructs future tactile changes conditioned on the current tactile state, visual observations, and executed actions. Unlike latent action models, which infer unobserved actions, our tokenizer is trained on demonstrations with known actions and therefore provides the actions to both the encoder and the decoder. With conditional reconstruction, the codes retain only the contact dynamics that the conditioning information cannot explain. Method sec:method In this section, we present in three parts ( ). First, formulates the problem and defines tactile innovation. Then, presents the tokenizer, which isolates tactile innovation from demonstrations and labels each demonstration frame with a discrete code. Finally, describes , which is trained to predict the code as an auxiliary objective. title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
summary: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build , which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, achieves a mean success rate of 93.75 across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations. Introduction sec:intro Humanoid robots could help people with a wide range of tasks in homes and workplaces. Many require whole-body loco-manipulation, in which the robot coordinates its steps and posture with its hand movements~ jiang2026wholebodyvla,li2026omega . Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ pi0,pi0.5,gr00t and world action models~ ye2026world,lingbotva,fastwam have shown that robots can learn diverse manipulation skills from demonstrations. For humanoids, however, the cost of whole-body teleoperation limits the range of tasks and environments represented in robot demonstrations~ he2024omnih2o,ze2026twist2 . Human experience of everyday activity offers a more scalable alternative to robot teleoperation. Recent work draws on the variety of activities and environments in these videos~ gigaworldpolicy,wu2024unleashing to pretrain manipulation policies~ wei2026psi0,zheng2026egoscale,li2026scalable . Despite this diversity, visual observations alone provide no explicit targets for whole-body motion. Prior work therefore retargets recorded human motion to obtain robot action targets~ chen2026egohumanoid,post2026a0 . However, differences in body proportions and joint structure can cause the resulting postures and hand trajectories to deviate from those in the human demonstration~ araujo2026retargeting . These deviations motivate retaining the original human motion as a training signal alongside the retargeted robot actions. Using that signal at scale requires egocentric video paired with synchronized whole-body motion across diverse tasks and environments. Yet many large egocentric datasets provide video alone or primarily track the head and hands~ grauman2022ego4d,hoque2026egodex , while datasets such as Nymeria~ ma2024nymeria offer only a few hundred hours of paired recordings. We address this data gap with , a dataset for humanoid pretraining that pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion. Collected under a common protocol using lightweight wearable sensors, the demonstrations cover more than 100 skills across homes, workplaces, retail spaces, and storage areas. We reconstruct 3D hand motion from the video and annotate the demonstrations with subtask descriptions and frame-level depth maps. For each demonstration, we retain the original human trajectory alongside the corresponding retargeted robot actions. Building on , we introduce , a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation. By predicting human motion alongside retargeted robot actions, its shared action expert receives direct supervision from the original human trajectories. During pretraining, the expert also predicts camera-frame wrist poses, while separate heads estimate current and future depth and describe the current subtask. We then post-train the policy on approximately 150 hours of T800 teleoperation data using the same robot action interface. We observe that 's robot action prediction error on held-out data follows an empirical scaling law, decreasing as the pretraining set grows from 5,000 to 50,000 hours of human demonstrations. With the same T800 demonstrations for post-training, more human pretraining data also raises the policy's mean success rate on three household tasks. Controlled ablations show that adding human motion supervision reduces action prediction error and improves real-robot task success compared with pretraining on retargeted actions alone. After full-corpus pretraining, we post-train on the same T800 demonstrations used for GR00T N1.7~ gr00t and ~ pi0.5 . outperforms both baselines on all eight individual loco-manipulation tasks, averaging 93.75 success. It retains this advantage on long-horizon industrial and household tasks. The policy also follows instructions that pair familiar objects and destinations in new ways and applies a learned manipulation skill to objects unseen during robot post-training. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce , a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and robot actions through a shared action expert. We build , a dataset pairing 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion across diverse tasks and environments. We find that as human pretraining data grows, action prediction error decreases according to an empirical scaling law and real-robot success rates rise. also generalizes to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations and to objects unseen during robot post-training. Related Work sec:related_work Foundation Models for Robot Control sec:related_foundation_models Generalist robot policies map observations and instructions to actions across a wide range of manipulation tasks~ brohan2022rt,team2024octo,kim2024openvla,pi0,wu2026foundation,gr00t,pi0.5 . For a humanoid, loco-manipulation additionally requires moving and staying balanced while adjusting posture to reach objects at different heights and distances. One line of work separates the control interfaces for the upper and lower body. WholeBodyVLA~ jiang2026wholebodyvla and ~ wei2026psi0 predict upper-body actions and coarse base commands, which a locomotion controller converts into lower-body motion. More recent approaches predict whole-body motion, enabling the policy to learn coordination between locomotion and manipulation~ zheng2026motionwam,li2026omega,post2026a0 . Our follows this approach and learns motion priors through large-scale human pretraining. Egocentric Data and Motion Alignment sec:related_motion_alignment Egocentric datasets have grown rapidly in scale, but largely at the cost of recorded whole-body motion or a consistent protocol. Nymeria~ ma2024nymeria uses an inertial motion-capture suit, and HumanVerse in ~ post2026a0 uses a headset with body-worn trackers, yet each covers only a few hundred hours. Larger datasets such as Ego4D~ grauman2022ego4d , EgoVerse~ punamiya2026egoverse , and EgoDex~ hoque2026egodex provide video with at most head, hand, or upper-body poses, while Ego-Exo4D~ grauman2024ego derives body pose from exocentric cameras. Pretraining corpora such as EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale and Ego4WAM~ sun2026ego4wam exceed 10,000 hours by aggregating many sources, which differ in sensors and annotation pipelines. We build to fill this gap with 50,000 hours of egocentric video and whole-body motion recorded by wearable trackers, all captured under the same protocol. Table~ tab:data_comparison compares with other egocentric datasets in terms of scale, capture setup, and annotation coverage. To construct robot-action supervision, human motion is mapped to robot embodiments through direct joint mappings~ fu2024humanplus or geometric retargeting, as in GMR~ araujo2026retargeting . Differences in body proportions and joint structure can alter the resulting postures and end-effector trajectories~ araujo2026retargeting,he2024learning . Controller dynamics introduce further discrepancies between references and execution~ chen2026egohumanoid,jiang2026egoalign . Controller-aware refinement~ chen2026egohumanoid,zhao2026halomi and causal state reconstruction, as in EgoAlign~ jiang2026egoalign , improve the consistency of human-derived supervision with robot behavior. Our annotation pipeline replaces noisy hand annotations with 3D hand poses reconstructed from egocentric video and uses them to refine end-effector alignment, reducing end-effector errors relative to GMR. Learning from Egocentric Demonstrations sec:related_egocentric_learning Human demonstrations are typically used in embodied learning to supervise perception, world modeling, and action learning. R3M~ nair2022r3m pretrains a visual encoder on egocentric human video so that manipulation policies can be learned from fewer robot demonstrations. World-action models instead use future frames as prediction targets, learning how scenes change as people interact with objects even without action labels~ zheng2026motionwam,sun2026ego4wam . When hand or body trajectories are available, human demonstrations can also supervise action learning~ qiu2025humanoid,yang2025egovla,wei2026psi0 . EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic aligns human hand trajectories with robot end-effector trajectories in a common coordinate frame to train a shared manipulation policy. EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale and ~ post2026a0 retarget human motion into robot hand or whole-body actions and train on these labels. However, constrained by morphological differences, retargeting inevitably introduces global errors and distorted postures~ araujo2026retargeting,chen2026egohumanoid . We therefore train on the original human motion together with the retargeted robot actions, learning motion priors directly from the demonstrations. sec:data Large-Scale Egocentric Corpus sec:egocentric_corpus We build to study how the scale of human demonstrations affects humanoid pretraining. The corpus pairs 50,000 hours of egocentric video with synchronized whole-body human motion recorded by wearable sensors, making it the largest such dataset to our knowledge. It comprises approximately 17.02 million episodes, 5.41 billion pose frames, and 11.18 million valid language instructions. Our setup consists of a PICO headset and five body-worn trackers, synchronously recording stereo RGB video and skeletal sequences from PICO’s body-tracking system~ chen2026egohumanoid,jiang2026egoalign . Collectors follow task goals and adapt their walking paths, stance, and grasping strategies to the scene, preserving natural repositioning and motion transitions within continuous interactions. The corresponding task instructions are retained alongside raw video, motion trajectories, and camera and device parameters for subsequent annotation and alignment. The demonstrations cover more than 100 skills across homes, workplaces, retail spaces, and storage areas. Activities range from picking up, carrying, and placing objects to folding garments and wiping surfaces. Continuous recordings capture how people coordinate walking, turning, and changes in posture with these hand movements. Figure~ fig:data_overview shows representative egocentric views, the distribution of interaction objects such as shelves, tables, boxes, and everyday containers, and episode counts for selected skills. It then performs temporal segmentation and semantic annotation, visual hand-motion reconstruction, and stereo depth estimation to produce time-aligned l

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
full_text: 1.0em \@plus @ 0.5em \@plus 4 @ @tocdepth>\@ne to 0.94 Introduction sec:scope ``Knowledge is the beginning of action and action is the completion of knowledge.'' --- Wang Yangming The central ambition of embodied intelligence is to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability. Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback~ wolpert2011principles,cisek2010neural,shadmehr2010error . In the cooking task of Fig.~ fig:report-overview , a robot must , , and . These requirements motivate three capabilities. decides what to do from earlier observations. produces the required physical effect in time. closes the loop, so that remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision. Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents~ liang2023cap , vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ kim2024openvla,pi2025pi05 , world-action models (WAMs)~ li2026wallwm,ye2026dreamzero , and hybrid architectures~ shi2025hirobot,gemini2025robotics15 have substantially advanced robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in , , and remain poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development. Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks~ libero,robocasa,behavior,robodojo,x2real explain why. First, conventional benchmarks often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether a task succeeds~ libero,rlbench,robocasa , so a failure cannot be traced to or . Second, although recent benchmarks have introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution~ robodojo,embodiedplayground,x2real,robocoliseum , they rarely evaluate , particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the others present but easy, a judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and a comparison of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms. To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark for , , and in robotic manipulation (Fig.~ fig:report-overview ). Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view emphasizes one demand by design. tasks keep physical operations simple, tasks state the required operation explicitly, and tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in a Clean and a Random scene, which share the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations (75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. A diagnosis harness combines rule-based analysis of the evaluator's stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of three representative systems to , , or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems in a per-model report called a model profile card (Fig.~ fig:eval-pipeline ; Appendix~ subsec:profile-cards ). Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals a clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across and , yet all struggle with . The strongest agent retains task state well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that pauses during inference. End-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second and execute practiced motions, but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization. Notably, on , the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0 of episodes, far below its 52.7 on and 39.0 on , and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6 . Competence in either capability therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates , , and . We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to , , or . The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies. We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which of and is weaker, and that all of them struggle with . Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , ~ pi2025pi05 , RDT2~ liu2026rdt2 and G0.5~ galaxea2026g05 improve instruction following and cross-task transfer, while world-action models such as LDA-1B~ lyu2026lda , Motus~ bi2026motus and DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero couple predictive modeling with control. Agent-based systems take a different route, turning language-model reasoning into executable programs~ liang2023cap and feeding success detection back into planning~ huang2022innermonologue,liu2023reflect . Recent work also addresses memory-augmented manipulation~ shi2025memoryvla,torne2026mem,sridhar2025memer , dynamic manipulation~ black2025rtc,xie2026dynamicvla , and force- or tactile-aware control~ yu2025forcevla,huang2025tactilevla . Despite this progress, each line is usually evaluated where only its own demand is hard: memory methods on tasks with simple execution, dynamic and contact-aware controllers on tasks whose target is given, and agents on tasks where perceiving the outcome is assumed. In practice, a failure may come from holding the wrong task state, missing the intended physical effect, or continuing without checking that the effect occurred. Mind2Act World therefore makes all three demands hard within the same tasks and evaluates agents, VLAs and WAMs on them. Evaluation for Manipulation and Embodied Agents Simulation benchmarks provide scalable testbeds for manipulation. RLBench~ rlbench , CALVIN~ mees2022calvin and LIBERO~ libero cover multi-task, language-conditioned and lifelong settings. RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin evaluates bimanual generalization, and THE COLOSSEUM~ pumacay2024colosseum stresses distribution shift. BEHAVIOR-1K~ behavior and RoboCasa~ robocasa pose long household activities. Memory benchmarks such as RMBench~ chen2026rmbench and RoboMME~ dai2026robomme isolate history-dependent decisions, the latter with Easy, Medium and Hard levels and timed stopping of moving objects. GeoMind~ wang2026geomind evaluates spatial reasoning and spatial memory through structured manipulation tasks, with controlled scene variations and diagnostic metrics for spatial understanding and execution failures. RoboDojo~ robodojo and RobotWorld~ robotworld diagnose capability dimensions with stage scores or execution traces, and real-world benchmarks such as RoboArena~ atreya2025roboarena assess deployed policies. For agents built on foundation models, EmbodiedBench~ yang2025embodiedbench spans high-level and low-level embodied tasks, and Embodied Playground~ embodiedplayground evaluates closed-loop behavior in which earlier actions set up later prerequisites. X2Real~ x2real records subtask failure nodes, separates reasoning from manipulation dimensions including dynamic operation, and compares VLA, WAM and agent routes. RoboColiseum~ robocoliseum reports a gap between task understanding and reliable execution. RLE-Bench~ rle and Embodied First Exam~ embodiedfirstexam instead evaluate agents that write and iterate on code to solve robot control and robot learning engineering problems. Most of these benchmarks entangle reasoning and execution within one task, so a failure cannot be attributed to either, or measure them in separate evaluations, leaving open whether they hold together when one realized outcome sets the conditions for the next decision. Mind2Act World addresses this gap by deriving tasks from real-world requirements and organizing them into Mind, Act and Mind2Act views with graded difficulty, so that the same demands are measured in isolation and in composition across architectures. Table~ tab:related-benchmark-facts compares Mind2Act World with 21 representative simulation benchmarks. Mind2Act World tasks also have long horizons, with training demonstrations averaging 60.7\,s overall and 99.6\,s in the Mind2Act view. Demonstrations in RoboTwin~2.0, RoboDojo, MIKASA-Robo-VLA and RoboCasa365 average 13 to 40\,s, and only BEHAVIOR-1K, whose tasks are full household activities, has longer ones. Mind2Act World Benchmark sec:benchmark Mind2Act World asks whether failures in manipulation tasks arise from incorrect reasoning, imprecise execution, or a poor composition of the two. The benchmark comprises 30 simulation tasks on a bimanual ARX X5 platform, organized into 3 views that place different demands on a system. Mind focuses on history-dependent reasoning, Act emphasizes constrained physical execution, and Mind2Act focuses on their composition. Each task has Easy, Medium, and Hard levels, and each level is evaluated in a Clean and a Random scene setting, yielding 180 configurations. Fig.~ fig:skill-diversity presents an overview of our 30 tasks. The following sections describe the design principles (Section~ subsec:design-principles ), task views (Section~ subsec:task-suite-design ), difficulty levels (Section~ subsec:pressure-design ), training data (Section~ subsec:training-data ), and evaluation setting (Section~ subsec:benchmark-evaluation-setting ). Design Principles subsec:design-principles Four principles guide the benchmark design: (i)~build tasks from real-world requirements, (ii)~evaluate reasoning and execution capabilities separately and in combination, (iii)~verify physical outcomes and record task progress, and (iv)~support evaluation across different model architectures. (i) Tasks are built from real-world requirements. Embodied agents in industry, homes, and service settings must follow instructions across multiple stages and produce the required physical effects at the right time. We construct tasks in three steps. First, we identify a practical requirement, such as remembering orders after they leave view, maintaining a target instrument reading, intercepting objects on a conveyor, or responding to appliance feedback. We then reproduce this requirement in a tabletop scene and define completion conditions based on physical outcomes. Table~ tab:application-domains groups the tasks into five application domains: home and food service, manufacturing and logistics, instrument operation and dexterous tool use, assembly and physical reasoning, and companion and edutainment. It also identifies the industrial or service requirement behind each task. In the companion and edutainment domain, structured activities such as card matching and paddle ball represent cognitive and sports training for older adults and children. title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

Introduction sec:intro Physical understanding has widely recognized as a cornerstone of language-conditioned robotic manipulation systems~ bousetouane2025physical, ye2026world, han2026geometric, pi2026pi07 . A broad spectrum of methods have emerged, ranging from hybrid frameworks~ xiao2026enpire,liang2023code to unified systems~ pi2026pi07,kim2024openvla,zitkovich2023rt , from vision-language architectures~ zhang2026dreamvla, bjorck2025gr00t,kim2026cosmos to multi-sensory models~ yu2026forcevla,niu2026t , and from static methods~ zhang2026dreamvla, bjorck2025gr00t,kim2026cosmos,qian2026geopredict,han2026geometric,qu2025spatialvla,li2026bridgevla,li2025spatial to dynamic paradigm~ zhang2025dynamic,li2025sim, liu2026rdt2,huang2026rt,tang2025vlash . Despite this great progress, recent works predominantly focus on the intrinsic gripper–object contact, whether in standard manipulation tasks such as Pick-and-Place, Re-orientation, and Opening Closing Articulated Objects~ liu2023libero,nasiriany2024robocasa,chen2025robotwin,zhang2025vlabench , or in contact-rich tasks such as Insertion, Fragile Grasping, and Wiping~ fang2026force,yu2026forcevla,huang2025tactile,li2026forcevla2,kim2026rldx,liu2024forcemimic,fang2023rh20t,niu2026t,shan2026learning . However, they largely overlook how the manipulators interacts with its surrounding environment (e.g., gravity, friction, inertia, aerodynamics, mass distribution, etc.), namely the newtonian mechanics underlying everyday physical interactions, which substantially limits their ability to reflect genuine physical intelligence.\\ To fill this gap, we recast language-conditioned robotic manipulation through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity~ dafle2014extrinsic , focusing on throwing-based object manipulation. In this setting, the manipulator must estimate the object's physical properties, such as its mass, center of mass (CoM), and friction, and plan the forces and contacts needed to send the object to a target location outside its own kinematic workspace.\\ We introduce , a high-fidelity synthetic manipulation dataset comprising 35k trajectories across 9 throwing tasks and 100 scenes. It covers rigid, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects, as well as diverse destination types, with all physical properties randomized. is generated by a fully decoupled, autonomous simulation pipeline that separates asset specification, skill policies, task composition, and rendering. Each task is built by retrieving embodiments, scenes, and objects from an asset library and composing scripted skill policies into complete behaviors. This compositional design enables automatic generation of object-level annotations, physical randomization, and collision-aware motion plans, supporting systematic VLA validation through fine-tuning and closed-loop evaluation. To evaluate the physical understanding of current policies, we select three representative policies: GR00T N1.7~ gr00t-n1 as a general-purpose policy, DynamicVLA~ xie2026dynamicvla as a high-frequency policy, and ForceVLA~ yu2026forcevla as a multi-sensory VLA. Our experiments show that current policies are not yet reliable for tasks requiring physical understanding, with average success rates below 10 . We further identify generalization and the probing of object physical properties as the main bottlenecks of current systems. To confirm that this trend holds beyond a single setup, we additionally conduct evaluations across multiple platforms, including a humanoid robot and real-world experiments. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We propose , a diverse and comprehensive dataset of nine throwing tasks for studying physical understanding in robot manipulation. We introduce a scalable construction pipeline that generates diverse, end-to-end data for throwing tasks. We conduct extensive evaluations across multiple embodiments, including robot arms and humanoids, in both simulation and real-world experiments. Our results show that data scarcity and physical blindness are the main bottlenecks keeping current policies from performing reliably on physical understanding tasks. Related Works Language-conditioned Robot Manipulation Recently, language-conditioned robot manipulation systems have attracted much attention and achieved great progress, owing to their generalizability, scalability, and potential for deployment in the physical world. Related methods can be roughly categorized into two branches: autoregressive-based approaches~ brohan2022rt,kim2024openvla,li2025unified,li2024manipllm,pertsch2025fast,wen2025tinyvla,goyal2025vla and diffusion-based approaches~ bjorck2025gr00t,pi2026pi07,li2024cogact,wen2025diffusionvla,ye2026world,kim2026cosmos,han2026geometric . While these methods have significantly advanced overall performance, their physical knowledge is interpolated from the training data distribution and its reliability remains unverified. Language-conditioned Dynamic Manipulation Our work is closely related to dynamic manipulation, which demands policies that are fast, reactive, and precise. Modeling such dynamics is challenging, as it relies on physical properties of both the objects and the manipulator that are difficult to estimate~ mason1993dynamic . In the language-conditioned setting, most recent work tracks a target object under static and predictable conditions~ zhang2025dynamic,li2025sim , adopts asynchronous inference to hide latency~ liu2026rdt2,huang2026rt,tang2025vlash , or extends control to more precise 6-DoF manipulation~ liao2026dynamicmanip,xie2026dynamicvla . While effective, these methods are evaluated primarily on kinematic accuracy. They optimize for trajectory matching and leave the understanding of physical properties implicit, so a failure cannot be attributed to kinematic error or to a misestimated physical property. In this work, we design a beyond-reach manipulation benchmark in which the object must be moved to a target location outside the kinematic range of the manipulator, making the understanding of physical properties a decisive factor for success. Physical Property Understanding To throw an object accurately to a target, a robot must first estimate the object's physical properties. Studies in cognitive science~ yuan2017connecting,mcadams1993recognition suggest that humans infer such properties not only from visual appearance but also from material experience. Existing approaches to physical property estimation fall into two main lines of work: those that encode an object's properties implicitly~ wu2016physics,bauza2019omnipush,purri2020teaching,yuan2017connecting and those that predict them explicitly~ liu2026vitacphys,yu2024octopi,sundaram2019learning,standley2017image2mass . While effective, these methods mostly target object-centric settings in general domains, and robotic scenarios remain underexplored. A few works in robot learning~ liu2026vitacphys,xie2024deligrasp have tackled this problem, but they are limited to simple pick-and-place or contact-rich manipulation tasks. These tasks are not demanding enough to properly evaluate a model's physical understanding. To fill this gap, we explicitly randomize object physical properties, such as mass, CoM, and friction, to evaluate a model's ability to accurately estimate object properties and reason about physics. In this section, we present the task taxonomy, detailed dataset statistics, and the data creation pipeline, which are illustrated in Figure fig:statistic and Figure fig:pipeline , respectively. Task Taxonomy Statistics comprises 9 tasks, 35 , 357 episodes, and 143.2 hours of data recorded at 10\,Hz. It is designed to evaluate how well policies estimate the physical properties of objects from different perspectives. . In , policies perform a throwing task at three levels of object difficulty: (1) Uniform Object (31.8 ): objects with uniformly distributed mass and a centered center of mass (CoM); (2) Irregular Object (39.2 ): objects with non-uniform mass distribution and a CoM offset toward one end; and (3) Dynamic Object (29.0 ): objects whose mass and CoM change during the interaction. In addition, to test generalization and timing, we use three destination settings: static single destination (31.76 ), static multiple destinations (29.77 ), and moving single destination (38.47 ). Assets. We provide 107 curated object assets, sourced from RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and Objaverse-XL~ deitke2023objaverse : 20 destination objects, 46 uniform objects, 37 irregular objects, and 4 dynamic objects. For environments, includes 100 RoboCasa kitchen scenes spanning diverse layouts and styles. Benchmark Construction Pipeline In this section, we describe the data synthesis pipeline of . We first construct the environment by specifying the task, target object, destination, and scene. We then apply domain randomization to diversify these environments. Finally, we generate approaching and throwing trajectories and define the procedures for storing the resulting data. Environment Construction As illustrated in Figure~ fig:pipeline , given a task description template, we first retrieve the task-relevant assets from the asset library: the target object, the destination object, and the scene. We use a UR5e arm equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper as the robot embodiment, represented as a stable USD asset. The scene assets are room-scale environments with diverse layouts and styles, each annotated with fine-grained manipulation areas to support natural, context-aware task construction. Our object library spans three mass categories (uniform, irregular, and dynamic) and covers a range of physical properties, sizes, and layouts. Objects are sampled equally across categories to keep the benchmark balanced. We also place distractor objects around the target object to encourage policy generalization. Destination objects likewise vary in motion direction, size, and layout. All functional annotations are managed through a unified interface, which makes asset configuration straightforward while keeping physical fidelity high.
