title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx
full_text: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at . Introduction Humanoid loco-manipulation for long-horizon tasks is central to embodied intelligence and generalist robotics, with applications in domestic assistance, healthcare, and industrial logistics. Yet even seemingly routine tasks in these domains demand complex, extended coordination between locomotion and manipulation. For instance, fetching a coffee or clearing a table interleaves walking, contact-rich manipulation, and precise object-part interaction over long action sequences. The challenge lies in jointly addressing three tightly coupled aspects: temporal structure, skill dynamics, and precise control, all of which must be grounded in physical interaction and integrated within a unified visuomotor control framework (see Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Traditional methods for loco-manipulation separate these concerns across modules: task and motion planning or behavior trees control timing~ garrett2021tamp, colledanchise2018behavior, ciebielski2025tamp , model-based whole-body control owns precision, and manipulation is realized by hand-designed motion primitives. These systems are transparent and precise, but every skill must be engineered for a specific object and scene, and contact-rich skills remain brittle. Learning-based methods offer a more generalizable alternative: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, intelligence2025pi05, bjorck2025groot, ding2025humanoidvla, xue2025leverb and learned whole-body controllers~ fu2024humanplus, ben2025homie, li2025amo acquire transferable manipulation skills and locomotion behaviors from data, reducing the need for task- or object-specific programming. However, learning and executing the entire long-horizon loco-manipulation task with a single policy introduces difficulties in maintaining task progress, coordinating reference frames, and handling highly imbalanced demonstrations. Without an explicit representation of task progress, visually similar observations from different stages can lead to incorrect skill execution~ ma2026furniturevla . Moreover, actions represented relative to the moving pelvis frame make precise manipulation difficult, since the action reference changes as the humanoid moves. Long-horizon demonstrations are also highly imbalanced: walking and low-motion segments dominate the trajectory, which can bias imitation learning toward conservative or near-static actions (e.g., standing still). Thus, these challenges remain major obstacles to reliable end-to-end long-horizon loco-manipulation, despite rapid progress in humanoid whole-body control~ cheng2024exbody, ben2025homie, li2025amo and VLAs. To this end, we aim to establish a physically grounded framework bridging robot foundation models (i.e., VLAs) and structured robot planning and control. Our insight is that the aspects a flat VLA handles least reliably, deciding when and where to act, can often be resolved directly from physical quantities, whereas learning how to execute a skill is precisely where VLAs are most effective. PGX therefore uses physical structure to determine task progress, skill initiation, and spatial grounding, while leaving the execution of transferable manipulation skills to the VLA. By decoupling timing and world-frame precision from the learned policy, we hypothesize that the same foundation-model backbone can execute long-horizon loco-manipulation more reliably. Building on this insight, we introduce (Physically Grounded eXecution), a training-free execution framework that separates deciding when and where to act from learning how to act. Rather than modifying the VLA, introducing a learned planner to infer sub-tasks from images~ huang2022innermonologue, shi2025hirobot, yuan2025being0 , or folding temporal structure into the policy itself~ fan2025longvla, shi2025memoryvla , PGX assigns task progression and spatial precision to physically grounded components while preserving the VLA as the manipulation skill executor. Specifically, PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers. 1) Timing: a predicate-gated finite state machine (FSM) maintains task progress and memory, representing each stage as a tuple of instruction, executor, guard predicate, timeout, and retry policy. 2) Skills: the VLA operates only within manipulation stages, while the execution layer re-establishes the starting conditions under which each skill was trained; failed guards trigger retries, and reverse transitions recover from prematurely entered stages. 3) Precision: world-coordinate locking (WCL) computes navigation goals from the current object pose, holds the base at its manipulation-entry position, and anchors precise contact targets in the world frame. In this way, physical structure governs task progression and spatial precision, allowing the VLA to focus on transferable manipulation dynamics. We evaluate in Isaac Lab Arena on three tasks (box transport, mug placement, and coffee fetching) and in a real-world coffee task using a Unitree G1 Humanoid Robot. We fine-tuned the state-of-the-art foundational VLA models and GR00T N1.6 on collected human demonstrations. On coffee fetching, improves the task success rate of a fine-tuned VLA from 35 to 80 with unchanged weights, and improves stage progression and success on all three tasks for both backbones. The real humanoid G1 experiment further demonstrates the effectiveness of the execution structure. In summary, the main contributions of our work are: We propose , a physically grounded execution framework that incorporates VLA models with a predicate-gated state machine and a world-coordinate locking layer, improving long-horizon capability. We develop predicate-gated stage sequencing with retry and reverse transitions, together with WCL components, and show that the decoupled layers supply structured robot behaviors and generalize across VLA backbones. We evaluate the effectiveness of on three simulated loco-manipulation tasks and on a real humanoid, where it turns near-failing flat policies into reliable long-horizon execution. Related Work Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Recent progress on humanoids builds on learned whole-body controllers that track retargeted human motion or teleoperation commands~ cheng2024exbody, he2024omnih2o, fu2024humanplus, ze2025twist, sleiman2026zest, luo2025sonic , with decoupled upper-body and locomotion interfaces that expose velocity and joint targets to a higher-level policy~ ben2025homie, li2025amo . On top of such controllers, generalist VLAs~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, intelligence2025pi05, bjorck2025groot, nvidia2025groot16 and humanoid-specific policies~ ding2025humanoidvla, xue2025leverb, hu2026openhlm learn manipulation and locomotion from demonstrations, while data-generation pipelines synthesize demonstrations in simulation through whole-body planning or procedural motion generation~ mandlekar2023mimicgen, lin2026humanoidmimicgen, kim2026legs . These works primarily improve the controller, the data, or the skill policy. Alternatively, our work takes a tuned VLA and a whole-body control stack as given and studies how to organize their skills into a long loco-manipulation task. Long-Horizon Manipulation with VLAs Many recent works tackle long-horizon tasks by decomposing them into sub-tasks, with the active sub-task inferred by an LLM or VLM planner~ ahn2022saycan, huang2022innermonologue, liang2023code, shi2025hirobot , by the VLA itself through embodied reasoning~ zawalski2024ecot, intelligence2025pi05 , or by a learned success or failure detector~ du2023successvqa . A second line strengthens the temporal representation inside the policy, through phase-aware input masking~ fan2025longvla , explicit memory~ shi2025memoryvla , or action chunking and flow-based decoders~ chi2023diffusionpolicy, black2024pi0 . A third line chains separately learned skills, regularizing terminal states so that one skill starts where the previous one ends~ lee2021skillchaining, agia2023stap, zhang2023boss, cheng2023league, ma2026furniturevla . These methods leave task progress, the switching decision, and the initial condition of each skill to a network or a semantic model, whereas chooses to keep task progress in an external state machine and switch skills on physical events rather than inferred semantics. Structured Robotic Execution and Hybrid Control Combining task structure with continuous control has been studied for years, and recent work replaces parts of this pipeline with learned or language-based components. Language models now generate the task structure as programs or plans and delegate execution to a library of learned skills~ liang2023code, ahn2022saycan, lu2025kitchenvla . ~ yuan2025being0 tracks progress from images with a foundation model and adjusts the stance with a VLM before manipulation, while our approach gates stages on physical predicates rather than image-based inference. Hybrid planners chain learned skills under feasibility checks~ agia2023stap, cheng2023league . These build on the classical machinery of task and motion planning~ garrett2021tamp, ciebielski2025tamp and behavior trees~ colledanchise2018behavior , which make the discrete structure explicit and hand execution to model-based control. On humanoids, large learned whole-body controllers now expose one command interface to teleoperation and VLA policies alike~ luo2025sonic, sleiman2026zest . For mobile manipulators, the standing position from which a skill starts is known to dominate its success, motivating coupled base-arm imitation policies~ fu2024mobilealoha , mostly on fixed or wheeled bases that do not drift during manipulation. Our work targets a biped whose stance is less stable than these bases, and builds the interface between learned skills and the legged control stack. Physically Grounded Execution Our goal is to use a hierarchical execution structure to address the key challenges of long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation, including task progress, spatial precision, and highly imbalanced demonstrations. The overall framework of is shown in Fig.~ fig:framework . A long-horizon loco-manipulation task is executed by three layers: a predicate state machine decides which stage is active and who executes it, the VLA acts inside manipulation stages, and a world-coordinate locking (WCL) layer keeps the base, the carried object, and device targets consistent in the world frame. The three layers are a division of responsibility rather than three networks that every action must pass through. This decomposition separates stages with distinct dynamics and learning requirement

title: SenseAlign: Learning Decision-Aligned Predictive Representations for Active Urban Sensing with UAVs
summary: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.

Urban transportation Active sensing Drones Reinforcement Learning Representation Learning Introduction sec: introduction Urban transportation networks are complex systems with spatio-temporal correlations, and their management builds upon the knowledge of network states and dynamics. Traditional solutions usually rely on fixed sensor infrastructure, e.g., loop detectors and surveillance cameras, where decent coverage requires substantial investments and continuous maintenance. Considering the complex spatio-temporal evolution of congestion and the inherent stochasticity of urban traffic system, sparse fixed sensors cannot always provide a reliable monitoring under the varying conditions. As a result, urban traffic sensing with aerial sensors has been gaining increasing attention in recent years barmpounakis2020pneuma,fonod2025advanced . Drone monitoring can better capture the onset of a traffic breakdown, queue dissipation and propagation of stop-and-go waves. They provide a more complete description and more precise measurements of traffic dynamics, particularly for the locations without loop detectors xiong2025multi . These observations are particularly valuable for microscopic traffic modeling, as the detailed trajectories reveal multi-agent interactions such as merging, lane changes, intersection queues, bus stops and turning maneuvers kim2026lane . Those high-quality vehicle trajectory data have supported many studies in microscopic traffic, including parameter extraction zhou2026itsm, sica2026setting , trajectory prediction mohebbi2025vehicle and traffic flow estimation song2026high . Meanwhile, trajectory data can also enable the research in consistent macro-micro traffic flow modeling wang2024integrated and analyzing the capacity drop in the infrastructure han2026capacity . On broader aspects, drone-based observations have created wider social-economic values in emission analysis pascual2026drone and sustainability barmpounakis2025new . Although aerial platforms have promising potential in urban sensing, full spatial coverage is hardly possible under realistic resource constraints. Therefore, the drone fleet must optimize the movements to actively inspect the most valuable areas according to the monitoring requirements. In this work, we study the problem of active urban sensing, where a swarm of drones moves over a city to monitor network conditions as they evolve. We consider two types of sensing tasks that are essential for understanding the system dynamics: detecting congestion-change events and estimating the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) geroliminis2008existence . The former aims to observe roads as congestion emerges or dissipates, while the latter requires measurements that represent the aggregate flow and density of the road network. Both tasks require the fleet to coordinate its movements based on partial observations and uncertain states, since traffic conditions in unobserved areas remain unknown and previously collected measurements become outdated. Thus, effective sensing depends on understanding how the network evolves and how this evolution changes the value of visiting different locations. The problem of modeling traffic evolution has long been a central topic in spatio-temporal forecasting, with graph-based methods learning dependencies across connected roads and successive observations li2018dcrnn . For active sensing, such predictive knowledge can help the fleet anticipate traffic conditions at the locations it will reach after moving. We therefore introduce traffic prediction as an auxiliary task for a reinforcement learning (RL) agent, teaching the model to understand traffic dynamics from partial observations. Since the ultimate goal is to allocate the drone fleet, prediction accuracy does not strictly translate to the value in decision-making. For example, a small error near a congestion transition can change which road should be visited, while a larger error at another location may have little influence. Therefore, an ideal predictor should provide decision-friendly forecasts, following the principle of Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) elmachtoub2022smart . Based on these observations, we propose SenseAlign, an RL-based framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for drone-based active urban sensing. A privileged teacher is first trained with access to future ground-truth (GT) traffic, giving it great advantage on the monitoring task chen2020cheating . We then train a student model to make decisions while having no privileged information. In addition to the standard RL training with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) schulman2017ppo , the student is augmented with three tasks for representation learning: Future traffic prediction, for understanding the dynamics and propagation of network traffic Knowledge distillation, for imitating the behavior of a privileged model while having only partial information SPO-inspired decision alignment, for preserving the traffic information most relevant to choosing the observations These objectives jointly shape the shared latent space, and allow the learned model to make better monitoring decisions. Experiments on a large-scale urban road network show that SenseAlign outperforms PPO and the other evaluated baselines on congestion-change monitoring and MFD estimation. Ablation studies have further verified the contribution of each module, showing the necessity of learning decision-aligned representations. Related work sec: related work Drone-based monitoring subsec: drone-based monitoring Drones are favorably utilized in inspection and monitoring across wide application domains. For landslide inspection, routing models maximize collected geological information while requiring visits to high-priority sites fang2023landslides . shen2020shipemissions adapt drone routes to changing vessel locations for air pollution surveillance, and~ liu2026seamonitoring schedule flights to continuously cover a sea area. Other applications include infrastructure inspection yang2025det , agriculture tang2025orchard, velusamy2021unmanned , maritime monitoring he2026maritime and wildfire monitoring merino2012fire . Specifically in the transportation domain, drone swarms have been adapted in smart cities for traffic monitoring khan2020smart . With the support of computer vision fonod2025advanced , that footage is particularly valuable for analysis of emissions espadaler2023traffic , travel behavior zhu2024real and road safety outay2020applications . With limited flight resources, drone-based traffic monitoring requires decisions about both spatial coverage and observation value. christodoulou2020tour plan tours that cover a prescribed road network with as few drones as possible under flight-time constraints. For traffic-responsive navigation, huang2021decentralized direct drones to gather around detected road blockages, while yahia2022estimation guide a drone toward observations that reduce uncertainty in traffic and incident estimates on a freeway. For network-level monitoring, wang2022rushhours optimize peak-hour monitoring routes using time-varying road profits, theocharides2024real aims to estimate per-region MFD with drones, and chow2016dynamic formulates repeated visits as information refreshes in a stochastic arc-inventory routing problem. Learning-based controllers prioritize event-arrival uncertainty under partial observability khamidehi2021traffic or combine changing traffic importance with observation age maljkovic2025monitoring . Since drones have become an important factor in urban logistic infrastructure tan2026uav , drone monitoring is often considered with other urban applications. bai2026TITS and xu2023gv propose to leverage the observations from existing ground vehicles to have better monitoring quality. lyu2026multiservice jointly optimize drone routes for urban monitoring, data collection, and parcel delivery. xu2026knowledge consider both monitoring and parcel delivery drones with rolling-horizon planning, and a follow-up work coordinates local detours to collect road information whose value grows over time zhu2026detour . Despite this progress, existing works either optimize geometric coverage without traffic dynamics, assume the system states are fully known, study traffic-responsive actions on limited road structures, or define monitoring utility according to predefined priorities and known information-growth models. However, a large-scale urban network can hardly be fully observed, and the predefined scores are not directly connected with the underlying network traffic. Therefore, we study the monitoring problem under dynamic traffic and partial observability, and define the monitoring utility using the evolving traffic states. Multi-agent planning subsec: multi-agent planning In general, coordinating a drone fleet to monitor an evolving road network is a multi-agent planning problem, whose central challenge is to define the value of obtained information and plan actions accordingly. Informative path planning (IPP) aims to plan trajectories for multiple robots to maximize collective information gain in an unknown environment while respecting resource constraints popovic2024informative . Some earlier works have derived their objectives using information theory, such as mutual information, for environment sensing with single or multiple robots singh2009informative, hitz2014focused . title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs)~ fastwam,fasterwam,openwam,lingbotva couple a video generator with an action decoder. Unlike a vision-language-action model (VLA), which maps observations to actions directly, a WAM is trained to predict how the scene evolves, and most WAMs also imagine the next few frames at test time and condition the action chunk on that imagination through attention. The imagined future is often argued to make policies more grounded, and it brings an apparent safety benefit: a human or an automated runtime monitor can inspect it before each chunk is executed and reject the chunk if the future looks wrong~ trustedimagination,badwam . Two existing attacks study how the imagined future relates to the executed action. BadWAM~ badwam gives a first indication that a WAM can ``dream right but act wrong'': small perturbations make the task fail while the predicted future stays close to the clean prediction. Attacking the Trusted Imagination~ trustedimagination shows that the reverse also holds: perturbations corrupt the imagined future while the action of the model barely changes. Both attacks optimize a new perturbation for every input, and neither can choose what the WAM does. It therefore remains open whether one perturbation can steer a WAM while its imagined future looks clean, and what role the imagined future plays in carrying such an attack to the action. We study a different threat: one fixed perturbation per model that steers the executed action. A single -bounded ( ) image perturbation, shared across every frame, task and camera, pushes the end effector of the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. It is trained in a white-box setting and needs no further optimization at deployment. Like BadWAM, the attack has a variant that also keeps the predicted future close to clean. Unlike BadWAM, this variant is universal and targeted. Because the attack has a target, its effect is a signed quantity, and every intervention inside the model has a quantitative outcome: the fraction of the targeted effect it removes or reproduces. We use this to trace the attack at three levels: the tokens whose keys and values the action expert reads, the FFN neurons of the video expert, and the directions of the residual stream. We call the attack together with this trace SteerTrace. We attack eight WAMs from four families on LIBERO~ libero and RoboTwin~ robotwin2 : FastWAM~ fastwam and its joint variant FastWAM-Joint, Faster-WAM~ fasterwam , OpenWAM in four variants that differ only in the attention mask~ openwam , and the autoregressive LingBot-VA~ lingbotva . A universal perturbation that steers the executed action. To our knowledge, this is the first universal perturbation that moves the executed action of a WAM toward an attacker-chosen target. It drives task success close to zero across the eight WAMs we evaluate ( ). The imagined future is the attack's preferred pathway. In all five models whose action expert attends to the imagined future, unconstrained attacks pass through it: restoring the future tokens removes -- of the targeted effect. When the predicted future is preserved near clean, the attack moves to the current frame in FastWAM-Joint, Faster-WAM and OpenWAM-MUT ( ). A small set of neurons carries the targeted effect. of the FFN neurons carry -- of the targeted effect in six models, and the set changes when the attack changes pathway ( ). Low-energy directions carry the targeted effect. Directions 2--16 of the residual shift hold only -- of its energy, yet removing them cancels -- of the targeted effect in seven models ( ). Related Work sec:related Video generation has served as a policy interface since UniPi~ du2023unipi , video pre-training improves manipulation policies~ wu2024gr1,hu2025vpp , and large video models~ bruce2024genie,agarwal2025cosmos,wan now serve as backbones of WAMs that predict future frames and actions together~ zhu2025uwm,bi2025motus,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,gigaworld2026 . These WAMs differ in how the action reads the imagined future: it attends to the imagined frames in the joint FastWAM~ fastwam and in the autoregressive LingBot-VA~ lingbotva , to a few selected future representations in Faster-WAM~ fasterwam , and not at all in the video-free FastWAM, which uses future prediction only as a training objective. OpenWAM~ openwam compares WAM designs in controlled experiments, including how the action relates to the imagined future. Our attacks span this range. Adversarial examples~ szegedy2014intriguing,goodfellow2015explaining,madry2018pgd extend to universal perturbations~ moosavi2017uap,doubletargeteduap , physical patches~ brown2017patch,eykholt2018robust and sequential decision making~ huang2017rl,gleave2020adversarial , and on vision-language-action models they cause task failure~ cheng2024manipulation,lu2026obeypatch , targeted motion~ wang2024vlaattack,huang2026trap or backdoor behavior~ zhou2025badvla . WAMs add an attack surface that these policies lack: the imagined future. BadWAM~ badwam keeps this future close to clean while making the task fail, and Attacking the Trusted Imagination~ trustedimagination corrupts it and detects such corruption with a denoiser. Both optimize a perturbation for every input. TAPDreamer~ tapdreamer and PASA-KV~ pasakv instead attack how the current observation is encoded, with patches that change the representation of a public visual encoder and the visual keys and values attended to by the action expert, respectively. A detailed comparison with these two concurrent attacks is in the Supplementary. None of these attacks steers the executed action toward a chosen target. Ours is, to our knowledge, the first targeted universal attack on WAMs, and we use it to examine what role the imagined future plays in carrying an attack to the action. Causal interventions on hidden states, including activation patching and causal tracing~ vig2020causal,meng2022rome , path patching~ wang2023ioi and automated circuit discovery~ conmy2023acdc , locate the components that drive a model output, and attribution patching approximates them to first order~ nanda2022attribution,syed2023attribution,kramar2024atp . At the level of units, FFN layers act as key--value memories~ geva2021ffn , and individual neurons carry specific knowledge~ dai2022knowledge or safety behavior~ chen2024safetyneurons . At the level of directions, behaviors such as refusal are mediated by low-dimensional subspaces of the residual stream~ arditi2024refusal,zou2023repe,turner2023activation , and features need not align with individual neurons~ elhage2022superposition . Adversarial perturbations exploit non-robust input features~ ilyas2019features . These analyses have not been used to trace a targeted effect on the action of a WAM. title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
summary: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA

Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6 on ScanRefer and 70.4 overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at . Introduction 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) links a natural-language description to its referent in 3D space chen2020scanrefer,achlioptas2020referit3d . In practical applications such as embodied intelligent navigation liu2025revisiting , human-robot collaborative interaction chen2025synergai , and augmented reality experiences arslan2025examining , intelligent systems must precisely localize and manipulate objects in complex, dynamic 3D environments based on natural language instructions provided by humans. Much of 3D-VG research has relied on supervised methods trained on large-scale annotated data wu2023eda,zhu2024scanreason,zhu2025llava . However, such methods are highly dependent on large-scale, high-quality 3D-text aligned annotated data, and the cost of annotating 3D data is 5–10 times that of 2D data dai2017scannet,wu2023self,liu2023inter,liu2025improving , which fundamentally limits the generalization performance of supervised methods in environments with open vocabularies. To overcome the bottleneck of scarce 3D annotated data, zero-shot 3D-VG has emerged as a hot research topic in recent years yang2024llm,yuan2024visual,zhang2024agent3d,xu2025vlm . These methods leverage the powerful generalization capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and visual-language models (VLMs) to achieve object grounding without the need for training on specific scenarios. TAB wang2026think formulates 3D-VG as active semantic reasoning and geometric reconstruction instead of static candidate-box matching. By directly processing raw RGB-D streams, it eliminates the reliance on preprocessed 3D point clouds. The proposed semantic-anchored geometric extension mechanism effectively addresses the issue of insufficient multi-view coverage in pure semantic tracking by projecting the 3D center of mass obtained from semantic tracking onto unobserved frames, achieving advanced performance among zero-shot methods on the ScanRefer chen2020scanrefer and Nr3D achlioptas2020referit3d benchmarks. However, although TAB has achieved remarkable progress, our in-depth analysis reveals three inherent limitations that restrict its applicability to real-world scenarios: 1. Error accumulation: TAB's anchor evidence flows from semantic temporal extension to centroid extraction and multi-view geometric extension, although the controller can retry calls or acquire a new reference. A wrong semantic association can bias the centroid and subsequent geometric retrieval. The one-way anchor transfer does not explicitly feed retrieved views back to correct that track. 2. Assumption limitations: TAB assumes that objects remain stationary within a sequence; its semantic temporal extension relies on frame-by-frame semantic consistency and does not model visual changes between the target and the camera caused by relative viewpoints. Changes in viewpoints may disrupt inter-frame semantic consistency, causing verification to fail and terminating tracking. 3. Projection vulnerability: TAB’s multi-view geometric extension relies entirely on a single 3D centroid for projection, ignoring spatial uncertainties caused by segmentation errors and object self-occlusion. Errors in the centroid can lead to inaccurate projections, especially under partial occlusion or noisy depth. In light of the above analysis, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA) framework, which upgrades zero-shot 3D-VG from a static serial paradigm to a dynamic interactive paradigm, as illustrated in Figure fig1 . Our core insight is that semantic understanding and geometric reconstruction are not a unidirectional dependency but rather a bidirectional process in which the two components mutually reinforce and correct each other. Specifically, DACA introduces a dual-anchor collaborative mechanism comprising semantic anchors and geometric anchors: semantic anchors capture the visual regions of interest (ROI) of a target and expand via VLM and optical flow, while geometric anchors model the target’s multi-view 3D spatial positions by multi-keypoint projection and voxelization. The agent can revisit acquisition with these observations, which creates a route to correct some errors propagated from the initial track. MG-STE and KA-MGE adapt existing optical-flow and geometric operators. The distinguishing hypothesis is that feeding new geometric observations back into semantic acquisition improves grounding. In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows: [leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt, itemsep=0pt] This work proposes the DACA framework, which introduces a semantic-geometric bidirectional collaborative agent in zero-shot 3D-VG, addressing the issue of unidirectional error accumulation. Motion-guided semantic temporal extension (MG-STE): Dense optical flow-driven semantic propagation is integrated with VLM to achieve continuous object grounding in 2D sequence consisting of images that cover a scene. Keypoint-aware multiview geometric extension (KA-MGE): Multi-point geometric representation is constructed with the corner points and centroid of the target’s 3D bounding box, which combined with volumetric scene modeling to achieve precise visibility determination. Zero-shot evaluation: The open-source model-based DACA outperforms existing zero-shot methods and surpasses fully supervised baselines in grounding 3D objects. Related Work 3D visual grounding. Based on the supervision setting, 3D-VG can be categorized into two major types: fully supervised and zero-shot. Fully supervised methods have been the mainstream in early research and primarily include two-stage and single-stage architectures: two-stage methods chen2022d,jain2022bottom first generate candidate regions using 3D detectors and then perform cross-modal feature matching; single-stage methods wu2023eda,qian2024multi directly fuse point cloud and text features to output the target bounding box. Although these methods achieve high grounding accuracy on closed datasets, their generalization ability is strictly limited by the coverage of the training data, making it difficult to transfer to unseen object categories and scenes. In contrast, the core objective of zero-shot 3D-VG is to overcome the bottleneck of 3D annotated data. Early zero-shot methods li2025seeground,jin2025spazer still relied on the input paradigm of pre-reconstructed 3D point clouds, simplifying the task to candidate region matching. In recent years, VLM-Grounder xu2025vlm and TAB wang2026think have pioneered the exploration of technical approaches for 3D localization directly from 2D image sequences. Among these, VLM-Grounder associates objects across different views through multi-view semantic matching; however, due to the lack of guidance from deterministic 3D geometric constraints, its performance drops sharply under extreme view changes. TAB is the first to reformulate 3D-VG as a process of active semantic reasoning and geometric reconstruction; however, it remains essentially a unidirectional, serial pipeline, suffering from inherent flaws such as unidirectional error accumulation and insufficient robustness. In contrast, our DACA framework proposed in this paper fundamentally resolves these issues through a dual-anchor collaboration mechanism. -based tool-calling agents. The rapid development of LLMs and VLMs has given rise to the paradigm of tool-calling agents. ReAct yao2023react first introduced the Reasoning Acting loop, enabling agents to interact with the environment by invoking external tools to perform complex reasoning tasks. In the visual domain, Voyager wang2023voyager and GPT-4V hurst2024gpt demonstrated the powerful capabilities of VLM agents in embodied navigation and visual reasoning. However, most VLM agents generally adopt a single serial architecture, relying on general-purpose modules to complete tasks, and lack decoupled and collaborative tools for specialized functions. In the 3D-VG task, semantic reasoning and geometric perception impose different demands on modeling capabilities, making it difficult for a single general-purpose module to effectively handle both types of tasks simultaneously. To address this, this paper introduces a dual-anchor collaboration mechanism within a single agent. By leveraging the division of labor and collaborative optimization between two specialized tools—semantic anchors and geometric anchors—we achieve superior semantic understanding and geometric localization performance compared to traditional agents. for 3d understanding. Current 3D VLMs can be broadly categorized into two types: one uses specialized 3D encoders to directly process point clouds such as PointLLM xu2024pointllm and SpatialLM mao2025spatiallm ; the other aggregates multi-view 2D image features into unified 3D spatial features such as 3D-LLM hong20233d and LLaVA-3D zhu2025llava . Although these models demonstrate powerful scene-level reasoning capabilities, they require resource-intensive cross-modal alignment training and rely on pre-reconstructed 3D inputs. Different from the aforementioned methods, the proposed DACA does not require 3D-specific pre-training. We leverage the reasoning capabilities of 2D VLMs within the agent loop and achieve precise 3D spatial understanding directly from raw RGB-D streams by combining the fundamental model with multi-view geometry and TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Function) voxelization. title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
summary: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
full_text: -1 Introduction VLN requires an embodied agent to connect movement decisions with precise movement~ cheng2024navila,qi2025vln,anderson2018r2r,ku2020rxr,krantz2020beyond,wang2025vlnpe . Representative methods adapt a general-purpose VLM through navigation-domain supervision to predict geometric goals for an action expert~ wei2025dualvln,gong2026abotn1 or generate numerical movement commands in a predefined format~ cheng2024navila . However, we observe substantial displacement of the base VLM's weights and degraded performance of general visual capability following this adaptation, as shown in Figure~ fig:dualvln_motivation . Inspired by DeepSeek-R1-Zero~ deepseekai2025r1 , which demonstrates that reasoning capabilities can emerge through RL directly from a base language model without prior SFT, we introduce , the first slow--fast navigation framework that learns navigation through environment interaction with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than adapting the brain to predict geometric goals, we introduce a semantic tool interface that connects it to a trainable flow-matching action expert~ yi2026flowpolicygradients . Through natural-language tool calls, the brain conveys movement decisions to the action expert, which translates them into continuous motion. Within this framework, we first construct reference trajectories from the brain's own movement requests, collected through online rollouts with the brain frozen. To ground these requests in executable motion, we design a privileged trajectory planner that leverages a semantic map derived from the scene mesh~ miao2025sage . The resulting reference trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision for the action expert. We then jointly optimize the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through multi-round agentic RL~ feng2026group,zheng2026pgpo . To address sparse success signals in challenging long-horizon navigation tasks, we design complementary process and outcome rewards that distinguish useful progress even when task completion fails. Beyond conventional slow--fast frameworks, our design provides two key benefits: (1) the semantic interface leverages the brain's native capabilities for flexible tool use and feedback-driven recovery~ yu2025correctnav,li2026agenticnav ; (2) Rather than specializing the model for navigation through SFT, builds upon its existing language and navigation decision-making capabilities, using RL to enhance navigation performance while largely preserving its general-purpose abilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce , the first slow--fast VLN framework that connects a VLM brain with an action expert policy through a semantic tool interface, achieving zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. We develop a two-stage training paradigm that first aligns continuous execution with the brain's semantic requests through request-grounded supervision and execution-prefix learning, then jointly optimizes the slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL. Across mainstream VLN-CE benchmarks, substantially outperforms representative SFT-based baselines trained on the same navigation episodes, with only 0.01497 VLM weight displacement while largely preserving general visual capabilities. Architecture sec:architecture Semantic Tool Calls and Contextual Queries. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:architecture , we separate movement decisions from continuous motion execution through a semantic tool-calling interface. Rather than predicting geometric goals, the VLM brain makes movement decisions via , specifying a target, its relative location, and a local plan for the action expert. The brain can also inspect the scene through or terminate navigation through , with prompts and tool schemas detailed in Appendix~ sec:navigation_system_prompt . At slow decision round , the brain policy generates a tool call from multimodal context , including the navigation instruction, RGB observations, tool history, and trajectory trace. For movement calls, denotes the natural-language arguments of . To convey the request and its navigation context to the action expert, we concatenate learnable query embeddings with the embedded context and tool call. The VLM contextualizes these queries, whose final-layer hidden states provide the action expert with semantic conditioning~ wei2025dualvln : Visual Execution at a Faster Timescale. While the brain specifies the intended movement, the action expert executes the call over multiple fast cycles. Throughout each call, the semantic condition and reference image remain fixed, while RGB observations are refreshed at each cycle~ wei2025dualvln . A frozen visual encoder and trainable fusion module combine both images into visual features . The semantic adapter projects into the visual conditioning space and adds a semantic-channel embedding, while adds a visual-channel embedding to . Concatenating the two streams forms the action expert's conditioning input: Conditioned on , the continuous-action expert integrates the flow velocities predicted by to generate an -step action sequence. After inverse normalization, each action specifies relative planar displacements and a heading change in the local frame defined by the agent's pose at the start of each cycle. At each cycle, we execute only the first steps, then refresh the observation and predict the next sequence, adapting motion while preserving the brain's intent. After each movement call, visual and trajectory feedback, including blocked motion or collisions, allows the brain to continue, inspect the scene, revise its request, or stop. Figure~ fig:action_expert_architecture details this execution path: semantic queries and visual tokens condition an -layer decoder, with an -layer flow-time MLP and flow integration steps. Appendix~ sec:visual_conditioning provides further details on the action expert's architecture and execution. Learning to Execute Semantic Requests sec:expert_adaptation Request-Grounded Anchoring. Our semantic interface also changes how action expert supervision must be constructed. Geometric-interface VLN frameworks can derive training conditions directly from scene meshes or ground-truth trajectories~ wei2025dualvln,gong2026abotn1,an2023etpnav , whereas our action expert follows natural-language requests issued online by the brain itself. Directly constructing semantic requests may not match the brain's actual request distribution, leaving the action expert exposed to out-of-distribution instructions at inference. Generating requests online along fixed trajectories also leaves the action labels independent of the requested movement. We report results for these alternatives, including CAST-inspired augmentation~ glossop2025cast and request transfer in Appendix~ sec:anchoring_alternatives . Built upon these insights, we propose a request-grounded data construction strategy that generates trajectories from the brain's actual requests. To realize this, we design a privileged semantic planner that uses a mesh-derived semantic map~ miao2025sage and training-only geometry to ground each request \(q_t\) at the agent's current state \(s_t\) into a reachable local goal \(g_t^ \), from which a reference trajectory \( _t\) is planned. The resulting execution-verified trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision for action expert adaptation. Further details of the semantic planner are provided in Appendix~ sec:semantic_teacher_details . Execution-Prefix Supervision. These request-grounded trajectories provide aligned training targets, but supervision must also match the action expert's execution criteria. For each verified trajectory , we construct -step reference action chunks across fast execution cycles, with action components per step, and pair them with the corresponding conditions . Additional details on action construction are provided in Appendix~ sec:action_target_details . Existing action-chunking methods supervise the full prediction horizon despite executing only a short prefix before replanning~ wei2025dualvln,chi2025diffusion,black2024pi_0 . Once new observations arrive, the remaining predictions are discarded, creating a mismatch between training and execution. We therefore retain full-horizon prediction while restricting flow-matching supervision to the executed -step prefix. At flow time sampled from a logit-normal distribution, we interpolate the full reference chunk with Gaussian noise , but compute the loss only over its first actions: During this stage, the VLM brain and visual encoder remain frozen, while the learnable queries and action expert parameters are optimized. Joint Slow--Fast Optimization via Agentic RL sec:credit Trajectory-Level Credit Assignment sec:credit_framework Supervised adaptation enables the action expert policy to execute individual movement requests, while successful navigation also depends on the VLM brain's ability to make movement decisions through semantic tool calls. To jointly improve movement decisions and continuous execution, we optimize the VLM brain policy and action expert policy using navigation feedback through closed-loop agentic RL~ feng2026group,zheng2026pgpo . Accurately estimating round-level advantages is challenging because task success depends on decisions and execution across multi-round interaction with the environment. We instead adopt trajectory-level credit assignment to evaluate their combined contribution to navigation success. For each navigation task, we sample independent long-horizon rollouts, with rollout comprising rounds of tool calls, corresponding action executions, and per-round environment feedback, which is used to compute the reward for each round. Using RLOO advantage estimation~ ahmadian2024back,shao2024deepseekmath , we compute the advantage by comparing its cumulative return with the mean return of the remaining rollouts: We use the same advantage to update both policies across all rounds of rollout , jointly improving semantic decisions and continuous execution for navigation success. Process and Outcome Rewards sec:round_rewards For challenging long-horizon navigation tasks, terminal success alone provides sparse supervision across the many decisions and actions made over multiple interaction rounds. We incorporate additional rewards derived from environment feedback at each interaction round. By distinguishing intermediate progress across rollouts, these rewards preserve relative learning signals even when no rollout reaches the goal, mitigating gradient degeneration when all rollouts fail: Terminal Success. We reward task success in the interaction round where it is confirmed by the environment's native success criterion: where indicates whether task success is confirmed at round of rollout . First Arrival. We reward the agent once when it first enters the goal region, which provides an outcome signal that is easier to obtain than terminal success. Let and indicate whether the goal has ever been reached before and after a call, respectively: Distance Progress. On challenging navigation tasks, both terminal success and first arrival can be difficult to achieve. We use process rewards to distinguish productive behavior even when neither outcome reward is obtained. We measure progress through a bounded proximity potential based on traversable distance to the goal region. title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Multimedia Signal Processing (MMSP 2026). Recipient of the Best Paper Award
summary:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution.
  Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models.
  Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.
full_text: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters. Gaussian Splatting, Super Resolution Gaussian splatting, super-resolution, Geometry aware super resolution Introduction sec:introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs introduced an explicit scene representation based on anisotropic Gaussian primitives and efficient -compositing rasterization, enabling real-time novel view synthesis at competitive visual quality. Subsequent work has improved its robustness, scalability, and rendering quality~ yu2023mipsplatting . A fundamental limitation persists: the projected covariance of each Gaussian determines its screen-space footprint and therefore influences the local frequency response of the rasterized representation. Although the complete alpha-composited renderer is nonlinear, larger projected footprints attenuate high-frequency image content by increasing the spatial support of individual Gaussian kernels~ yu2023mipsplatting,goodman2005fourier . Consequently, high-frequency scene content, including sharp boundaries, fine surface texture, and sub-pixel geometric structure, can be attenuated by the finite spatial support of projected Gaussian primitives~ goodman2005fourier,gonzalez2018digital . Addressing this limitation, therefore, requires either increasing the representational capacity of the underlying scene model, often at additional computational and memory cost, or exploiting residual high-frequency cues that remain implicitly encoded within the rendered observations. The most direct response to this limitation is primitive densification~ kerbl20233dgs , which introduces additional Gaussian primitives to increase local representational capacity. While effective in principle, densification scales poorly: capturing increasingly fine geometric detail typically requires substantially more primitives, resulting in higher memory consumption, storage requirements, and rendering overhead~ fan2024lightgaussian,papantonakis2024reduced3dgs,hanson2025pup3dgs . Recent 3DGS super-resolution methods~ yu2024gaussiansr,xie2024supergs,feng2024srgs,asthana2025splatsure improve reconstruction fidelity through additional scene-level optimization and the incorporation of learned super-resolution priors. Although effective, these approaches increase reconstruction complexity, optimization time, and training overhead, limiting their practicality as lightweight inference-time solutions. Alternatively, lightweight 2D super-resolution networks~ dong2016fsrcnn,shi2016espcn,sun2023safmn can enhance rendered views with relatively modest inference overhead. However, because they operate solely in image space, they lack explicit geometric constraints and may produce perceptually plausible yet geometrically unconstrained high-frequency detail~ blau2018perception,ren2025hallucination . We observe that the information required to recover high-frequency scene detail is not necessarily absent from the representation, but may instead be attenuated by the finite spatial extent of the rendering primitives, as shown in Fig.~ fig:theory_insight . Specifically, the projected covariance of each Gaussian determines the screen-space footprint of the rasterized primitive~ kerbl20233dgs,yu2023mipsplatting . Although the 3DGS rasterization process is not strictly linear, larger projected footprints act analogously to low-pass smoothing operators, attenuating fine-scale image structure while preserving coarse scene content~ goodman2005fourier,born1999principles,gonzalez2018digital . To probe this behavior, we systematically contract during rasterization, generating a hierarchy of renderings with progressively smaller Gaussian footprints. We refer to this hierarchy as a multi-aperture rendering sequence, where the term aperture denotes the effective screen-space footprint scale of the rendering primitives, drawing inspiration from the role of aperture in controlling blur scale within optical imaging systems~ goodman2005fourier . The resulting image variations are not uniformly distributed across the scene: some regions remain comparatively stable across scales, whereas others exhibit pronounced sensitivity to footprint perturbations. We interpret this per-pixel variation as a structural uncertainty field, , which localizes regions that are likely under-resolved by the native representation and can therefore benefit most from targeted enhancement. The main contributions of this work are as follows: A bandwidth-aware interpretation of Gaussian rasterization. We provide a bandwidth-oriented interpretation of Gaussian rasterization, showing how projected Gaussian covariances influence the effective frequency response of individual rasterization kernels and how covariance contraction can probe bandwidth-sensitive scene structure. A structural uncertainty field from multi-aperture rendering. We introduce a parameter-free uncertainty measure derived from cross-aperture rendering variation that localizes potentially under-resolved scene regions and provides a compact geometric prior for reconstruction. Aperture-guided super-resolution for Gaussian Splatting. We propose a lightweight architecture that progressively fuses multi-aperture observations conditioned on uncertainty, transmittance, and positional-encoded depth cues to enhance rendered 3DGS views without modifying the underlying representation. Validation across degradation and rendering scales. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360 demonstrate increasing improvements under moderate and severe representation degradation. Theoretical Foundation sec:theory Projected Gaussian footprints act as spatially varying reconstruction kernels whose frequency response influences the local frequency content of rendered images~ yu2023mipsplatting . For an isolated projected Gaussian, where and denote the projected mean and projected covariance, respectively. The covariance controls the spatial extent of the footprint and, therefore, the local image resolution. The Fourier transform of a two-dimensional Gaussian is Since the Fourier transform of a Gaussian is also Gaussian, larger projected covariances produce broader spatial footprints and stronger attenuation of high-frequency components, whereas smaller covariances increase the effective bandwidth. Consequently, projected Gaussian footprints behave as local low-pass filters that attenuate high-frequency scene detail~ gonzalez2018digital,pratt2007digital . Practical 3DGS implementations further enforce a minimum projected footprint during rasterization~ kerbl20233dgs , increasing covariance and suppressing frequencies near the Nyquist limit. Although the renderings remain sampled on the same pixel lattice, the newly exposed responses appear as cross-aperture variations that provide evidence of potentially unresolved scene content.
