title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
summary: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.
full_text: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet\\ for 3D Virtual Try-On Sarthak Batra Armin Mustafa Adrian Hilton University of Surrey, Guildford, UK\\ \ s.batra,armin.mustafa,a.hilton\ @surrey.ac.uk Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods. Introduction sec:intro Virtual try-on (VTON) lets a user see how a garment would look on their own body without a physical fitting. Beyond e-commerce, it is increasingly relevant to AR/VR avatars and telepresence, where a garment must remain plausible as the viewpoint and the body move. The task is difficult because it couples fine-grained appearance transfer (textures, logos, prints) with strict geometric and identity constraints (body shape, pose, self-occlusion, and preservation of the face, hair, and background). Most research has focused on 2D try-on, which has evolved from warping-and-compositing pipelines built on human parsing and dense correspondence~ han2018viton,choi2021vitonhd,issenhuth2020parserfree to diffusion models~ ho2020ddpm,song2021ddim,rombach2022ldm that cast try-on as conditional generation or inpainting~ zhu2023tryondiffusion,kim2024stableviton,choi2024improving,xu2024ootdiffusion,zeng2024catdm . These models produce highly realistic single images, but they have no mechanism for keeping a garment coherent across viewpoints, which is exactly what a user expects when turning around to see the side or back. Moving to 3D adds two requirements. Multi-view consistency: garment details such as patterns, seams, and prints must persist across views without flicker or drift. Geometric plausibility: the garment must drape and occlude correctly around the body, including under self-occlusions such as crossed arms or strong torso rotation. The two are tightly coupled: small inconsistencies among edited training images become persistent artifacts in the reconstructed 3D representation, and weak geometric reasoning produces distortions that are most visible in novel views. In parallel, 3D scene editing has advanced on top of differentiable representations such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussiansplatting . The dominant paradigm renders the current 3D scene, edits the renderings with a 2D diffusion model, and distills the edits back into the scene parameters~ haque2023instructnerf2nerf,zhhuang2023dreameditor,chen2023gaussianeditor,wu2024gaussctrl . Try-on is a demanding instance of this problem: the edit must be local (the garment region only), identity-preserving (face, hair, body, and background stay fixed), and faithful to a garment image rather than to a coarse text prompt, which is why image-prompted 3D editing has become an important direction~ zhhuang2024tipeditor . Recent 3DGS-based try-on methods~ chen2024gaussianvton,gsvton2024 adapt this paradigm to garments, but several of their key components are hand-designed rather than learned. (i) Cross-view consistency of the edited training set is encouraged by concatenating attention features from manually selected reference views, rather than by learning correspondences between views. (ii) During 3DGS editing, the diffusion model is conditioned on garment appearance alone and must infer surface orientation, depth ordering, and occlusion boundaries implicitly. (iii) Current-view and reference-view attention features are blended with a fixed weight that ignores camera pose, so every reference view is trusted equally regardless of how close it is to the current viewpoint~ gsvton2024 . We address these limitations with GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit 3D reasoning learned through multi-view attention with explicit geometric guidance through multi-modal conditioning. Our guiding principle is that consistency should be learned where supervision is strongest (the observed training views) and enforced where generalization is hardest (novel views). (1) Multi-view inpainting transformer. Rather than editing each training view separately and reconciling the results post hoc, we edit several views jointly. All views are tokenized into a single sequence and processed with cross-view self-attention, so that any patch can attend to every patch in every other view. Multi-view alignment thereby becomes a learnable correspondence problem: attention can discover which regions depict the same garment surface under different viewpoints. The resulting edited set is more coherent and provides a cleaner supervision signal for LoRA personalization~ hu2021lora and 3D optimization. (2) Geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet. Cross-view attention is effective for observed views, but the iterative 3DGS editing stage must also synthesize the garment from viewpoints without direct visual evidence, where the diffusion model has to decide how textures warp and where folds form. We therefore condition the editor with a multi-modal ControlNet~ zhang2023controlnet that receives, in addition to the garment image, depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state. The garment branch supplies appearance; the normal branch supplies local surface orientation, which governs shading and fold direction; and the depth branch supplies spatial ordering and occlusion boundaries. (3) Pose-adaptive persona-aware attention. Finally, we revisit how reference views are aggregated during 3DGS editing. A fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view attention implicitly assumes that every reference view is equally informative from every camera pose, which is rarely true. We instead weight reference views by camera proximity (a softmin over pose distances) and predict the overall blending ratio with a lightweight MLP conditioned on the current pose. The editor thus relies on reference evidence when the camera is close to a training viewpoint and on its generative prior when the viewpoint is genuinely novel. Together, these components form a hybrid 3D reasoning scheme: cross-view attention provides implicit 3D awareness when editing training views, and geometry-conditioned diffusion provides explicit structure during novel-view editing. On 3D-VTONBench~ gsvton2024 , GS-VTON-MVT improves multi-view consistency and geometric fidelity over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods, with the largest gains under self-occlusion and challenging poses. Contributions. In summary: We propose a multi-view inpainting transformer for constructing the edited training set in 3D try-on, replacing heuristic reference-feature concatenation with cross-view correspondence learned through joint attention. We introduce a geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet for 3DGS try-on that extends garment-image conditioning with depth and normal maps rendered from the evolving 3D representation, rather than from a fitted body model. We develop a pose-adaptive persona-aware attention that weights reference views by camera proximity and predicts the current/reference blending ratio from the camera pose. We show empirically that combining implicit (attention-based) and explicit (geometry-conditioned) reasoning yields consistent gains in perceptual quality and cross-view consistency for diffusion-based 3D try-on. Related Work sec:related_work Diffusion Models, Personalization, and Controllable Generation Denoising diffusion models~ ho2020ddpm have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image synthesis and editing; faster samplers~ song2021ddim made them practical for interactive editing, and latent diffusion~ rombach2022ldm made high-resolution synthesis affordable by denoising in a compact VAE latent space. Vision-language representations such as CLIP~ radford2021clip ground generation in text or image conditions. Personalization adapts a pretrained model to a specific subject: DreamBooth~ ruiz2023dreambooth fine-tunes the full model, while LoRA~ hu2021lora learns low-rank weight updates at a fraction of the cost. Controllable generation adds structural constraints; ControlNet~ zhang2023controlnet attaches a trainable copy of the UNet encoder that injects spatial conditions such as edges, depth, or pose through zero-initialized convolutions. Multiple geometric conditions have been fused for human generation: Champ~ zhu2024champ conditions human animation on depth, normal, and semantic maps rendered from a parametric body model, and multi-view generators such as MV-Adapter~ huang2025mvadapter condition on rendered position and normal maps. Our multi-modal ControlNet follows this line but derives depth and normals from the evolving 3DGS scene rather than from a template body or a fixed mesh. 2D Image-Based Virtual Try-On Classical 2D try-on decomposes the task into human parsing, garment warping, and compositing~ han2018viton ; high-resolution variants reduce misalignment artifacts~ choi2021vitonhd , and parser-free formulations remove the dependence on brittle segmentation~ issenhuth2020parserfree . Diffusion-based methods replace explicit warping with conditional generation, producing realistic wrinkles, shading, and fine patterns~ zhu2023tryondiffusion . Subsequent work improves garment correspondence and identity preservation~ kim2024stableviton,choi2024improving , controllability and efficiency~ xu2024ootdiffusion,zeng2024catdm , and architectural simplicity: CatVTON~ chong2025catvton conditions by simply concatenating person and garment latents, and Leffa~ zhou2025leffa regularizes attention to behave like a flow field, which sharpens fine garment details. Multi-view try-on has also emerged in 2D: MV-VTON~ wang2025mvvton uses front and back garment images to dress a person seen from different viewpoints. These models, however, still generate each image independently and provide no guarantee of cross-view coherence, which becomes the main failure mode when their outputs supervise a 3D representation. Multi-View Consistent 3D Editing NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3DGS~ kerbl2023gaussiansplatting have enabled diffusion-driven 3D editing, in which renderings are edited in 2D and the edits are distilled back into the scene, either through iterative dataset updates~ haque2023instructnerf2nerf,instructgs2gs2024,dong2024vicanerf or score distillation~ zhhuang2023dreameditor,chen2023gaussianeditor ; TIP-Editor~ zhhuang2024tipeditor additionally accepts an image prompt. Because independently edited views disagree, much recent work enforces consistency during 2D editing itself. title: PaveSplat: Resolution-Robust Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting with Residually Corrected Surface-Aligned Covariances
comment: Accepted to ACCV 2026. 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://janghunn.github.io/pavesplat/ ; code: https://github.com/janghunn/pavesplat
summary: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale (1x-8x). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.
full_text: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale ( -- ). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering. Introduction sec:intro Feed-forward Gaussian splatting reconstructs a renderable 3D scene from a few images in a single network pass. Pixel-aligned primitives are predicted from image features~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,xu2025depthsplat and rendered with a differentiable rasterizer~ kerbl3dgs . Among these methods, how each primitive's covariance is obtained spans two regimes. First, fully learned covariances --- a free quaternion and scale regressed per pixel~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat --- provide high flexibility but no explicit surface grounding. With nothing tying the scale to the local surface, the per-pixel sizes vary without control: some surfels grow into long needles that over-spread into blur, while others stay too small to fill the surface (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)). This looks adequate at the training resolution, but the uneven, surface-agnostic scales leave holes once the prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. Second, the analytic regime, SurfSplat~ he2026surfsplat derives the covariance analytically from predicted depth: surface tangents come from the unprojected point map, their cross product gives a normal, and the released SurfSplat normal-alignment step (described in that paper as a Rodrigues rotation) ties the surfel frame to that local surface. This imposes a surface-continuity prior that makes the covariance tied to the predicted local surface. The analytic regime, however, trades correctability for its prior: the covariance is a deterministic function of predicted depth. Where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed --- at depth edges, thin structures, or textureless slopes --- the surfel orientation can be misaligned; since the only trainable covariance parameters are two bounded scale multipliers, there is no learned orientation variable at a given predicted depth. The prior also leaves an in-plane misalignment: the analytic rotation is built from the normal alone, so its two in-plane axes are fixed by the normal rather than aligned with the tangent directions from which the radii are measured. This would be harmless for an isotropic disk, but the in-plane radii are anisotropic: an elongated surfel has a meaningful long axis, and nothing ties it to the surface tangents it was derived from. The ``surface-aligned'' covariance is therefore not aligned with those tangents (Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)). On a surface seen at an oblique angle the two tangents differ in length, so a surfel whose long axis falls across the short tangent over-spreads there while leaving gaps along the long one. Such surfels cover the surface loosely --- adequate at the training resolution but exposed as holes once the prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. This paper presents PaveSplat, a residually corrected surface-aligned covariance that places anisotropic surfels between the fully learned and fully analytic regimes, paving the visible surface (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Unlike the analytic baseline, our approach does not treat the analytic prior as a hard constraint; we keep it as an initialization and act on the two separable aspects of a surfel's covariance, its in-plane extent and its orientation. For shape, we keep the analytic in-plane radii and their bounded multipliers, but build the frame so its in-plane axes align with the projected surface tangents; we refer to this geometry-consistent stage as the surface-aligned prior. For orientation, we add a residual reorientation, our only newly learned covariance parameter: a per-pixel rotation residual that post-composes the analytic rotation and is initialized to identity. The first forward pass thus reproduces the analytic frame exactly, and training reorients a surfel only where rendering evidence demands (Fig.~ fig:teaser (c)), preserving the anisotropic surface support that degenerate surfels lose, so that coverage holds when the prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. Consequently, PaveSplat does not replace the surface prior with a free covariance; it opens only the missing orientation degree of freedom around an analytic operating point. We therefore measure whether the residual is used or collapses to identity: we log the residual rotation-angle distribution throughout training, report full-test per-scene statistics against a sample-matched SurfSplat under a single controlled recipe (the covariance derivation is the only variable), and instrument the geometry pipeline with diagnostics that tie the metric differences to the mechanism. Our contributions are summarized as follows: a residually corrected surface-aligned covariance for feed-forward surfel splatting that keeps the analytic extent prior and corrects only the surfel orientation with a lightweight, identity-initialized quaternion residual, placed between the fully learned and fully analytic regimes; a geometry-consistent analytic initialization of that prior --- a tangent-aligned frame with explicit degeneracy handling --- so the in-plane anisotropy acts along the surface tangents it was measured on rather than along axes fixed by the normal alone; mechanistic validation beyond image metrics: the residual does not collapse, in-plane anisotropy and coverage holes move as predicted, and PaveSplat reports the best RealEstate10K PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every render scale ( -- ), winning on most test scenes against the same-recipe analytic baseline at each scale; on zero-shot ScanNet, a ground-truth normal check (supplement) further shows lower rendered-normal error, consistent with reorienting covariance for coverage. Related work sec:related Gaussian splatting and surface-aligned primitives 3D Gaussian splatting~ kerbl3dgs represents a scene with anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them with an EWA-style differentiable rasterizer~ zwicker2001ewa . However, per-scene optimization and single-pass prediction constrain each primitive's covariance very differently. Surface-oriented variants add geometric structure to the per-scene setting: 2DGS~ huang2dgs flattens Gaussians into disks; Gaussian surfels~ dai2024surfels use surfel primitives for surface reconstruction; SuGaR~ guedon2024sugar regularizes Gaussians toward an extractable surface. These methods optimize each scene from many posed views, so the primitive support is adjusted through repeated rendering losses. In feed-forward reconstruction, the same kind of support must be predicted from a few posed images without per-scene refinement. Feed-forward sparse-view novel view synthesis Generalizable novel view synthesis predicts a renderable scene from sparse posed images, with early systems built on NeRF-style radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf,yu2021pixelnerf,chen2021mvsnerf,suhail2022gpnr,du2023attnrend,xu2024murf . However, replacing iterative per-scene fitting with a feed-forward predictor makes the primitive covariance a learned quantity inferred from limited evidence. pixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat introduced pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives to this regime; MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat uses plane-sweep cost volumes~ yao2018mvsnet,wang2026mvssurvey ; TranSplat~ zhang2025transplat and HiSplat~ tang2025hisplat refine matching and hierarchy; DepthSplat~ xu2025depthsplat connects the Gaussian head to monocular and multi-view depth cues~ yang2024depthanythingv2,xu2023unimatch ; Splatter Image~ szymanowicz2024splatter , GS-LRM~ zhang2024gslrm , and SparseSplat~ zhang2026sparsesplat change the prediction layout. In these Gaussian feed-forward methods, rotation and scale are commonly regressed as free per-pixel outputs. This gives the network capacity, but the covariance is not explicitly tied to the local surface frame. Analytic vs.\ learned covariance A Gaussian covariance defines the spatial support used to cover the predicted surface, and therefore forms a separate design axis from depth, opacity, and color. SurfSplat~ he2026surfsplat moves from free covariance regression to a feed-forward surfel representation: the local tangents and normal are computed from predicted depth, the surfel rotation and in-plane scales are derived analytically, and alpha blending is constrained to use multiple layers. However, this analytic choice also makes the covariance a deterministic function of the depth-derived frame. Where that frame is ambiguous, the representation has no learned orientation parameter analogous to the free quaternion used by pixel-aligned 3DGS predictors. Residual refinement has been used in feed-forward pipelines for positions or features~ tang2025hisplat , but covariance orientation remains less directly separated from the analytic surface prior. While existing feed-forward Gaussian methods either learn the covariance freely or derive it analytically from predicted depth, PaveSplat treats the analytic surfel covariance as an operating point. SurfSplat is the same-recipe analytic baseline in our experiments; we align the in-plane axes with the measured tangents and learn only an identity-initialized residual orientation around that frame (Sec.~ sec:method ). Given input images with camera intrinsics and camera-to-world extrinsics , a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting network predicts one pixel-aligned primitive per pixel, with center , opacity , rotation , per-axis scales , and spherical-harmonics color , rendered by a differentiable rasterizer~ kerbl3dgs . We follow the surfel (2D Gaussian) formulation~ huang2dgs,he2026surfsplat : the third scale is pinned to a small constant, so each primitive is a thin disk whose orientation is the local surface geometry. title: CryoGaussian: Heterogeneous Cryo-EM Reconstruction Made Explicit with Gaussian Splatting
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) determines macromolecular structures from noisy particle images. However, rare, transient compositional states and subtle, continuous conformational variation are difficult to resolve. We present CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to the particle images through a differentiable rasterizer rendering orthographic line integrals modulated by the contrast transfer function. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To capture the compositional and conformational variation across particle images, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. Each structural state is then reconstructed by fitting the Gaussians conditioned on its inferred latent. On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity. On experimental data, it resolves a rare compositional state of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3% of particles) with rRNA helix 68 docked in the absence of the central protuberance, and continuous conformational motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. We further optimize the rasterizer for additive cryo-EM projection, reducing training time by 12.8-28.0$\times$.
full_text: .toc mainmatter Introduction Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reconstructs three-dimensional biomolecular density at near-atomic resolution from noisy two-dimensional particle images~ cheng2015primer,yip2020atomic . Resolving compositional and conformational heterogeneity reveals molecular organization and function, as illustrated by respiratory supercomplexes and proteasome states~ zheng2024supercomplexes,dong2019proteasome . Biological interpretation requires both reliable structural detail and an account of the compositional and conformational states of the imaged biomolecules. Each particle image is a noisy projection of an unknown density modulated by the contrast transfer function (CTF), and the structural state underlying each particle image is also unknown. Signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) as low as 0.01 obscure fine features~ bendory2020single , while overfitting can introduce misleading density~ scheres2012overfitting . Discrete classification can miss rare, transient states or average over continuous variation~ rabuckgibbons2022mining,punjani20233dflex . Density-preserving deformation models including 3DFlex capture motion but are ill-suited to compositional changes~ punjani20233dflex . Other continuous representations accommodate compositional and conformational heterogeneity~ zhong2021cryodrgn,gilles2025recovar,luo2023opusdsd , yet resolving heterogeneity alone does not ensure faithful per-state reconstruction: even with identical latents, reconstruction procedures recover different structural detail~ gilles2025recovar . Accurate heterogeneity estimation and high-quality per-state reconstruction pose distinct challenges. Gaussian mixtures provide physically motivated representations of molecular density and structural variation~ doyle1968relativistic,peng1996robust,chen2021e2gmm , and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes explicit Gaussians computationally attractive through differentiable rasterization~ kerbl2023gaussian . Cryo-EM, however, records orthographic line integrals modulated by the CTF, so projected Gaussians add without occlusion and require a rasterizer adapted to cryo-EM image formation~ singer2020computational . CryoSplat adapts Gaussian splatting to this projection model for homogeneous , the special case of a single structural state, from randomly initialized Gaussians~ chen2026cryosplat , whereas Gaussian-based heterogeneity methods such as e2gmm, DynaMight, CryoSPIRE, and GaussianEM still require initialization from a reference map or atomic structure~ chen2021e2gmm,schwab2024dynamight,shekarforoush2025cryospire,he2025gaussianem . These limitations motivate us to employ Gaussian splatting, free of structural priors and grounded in the physics of cryo-EM image formation, to achieve both accurate heterogeneity estimation and high-quality per-state reconstruction. We introduce CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to particle images. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, without prior structural information, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To estimate compositional and conformational heterogeneity, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. To reconstruct each structural state, we fit the latent-conditioned Gaussians at its inferred latent. contributions. (i) We introduce CryoGaussian, which fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to particle images from random initialization under data-derived constraints. (ii) We model both compositional and conformational heterogeneity with latent-conditioned Gaussians and reconstruct each structural state from the inferred latents. (iii) We optimize differentiable rasterization for additive cryo-EM projection, whose linearity permits per-Gaussian gradient accumulation and projection scheduling, and distribute training, reducing end-to-end training time by 12.8--28.0 on one GPU and a further 5.1--6.5 on eight GPUs (Table~ tab:rasterizer_speedup ). (iv) On CryoBench, we demonstrate accurate heterogeneity estimation and state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity; on experimental data, we resolve a rare assembly intermediate of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3 of particles) and continuous motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. title: SpatialScout-V2: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore Real-World 3D Scenes and Localize Objects?
summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20\%. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches only 22.52\%, with just 18.36\% of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes.
full_text: Overview of SpatialScout-V2, a benchmark built from real-world scenes for 3D object localization. A VLM agent controls the camera, conducts automated reasoning, and submits the world coordinates of all spotted objects. fig:spatialscout-teaser Spatial intelligence requires agents to acquire visual evidence and integrate partial observations into coherent three-dimensional representations. We introduce SpatialScout-V2, which extends SpatialScout's active mapping task from simulation to real residential scenes through three advances: real visual observations, preservation of original scene content, and interactive exploration of recorded views. Built from 100 homes in Realsee3D, the benchmark covers 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. Given a fixed target inventory, agents autonomously select recorded viewpoints and viewing directions, integrate calibrated RGB observations, and iteratively estimate and revise object centers within a fixed interaction budget. We evaluate the localization accuracy and completeness of object-center maps using mean IoU, IoU-threshold hit rates, and target coverage. Evaluating seven frontier vision-language models (VLMs), we find that six achieve an all-target mean IoU below 20 . Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus~5.5, reaches only 22.52 , with just 18.36 of targets exceeding an IoU of 0.5. Further analysis shows that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy, while target omissions further reduce overall scores. These results highlight substantial challenges in constructing accurate and complete object-center maps through active exploration of real scenes. Introduction sec:introduction Spatial intelligence enables agents to understand the spatial layout of their surroundings and use that understanding to guide their actions. When observations are partial, this understanding must be built incrementally~ theoryofspace . Agents need to decide which regions warrant further exploration, recognize the same objects across viewpoints, and integrate local position estimates into a shared three-dimensional representation~ conceptgraphs . As evidence accumulates, this representation must also be revised. Spatial intelligence thus couples exploration and representation: the current scene understanding guides subsequent observations, which in turn update that understanding~ bajcsy1988active,naruto . Evaluating this capability requires examining both how agents acquire evidence and how they use it to construct spatial representations. Spatial question answering can test specific judgments about distance, direction, and object relations~ vsi , but correctly answering individual questions does not establish whether vision-language model (VLM) agents can complete long-horizon spatial interaction tasks. SpatialScout~ spatialscout introduced a concrete evaluation of this capability in simulation: agents autonomously explore indoor scenes and reconstruct their spatial layouts by estimating three-dimensional object positions. This task provides a foundation for evaluating active spatial construction, but agents' performance on this task with real-world observations remains to be examined. We therefore ask: can agents construct accurate and complete object-center maps from observations of real homes? SpatialScout-V2 extends SpatialScout's active spatial construction task from simulation to real residential captures. While retaining autonomous observation, evidence integration, and map revision, v2 advances the evaluation setting in three respects: Real visual observations. We replace images rendered from simulated assets with views from real captures, preserving the appearance of objects and the lighting conditions of actual homes. Preservation of original scene content. Whereas v1 hides unselected candidate objects during rendering~ spatialscout , v2 retains the original scene content in the captures, including both target and non-target objects and their occlusion relationships. Agents therefore explore and localize objects within their natural scene context. Interactive exploration of recorded views. We organize panoramic captures taken at multiple positions in real homes into an interactive environment. Guided by prior observations and the current map, agents select subsequent viewing positions from the recorded locations and adjust viewing directions to gather further evidence and refine spatial estimates. These advances combine real visual observations, autonomous evidence acquisition, and explicit spatial evaluation to assess whether agents can construct accurate and complete spatial representations. VSI-Bench~ vsi evaluates spatial reasoning over fixed video observations, while OpenEQA's active setting~ openeqa and E3VS-Bench~ e3vs allow agents to acquire evidence for question answering. SpatialScout-V2 instead evaluates the object-center map progressively constructed through interaction, jointly measuring localization accuracy and target coverage. Agents must select informative viewpoints, associate evidence across views, and continually refine position estimates amid non-target objects and occlusions, balancing map completeness and accuracy within a limited interaction budget. SpatialScout-V2 uses 100 real residential scenes from Realsee3D~ Li2025realsee3d_data,li2026argus , covering 3,171 target objects across 29 categories. The evaluation environment combines registered panoramic observations with reference geometry derived from real captures, enabling quantitative evaluation of SpatialScout's active mapping task in real scenes. Agents have access to a fixed target inventory, available camera positions, and calibrated RGB views. Each episode allows up to 120 model turns, during which agents select recorded viewpoints, adjust viewing directions, acquire images, and submit or revise three-dimensional object centers. Agents determine their own observation sequences, so each new view can inform both map updates and subsequent exploration. A triangulation tool supports geometric estimation from agent-selected point correspondences, while depth maps and reference annotations remain unavailable to the agents. We use the source dataset's multi-view 3D annotations as evaluation references and assess localization relative to object size using 3D bounding-box intersection over union (IoU). For scoring, each submitted identifier's reference-sized box is translated to the predicted center and matched one-to-one within its category. Scores over both all targets and submitted targets distinguish the effect of target omissions from the localization qualitya. Our evaluation of seven VLM agents reveals substantial limitations in spatial localization under this real-scene protocol. Among completed episodes that satisfy the scoring criteria, Claude Opus~5.5 achieves the highest all-target mean IoU at 22.52 ; only 18.36 of targets exceed an IoU of 0.5, and just 0.19 exceed 0.9. Its submitted-target mean IoU is nearly identical at 22.58 , showing that broad submission coverage can coexist with limited localization accuracy. GPT-6 Astra reaches a mean IoU of 21.65 over submitted targets but 15.50 over all targets, reflecting the additional effect of target omissions. Tool-use analysis further reveals differences in how agents allocate interactions to image acquisition and triangulation, as well as repeated operations. These findings underscore the need to evaluate agents' acquisition and integration of visual evidence together with the accuracy and completeness of their final spatial estimates. Our contributions are threefold. First, we extend SpatialScout from active mapping in simulation to interactive mapping from real residential captures, retaining autonomous exploration and map revision while incorporating real appearance, lighting, and non-target scene content into the evaluation. Second, we combine autonomous view selection from registered panoramas with source-dataset 3D annotations to quantify localization accuracy and inventory coverage across 100 homes and 3,171 target objects. Third, we evaluate seven VLM agents and analyze their localization results, coverage, and tool-use behavior, revealing persistent difficulty in constructing precise object-center maps even when submission coverage is high. Benchmark Construction sec:method sec:benchmark_construction SpatialScout-V2 evaluates active object-center mapping on the 100 test scenes of Realsee3D's real-world subset~ Li2025realsee3d_data,li2026argus . Given a target inventory and RGB observations with known camera poses and intrinsics, an agent selects among recorded camera positions and estimates the targets' three-dimensional centers. The benchmark measures both localization accuracy and coverage of the inventory. Real-World Scene Data sec:real_scene_data The real-world subset of Realsee3D contains 1,000 residential scenes, partitioned at scene level into training and test sets in a 9:1 ratio~ li2026argus . We use its 100 test scenes as a fixed evaluation catalog. Realsee captures these interiors using tripod-mounted Galois 3D LiDAR cameras. The released data provide equirectangular RGB panoramas, sparse depth maps, and camera-to-world transformations for each scan position. Metric depth is recovered using the supplied depth scale. The aligned RGB images and depth maps support the multi-view 3D object annotations described below. Object Annotations sec:object_annotations The reference boxes are produced by an automatic multi-view annotation pipeline, as depicted in Fig.~ fig:construction . We manually inspect each box from at least two viewpoints and remove inaccurate annotations. The resulting inventory contains 3,171 objects across 29 categories, as presented in Fig.~ fig:wordcloud . We use the resulting boxes as evaluation references after visual inspection. Panoramic instance segmentation. A proprietary panoramic segmentation model developed by Realsee Li2025realsee3d_data predicts semantic regions, instance masks, and confidence scores directly on the full panoramas. Low-confidence detections are removed, and masks are refined using geometric and semantic cues. Mirrors and glass can cause erroneous laser range measurements~ koch2017reflections . The annotation pipeline suppresses pixels on these surfaces. Masks crossing the panorama seam and masks that combine distinct objects are repartitioned before lifting to 3D. Lifting and association across views. Each refined mask is back-projected using the aligned metric depth and the corresponding camera-to-world pose. Bidirectional reprojection consistency associates observations of the same physical object across views. Their 3D points are fused, and outlier removal reduces depth noise and points included through segmentation errors. A gravity-aligned bounding box is fitted to each fused instance. Fragments with strongly overlapping footprints are merged, and box centers and orientations are refined using the dominant scene axes. Category-specific size priors, duplicate removal, and correction of category confusions complete the annotation. The source 3D annotation vocabulary contains 102 indoor object categories drawn from the segmentation model's 130 categories. Each annotated instance includes its category, 3D box, confidence aggregated over its 2D observations, visible-viewpoint identifiers, and floor index. These scene-level instances provide a reference for mapping the same object across multiple photographs. title: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.

Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models~ black2024pi_0,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,team2024octo,bousmalis2023robocat,brohan2023rt,vuong2023open,team2025gemini have enabled a single policy to perform a broad range of robotic manipulation tasks, highlighting their potential as general-purpose robotic control policies. However, even strong pre-trained VLAs often require substantial fine-tuning or retraining to maintain reliable performance under distribution shifts, such as new environments, unseen objects, or novel task instructions~ zhang2026retrieval , limiting their ability to rapidly adapt at deployment time. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) can adapt to new tasks at inference time through in-context learning (ICL): given only a small number of input-output demonstrations as context, an LLM can adjust its behavior without updating its model parameters~ brown2020language,dong2024survey,mao2025survey . Inspired by this paradigm, recent work such as RICL~ sridhar2025ricl introduces in-context adaptation to pre-trained VLAs. Specifically, RICL maintains a compact retrieval buffer of expert demonstrations and, at each decision step, retrieves demonstrations relevant to the current observation as additional context for the VLA policy, enabling effective adaptation to previously unseen deployment conditions without parameter updates. The effectiveness of retrieval-based in-context adaptation depends critically on which demonstrations are retrieved, since these examples determine what task-specific information is provided to the VLA at deployment. Prior work~ sridhar2025ricl,zhang2026retrieval , including RICL, relies on visual similarity between the current observation and observations in the retrieval buffer to select relevant demonstrations. Recent approaches have explored improved retrieval mechanisms~ jang2026ra,yang2026ici,liu2026robota , such as incorporating task instructions and learning embeddings that better capture behavioral relevance. However, improving retrieval quality does not necessarily guarantee successful task execution~ liu2026does . Even when the retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may still fail to translate the retrieved information into appropriate actions for its current state. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:qualitative (a), RICL retrieves behaviorally relevant demonstrations but nevertheless moves the bowl in the wrong direction, ultimately leading to task failure. This suggests the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations depends not solely on their relevance to the current task, but ultimately on whether they enable the VLA to successfully complete it. In this work, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate. As discussed above, retrieving relevant demonstrations alone is insufficient for successful task execution, as the VLA may still fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information. Therefore, R2-VLA enables the VLA to determine when it can act autonomously and when additional assistance is necessary to successfully complete the task. To this end, we augment the VLA with a learned uncertainty predictor that estimates how uncertain the VLA is about its predicted actions, given the current observation, retrieved demonstrations, and its own prior knowledge. When the predicted uncertainty is below a specified threshold, the VLA executes its own action autonomously ( ). Otherwise, it requests expert assistance ( ) to avoid potentially incorrect actions, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:qualitative (b). However, determining an appropriate uncertainty threshold is nontrivial, as the predicted uncertainty does not directly correspond to task-level success. We therefore introduce a risk-control procedure that calibrates the threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. In this way, R2-VLA directly connects the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations to their ability to support successful task completion. To summarize, our contributions are as follows: 1. We propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that learns to estimate the uncertainty of its predicted actions given retrieved demonstrations and determines when to or to satisfy a user-specified task-level failure risk requirement. 2. We theoretically establish a connection between uncertainty prediction accuracy and task-level failure risk (Theorem~ thm:risk-bound ). We further extend R2-VLA to continual adaptation by incorporating expert corrections into the retrieval buffer and theoretically establish that the prescribed task-level risk can be preserved throughout adaptation (Theorem~ thm:continual-risk-main ). 3. We conduct extensive experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites, demonstrating consistent improvements of \(9.2\)--\(11.2\) percentage points in average task success over RICL, while meeting the desired target in most settings with minimal expert assistance. We provide a more detailed discussion of related work on retrieval-augmented VLA and risk control in Appendix~ app:related-work . Risk-Controlled Retrieval-Augmented VLA Even behaviorally relevant demonstrations do not necessarily enable a retrieval-augmented VLA to complete a task successfully. We therefore propose R2-VLA, which determines when the VLA can act autonomously and when it should request expert assistance, with the goal of satisfying a user-specified task success requirement while minimizing the frequency of expert assistance. We first formulate the R2-VLA policy (Section~ sec:framework ), then describe how the uncertainty predictor is learned (Section~ sec:uncertain ) and how its threshold is calibrated using task outcomes (Section~ sec:risk-control ). Finally, we introduce continual deployment adaptation (Section~ sec:algorithm ) and present the theoretical results (Section~ sec:theory ).
